paragraphs: This paper describes Wattle, a low-power analog neural network chip intended to classify intracardiac electrograms within an implantable pacemaker or defibrillator system. It implements a three-layer perceptron with 10 input, 6 hidden, and 4 output units. The hardware uses multiplying digital-to-analog converter synapses and switched-capacitor neurons fabricated in a 1.2 μm CMOS process.

The on-chip neurons provide individually variable gain, allowing each neuron's response to be adjusted. The design also reduces energy per connection relative to previous designs. These features connect the chip's learning capabilities with the low-power requirements of its intended application, where neural classification is one component of an integrated device.

Measurements indicate that an energy cost of 10 pJ per connection is achievable within an integrated system. Wattle was successfully trained with the chip in the learning loop on four-input parity and electrogram morphology classification tasks. These results establish trainability on both a parity problem and the signal-shape classification problem relevant to the proposed application.
summary.tldr: Wattle is a trainable low-power analog neural chip designed for cardiac signal classification, with measurements indicating 10 pJ per connection.

title: WATTLE: A Trainable Gain Analogue VLSI Neural Network

abstract: The parietal cortex is thought to represent the egocentric posi(cid:173) tions of objects in particular coordinate systems. We propose an alternative approach to spatial perception of objects in the pari(cid:173) etal cortex from the perspective of sensorimotor transformations. The responses of single parietal neurons can be modeled as a gaus(cid:173) sian function of retinal position multiplied by a sigmoid function of eye position, which form a set of basis functions. We show here how these basis functions can be used to generate receptive fields in either retinotopic or head-centered coordinates by simple linear transformations. This raises the possibility that the parietal cortex does not attempt to compute the positions of objects in a partic(cid:173) ular frame of reference but instead computes a general purpose representation of the retinal location and eye position from which any transformation can be synthesized by direct projection. This representation predicts that hemineglect, a neurological syndrome produced by parietal lesions, should not be confined to egocentric coordinates, but should be observed in multiple frames of reference in single patients, a prediction supported by several experiments. 158 Alexandre Pouget, Terrence J. Sejnowski

paragraphs: The paper proposes that parietal cortex represents spatial information in a form that supports multiple sensorimotor transformations. The key ingredients are an object's retinal location and the position of the eyes. Together, these can provide information from which different coordinate descriptions are constructed, rather than requiring a single dedicated spatial frame.

The authors model a neuron's response as a Gaussian function of retinal position multiplied by a sigmoid function of eye position. A collection of these responses forms a set of basis functions. They show that simple linear transformations of this representation can generate receptive fields expressed either relative to the retina or relative to the head.

The proposal also yields a prediction about hemineglect following parietal damage. If the underlying representation serves several coordinate transformations, neglect should appear in multiple reference frames within one patient. The authors report that several experiments support this prediction. The contribution connects a mathematical representation of neuronal responses to both flexible spatial computation and an observable consequence of brain injury.
summary.tldr: A basis-function model explains how parietal activity could support multiple spatial reference frames and predicts multi-frame hemineglect.

title: Spatial Representations in the Parietal Cortex May Use Basis Functions

abstract: Scale invariance is a fundamental property of ensembles of nat(cid:173) ural images [1]. Their non Gaussian properties [15, 16] are less well understood, but they indicate the existence of a rich statis(cid:173) tical structure. In this work we present a detailed study of the marginal statistics of a variable related to the edges in the images. A numerical analysis shows that it exhibits extended self-similarity [3, 4, 5]. This is a scaling property stronger than self-similarity: all its moments can be expressed as a power of any given moment. More interesting, all the exponents can be predicted in terms of a multiplicative log-Poisson process. This is the very same model that was used very recently to predict the correct exponents of the structure functions of turbulent flows [6]. These results allow us to study the underlying multifractal singularities. In particular we find that the most singular structures are one-dimensional: the most singular manifold consists of sharp edges. Category: Visual Processing.

paragraphs: Natural images exhibit statistical regularities across scales, but their non-Gaussian structure contains more detail than scale invariance alone describes. This paper studies the marginal statistics of a variable related to image edges. The aim is to characterize how different statistical measures of that variable relate to one another.

Numerical analysis reveals extended self-similarity: each moment can be expressed as a power of another chosen moment. Moments describe different aspects of a distribution, so this finding connects an entire family of statistical measurements through scaling relationships. The authors show that the corresponding exponents can be predicted by a multiplicative log-Poisson process, a model also used for turbulent flows.

These relationships allow the authors to investigate the images' multifractal singularities, or structures with different local scaling behavior. They find that the most singular structures are one-dimensional and consist of sharp edges. The result ties a statistical description across scales to a recognizable image feature, identifying edges as the strongest singular structures in the analysis.
summary.tldr: Edge-related natural-image statistics exhibit extended self-similarity, with log-Poisson scaling that identifies sharp edges as the most singular structures.

title: Self-similarity Properties of Natural Images

abstract: The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) (9) is an objective method for quantifying facial movement in terms of component actions. This system is widely used in behavioral investigations of emotion, cognitive processes, and social interaction. The cod(cid:173) ing is presently performed by highly trained human experts. This paper explores and compares techniques for automatically recog(cid:173) nizing facial actions in sequences of images. These methods include unsupervised learning techniques for finding basis images such as principal component analysis, independent component analysis and local feature analysis, and supervised learning techniques such as Fisher's linear discriminants. These data-driven bases are com(cid:173) pared to Gabor wavelets, in which the basis images are predefined. Best performances were obtained using the Gabor wavelet repre(cid:173) sentation and the independent component representation, both of which achieved 96% accuracy for classifying 12 facial actions. The ICA representation employs 2 orders of magnitude fewer basis im(cid:173) ages than the Gabor representation and takes 90% less CPU time to compute for new images. The results provide converging support for using local basis images, high spatial frequencies, and statistical independence for classifying facial actions.

paragraphs: This paper compares image representations for automatically identifying facial actions in image sequences. The target is the Facial Action Coding System, which describes facial movement through component actions and ordinarily requires highly trained human coders. Automating those component labels could support the kinds of behavioral investigations that already use the coding system.

The comparison includes representations learned through principal component analysis, independent component analysis, local feature analysis, and Fisher's linear discriminants. It also includes Gabor wavelets, whose basis images are predefined. The central question is how these different ways of representing facial images affect recognition of the underlying facial actions.

Gabor wavelets and independent component analysis perform best in the reported comparison, each reaching 96% accuracy on 12 facial actions. The independent component representation uses roughly 100 times fewer basis images and requires 90% less CPU time to compute for new images than the Gabor representation. The findings support the usefulness of local image components, high spatial frequencies, and statistical independence for this classification task.
summary.tldr: ICA and Gabor representations both achieved 96% accuracy on 12 facial actions, with ICA requiring substantially fewer basis images and less computation.

title: Image Representations for Facial Expression Coding

abstract: We describe a class of probabilistic models that we call credibility networks. Using parse trees as internal representations of images, credibility networks are able to perform segmentation and recog(cid:173) nition simultaneously, removing the need for ad hoc segmentation heuristics. Promising results in the problem of segmenting hand(cid:173) written digits were obtained. 1

paragraphs: Recognizing an image can involve deciding both how to divide it into meaningful pieces and what those pieces represent. This paper introduces probabilistic models called credibility networks that address these two tasks together. Their internal representation of an image is a parse tree, which expresses an interpretation through a structured arrangement of parts.

Using that representation, the model can perform segmentation and recognition simultaneously. The significance is that segmentation becomes part of the probabilistic interpretation of the image. The approach therefore removes the need for ad hoc segmentation heuristics that would otherwise specify how the image should be divided.

The authors report promising results for segmenting handwritten digits. This provides evidence for the proposed approach in a concrete recognition setting, with the strength of the result described as promising rather than definitive. The broader contribution is a modeling framework in which image structure and object identity are handled together, allowing the segmentation task to be addressed within the same representation used for recognition.
summary.tldr: Credibility networks use probabilistic image parse trees to combine segmentation and recognition, with promising handwritten-digit results.

title: Learning to Parse Images

abstract: Dual estimation refers to the problem of simultaneously estimating the state of a dynamic system and the model which gives rise to the dynam(cid:173) ics. Algorithms include expectation-maximization (EM), dual Kalman filtering, and joint Kalman methods. These methods have recently been explored in the context of nonlinear modeling, where a neural network is used as the functional form of the unknown model. Typically, an ex(cid:173) tended Kalman filter (EKF) or smoother is used for the part of the al(cid:173) gorithm that estimates the clean state given the current estimated model. An EKF may also be used to estimate the weights of the network. This paper points out the flaws in using the EKF, and proposes an improve(cid:173) ment based on a new approach called the unscented transformation (UT) [3]. A substantial performance gain is achieved with the same order of computational complexity as that of the standard EKF. The approach is illustrated on several dual estimation methods.

paragraphs: Dual estimation means learning both a dynamic system's state and the model governing how that state evolves. These estimates depend on one another: estimating the clean state uses the current model, while learning the model depends on understanding the system's trajectory. The paper considers this problem in nonlinear settings where a neural network represents the unknown dynamics.

Existing approaches include expectation-maximization, dual Kalman filtering, and joint Kalman methods. An extended Kalman filter or smoother commonly estimates the state from the current model, and an extended Kalman filter can also estimate the neural network's weights. The authors identify flaws in using this filtering approach for the problem.

They propose an improvement based on the unscented transformation and illustrate it across several dual estimation methods. The abstract reports a substantial performance gain while retaining the same order of computational complexity as the standard extended Kalman filter. The practical significance is an improvement to the estimation machinery that does not require moving to a higher computational complexity class.
summary.tldr: The unscented transformation improves several dual estimation methods while preserving the computational complexity order of extended Kalman filtering.

title: Dual Estimation and the Unscented Transformation

abstract: One way to approximate inference in richly-connected graphical models is to apply the sum-product algorithm (a.k.a. probabil(cid:173) ity propagation algorithm), while ignoring the fact that the graph has cycles. The sum-product algorithm can be directly applied in Gaussian networks and in graphs for coding, but for many condi(cid:173) tional probability functions - including the sigmoid function - di(cid:173) rect application of the sum-product algorithm is not possible. We introduce "accumulator networks" that have low local complexity (but exponential global complexity) so the sum-product algorithm can be directly applied. In an accumulator network, the probability of a child given its parents is computed by accumulating the inputs from the parents in a Markov chain or more generally a tree. After giving expressions for inference and learning in accumulator net(cid:173) works, we give results on the "bars problem" and on the problem of extracting translated, overlapping faces from an image.

paragraphs: The paper addresses an obstacle to using sum-product message passing in richly connected probabilistic models. Applying this algorithm while ignoring cycles is one way to approximate inference. However, many conditional probability functions, including the sigmoid function, do not allow the algorithm to be applied directly in the form considered here.

Accumulator networks reorganize how a child variable depends on its parents. Their inputs are combined through a Markov chain, or more generally through a tree, to determine the child's probability. This gives the network low local complexity, making direct sum-product updates possible. Its overall complexity can still be exponential, so tractable local computations do not eliminate the difficulty of the global problem.

The authors derive expressions for both inference and learning in these networks. They also report results on the bars problem and on extracting translated, overlapping faces from an image. The contribution is a model structure designed to accommodate local probability propagation, together with applications illustrating its use in recovering overlapping visual components.
summary.tldr: Accumulator networks combine parent inputs through chains or trees, enabling direct sum-product updates despite potentially exponential global complexity.

title: Accumulator Networks: Suitors of Local Probability Propagation

abstract: How do cortical neurons represent the acoustic environment? This ques- tion is often addressed by probing with simple stimuli such as clicks or tone pips. Such stimuli have the advantage of yielding easily interpreted answers, but have the disadvantage that they may fail to uncover complex or higher-order neuronal response properties. Here we adopt an alternative approach, probing neuronal responses with complex acoustic stimuli, including animal vocalizations and music. We have used in vivo whole cell methods in the rat auditory cortex to record subthreshold membrane potential ﬂuctuations elicited by these stimuli. Whole cell recording reveals the total synaptic input to a neuron from all the other neurons in the circuit, instead of just its output—a sparse bi- nary spike train—as in conventional single unit physiological recordings. Whole cell recording thus provides a much richer source of information about the neuron’s response. Many neurons responded robustly and reliably to the complex stimuli in our ensemble. Here we analyze the linear component—the spectro- temporal receptive ﬁeld (STRF)—of the transformation from the sound (as represented by its time-varying spectrogram) to the neuron’s mem- brane potential. We ﬁnd that the STRF has a rich dynamical structure, including excitatory regions positioned in general accord with the predic- tion of the simple tuning curve. We also ﬁnd that in many cases, much of the neuron’s response, although deterministically related to the stimulus, cannot be predicted by the linear component, indicating the presence of as-yet-uncharacterized nonlinear response properties.

paragraphs: Simple sounds such as clicks and brief tones are easy to interpret experimentally, but they may miss complex neural response properties. This study instead probes rat auditory cortex with richer sounds, including animal vocalizations and music. It uses in vivo whole-cell recordings to measure membrane-potential fluctuations below the threshold for producing spikes.

These recordings reveal synaptic input to a neuron, providing a richer view than its sparse sequence of output spikes alone. Many neurons respond robustly and reliably to the complex stimuli. The authors analyze the linear part of the relationship between each sound's time-varying spectrogram and the recorded membrane potential through spectrotemporal receptive fields.

The receptive fields show rich temporal structure, with excitatory regions generally consistent with simple tuning-curve predictions. Yet in many cases, substantial stimulus-determined responses cannot be predicted by the linear component. This combination shows both the usefulness and the limits of the linear description: it captures meaningful response organization while leaving nonlinear properties that remain uncharacterized.
summary.tldr: Whole-cell recordings reveal reliable responses to complex sounds, with substantial nonlinear structure beyond what linear receptive fields predict.

title: Spectro-Temporal Receptive Fields of Subthreshold Responses in Auditory Cortex

abstract: A framework is introduced for assessing the encoding accuracy and the discriminational ability of a population of neurons upon simul- taneous presentation of multiple stimuli. Minimal square estima- tion errors are obtained from a Fisher information analysis in an abstract compound space comprising the features of all stimuli. Even for the simplest case of linear superposition of responses and Gaussian tuning, the symmetries in the compound space are very di(cid:11)erent from those in the case of a single stimulus. The analysis allows for a quantitative description of attentional e(cid:11)ects and can be extended to include neural nonlinearities such as nonclassical receptive (cid:12)elds.

paragraphs: The paper asks how accurately a population of neurons can represent and distinguish several stimuli presented at the same time. It introduces a framework that treats the features of all those stimuli together. The goal is to assess the information available about a combined presentation, rather than analyzing each stimulus as though it appeared alone.

The authors construct a compound space whose coordinates describe the features of every stimulus. They use Fisher information in that space to obtain minimal squared estimation errors. Even when neural responses simply add together and tuning follows a Gaussian shape, the resulting symmetries differ substantially from those for a single stimulus. Thus, simple response rules do not make the multiple-stimulus problem equivalent to separate single-stimulus problems.

The framework also permits a quantitative description of attentional effects. The authors state that it can be extended to incorporate neural nonlinearities, including nonclassical receptive fields. Its contribution is an estimation-based way to connect population responses with encoding accuracy and discrimination while explicitly retaining the structure introduced by simultaneous stimuli.
summary.tldr: A Fisher-information framework analyzes how neural populations encode multiple simultaneous stimuli and how their joint structure changes estimation accuracy.

title: An Estimation-Theoretic Framework for the Presentation of Multiple Stimuli

abstract: We present a biophysically constrained cerebellar model of classical conditioning, implemented using a neuromorphic analog VLSI (aVLSI) chip. Like its biological counterpart, our cerebellar model is able to control adaptive behavior by predicting the precise timing of events. Here we describe the functionality of the chip and present its learning performance, as evaluated in simulated conditioning experiments at the circuit level and in behavioral experiments using a mobile robot. We show that this aVLSI model supports the acquisition and extinction of adaptively timed conditioned responses under real-world conditions with ultra-low power consumption.

paragraphs: Classical conditioning involves learning responses to predictive events, and useful behavior can depend on responding at the right moment. This paper implements a biophysically constrained cerebellar model on a neuromorphic analog VLSI chip. The model controls adaptive behavior by learning to predict the precise timing of events.

The authors describe the chip's operation and evaluate its learning in two settings: circuit-level simulations of conditioning and behavioral experiments with a mobile robot. These evaluations connect the circuitry's learning behavior to its use in an acting system, where a conditioned response must be coordinated with events outside the chip.

The reported results demonstrate both acquisition and extinction of adaptively timed conditioned responses under real-world conditions, with ultra-low power consumption. Acquisition shows that the system can learn the response, while extinction shows that the learned behavior can diminish through conditioning experience. The contribution is a hardware realization of a cerebellar learning model that combines timing-sensitive adaptation with low-power operation in a physical robotic setting.
summary.tldr: A low-power analog cerebellum chip learns and extinguishes precisely timed conditioned responses in simulations and mobile-robot experiments.

title: The Cerebellum Chip: an Analog VLSI Implementation of a Cerebellar Model of Classical Conditioning

abstract: What makes a neural microcircuit computationally powerful? Or more precisely, which measurable quantities could explain why one microcircuit C is better suited for a particular family of computational tasks than another microcircuit C 0 ? We propose in this article quantitative measures for evaluating the computational power and generalization capability of a neural microcircuit, and apply them to generic neural microcircuit models drawn from different distributions. We validate the proposed measures by comparing their prediction with direct evaluations of the computational performance of these microcircuit models. This procedure is applied first to microcircuit models that differ with regard to the spatial range of synaptic connections and with regard to the scale of synaptic efficacies in the circuit, and then to microcircuit models that differ with regard to the level of background input currents and the level of noise on the membrane potential of neurons. In this case the proposed method allows us to quantify differences in the computational power and generalization capability of circuits in different dynamic regimes (UP- and DOWN-states) that have been demonstrated through intracellular recordings in vivo.

paragraphs: The paper asks what measurable properties make one neural microcircuit better suited than another to a family of computational tasks. It proposes quantitative measures of computational power and generalization capability. The purpose is to evaluate circuits through quantities that predict their usefulness, alongside directly measuring how well they perform computations.

The authors apply the measures to generic microcircuit models drawn from different distributions and validate them against direct performance evaluations. One set of comparisons changes the spatial reach of synaptic connections and the scale of synaptic strengths. Another changes background input currents and the amount of noise affecting neuronal membrane potentials.

The latter comparisons allow the method to quantify computational and generalization differences between circuits in UP and DOWN dynamic regimes. These regimes have been observed in biological recordings, while the described evaluation applies the proposed measures to circuit models. The contribution is a framework connecting circuit properties and activity conditions to task suitability, supported by comparisons between predicted and directly evaluated computational performance.
summary.tldr: Quantitative measures predict and compare neural microcircuit models' computational power and generalization across connectivity, input, and noise conditions.

title: Methods for Estimating the Computational Power and Generalization Capability of Neural Microcircuits

abstract: This paper proposes a new approach to model-based clustering under prior knowl- edge. The proposed formulation can be interpreted from two different angles: as penalized logistic regression, where the class labels are only indirectly observed (via the probability density of each class); as ﬁnite mixture learning under a group- ing prior. To estimate the parameters of the proposed model, we derive a (gener- alized) EM algorithm with a closed-form E-step, in contrast with other recent approaches to semi-supervised probabilistic clustering which require Gibbs sam- pling or suboptimal shortcuts. We show that our approach is ideally suited for image segmentation: it avoids the combinatorial nature Markov random ﬁeld pri- ors, and opens the door to more sophisticated spatial priors (e.g., wavelet-based) in a simple and computationally efﬁcient way. Finally, we extend our formulation to work in unsupervised, semi-supervised, or discriminative modes.

To estimate the parameters of the proposed model, we derive a (gener- alized) EM algorithm with a closed-form E-step, in contrast with other recent approaches to semi-supervised probabilistic clustering which require Gibbs sam- pling or suboptimal shortcuts. paragraphs: Clustering often benefits from prior knowledge about which observations should belong together. This paper develops a probabilistic formulation that incorporates such grouping information. It has two interpretations: a finite mixture model with a grouping prior, or penalized logistic regression in which labels are observed only indirectly through the probability distributions associated with the classes.

The authors derive a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm for estimating the model parameters. Its expectation step has a closed-form solution. This is a practical distinction from the recent probabilistic clustering approaches discussed in the abstract, which rely on Gibbs sampling or shortcuts described as suboptimal to carry out their inference.

Image segmentation is a central application because spatial relationships can guide the grouping of image regions. The formulation avoids the combinatorial character of Markov random field priors and permits more sophisticated spatial priors, including wavelet-based ones, in a computationally efficient way. The authors also extend the framework to unsupervised, semi-supervised, and discriminative modes, allowing related modeling machinery to serve different levels of label availability.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic clustering framework incorporates grouping knowledge with efficient inference and flexible spatial priors.

title: Clustering Under Prior Knowledge with Application to Image Segmentation

abstract: We present four new reinforcement learning algorithms based on actor-critic and natural-gradient ideas, and provide their convergence proofs. Actor-critic rein- forcement learning methods are online approximations to policy iteration in which the value-function parameters are estimated using temporal difference learning and the policy parameters are updated by stochastic gradient descent. Methods based on policy gradients in this way are of special interest because of their com- patibility with function approximation methods, which are needed to handle large or in(cid:2)nite state spaces. The use of temporal difference learning in this way is of interest because in many applications it dramatically reduces the variance of the gradient estimates. The use of the natural gradient is of interest because it can produce better conditioned parameterizations and has been shown to further re- duce variance in some cases. Our results extend prior two-timescale convergence results for actor-critic methods by Konda and Tsitsiklis by using temporal differ- ence learning in the actor and by incorporating natural gradients, and they extend prior empirical studies of natural actor-critic methods by Peters, Vijayakumar and Schaal by providing the (cid:2)rst convergence proofs and the (cid:2)rst fully incremental algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper introduces four reinforcement-learning algorithms combining actor-critic methods with natural gradients and proves their convergence. In actor-critic learning, a critic estimates a value function through temporal-difference learning, while an actor updates the policy. This arrangement supports online approximations to policy iteration and is compatible with function approximation for large or infinite state spaces.

The motivation combines several benefits with different strengths of evidence. Temporal-difference learning can dramatically reduce gradient-estimate variance in many applications. Natural gradients can improve the conditioning of the parameterization and have reduced variance in some cases. The proposed algorithms bring these ideas together in fully incremental procedures, allowing learning to proceed through successive updates.

The theoretical results extend earlier two-timescale convergence analyses by incorporating natural gradients and using temporal-difference learning in the actor. They also add convergence proofs and fully incremental algorithms to a line of work previously supported by empirical natural actor-critic studies. The main advance is thus both a set of learning procedures and a formal foundation for their convergence.
summary.tldr: Four fully incremental natural actor-critic algorithms combine online reinforcement learning with convergence proofs.

title: Incremental Natural Actor-Critic Algorithms

abstract: Bandpass filtering, orientation selectivity, and contrast gain control are prominent features of sensory coding at the level of V1 simple cells. While the effect of bandpass filtering and orientation selectivity can be assessed within a linear model, contrast gain control is an inherently nonlinear computation. Here we employ the class of $L_p$ elliptically contoured distributions to investigate the extent to which the two features---orientation selectivity and contrast gain control---are suited to model the statistics of natural images. Within this framework we find that contrast gain control can play a significant role for the removal of redundancies in natural images. Orientation selectivity, in contrast, has only a very limited potential for redundancy reduction.

paragraphs: Simple cells in the primary visual cortex exhibit bandpass filtering, orientation selectivity, and contrast gain control. The paper asks how well orientation selectivity and contrast gain control account for statistical structure in natural images. Its focus is redundancy reduction: removing statistical dependence or repeated information in the image representation.

The distinction between the mechanisms matters mathematically. Orientation selectivity can be assessed in a linear model, while contrast gain control requires a nonlinear computation. The authors use Lp elliptically contoured distributions as a common framework for examining their suitability for modeling natural-image statistics.

Within that framework, contrast gain control can contribute substantially to redundancy removal, whereas orientation selectivity has only limited potential for that purpose. The finding assigns different explanatory weight to two prominent features of early visual processing. Its scope is the redundancy-reduction question within the chosen statistical framework; it does not imply that orientation selectivity has little value for every function of vision.
summary.tldr: Within the studied image-statistics framework, contrast gain control has substantially more redundancy-reduction potential than orientation selectivity.

title: The Conjoint Effect of Divisive Normalization and Orientation Selectivity on Redundancy Reduction

abstract: A visual attention system should respond placidly when common stimuli are presented, while at the same time keep alert to anomalous visual inputs. In this paper, a dynamic visual attention model based on the rarity of features is proposed. We introduce the Incremental Coding Length (ICL) to measure the perspective entropy gain of each feature. The objective of our model is to maximize the entropy of the sampled visual features. In order to optimize energy consumption, the limit amount of energy of the system is re-distributed amongst features according to their Incremental Coding Length. By selecting features with large coding length increments, the computational system can achieve attention selectivity in both static and dynamic scenes. We demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior accuracy in comparison to mainstream approaches in static saliency map generation. Moreover, we also show that our model captures several less-reported dynamic visual search behaviors, such as attentional swing and inhibition of return.

paragraphs: The paper models visual attention as a process that stays relatively unresponsive to common inputs while remaining sensitive to unusual ones. Its central idea is to base attention on feature rarity. The model aims to maximize the entropy of sampled visual features, connecting selective attention to the information represented in what gets sampled.

To guide selection, the authors introduce Incremental Coding Length, a measure of the entropy gain associated with each feature. The system redistributes its limited energy among features according to this measure. Selecting features with large coding-length increments produces attention selectivity in both static images and changing scenes within the same framework.

For static saliency maps, the authors report higher accuracy than mainstream approaches. They also show that the model captures dynamic search behaviors including attentional swing and inhibition of return. These findings link the information-based selection rule to both spatial saliency and changes in attention over time. The model’s contribution is a common objective for these behaviors together with an explicit allocation of limited computational energy.
summary.tldr: A rarity-based attention model allocates limited energy using coding-length increments and captures both static saliency and dynamic search behaviors.

title: Dynamic visual attention: searching for coding length increments

abstract: Humans are typically able to infer how many objects their environment contains and to recognize when the same object is encountered twice. We present a simple statistical model that helps to explain these abilities and evaluate it in three behavioral experiments. Our first experiment suggests that humans rely on prior knowledge when deciding whether an object token has been previously encountered. Our second and third experiments suggest that humans can infer how many objects they have seen and can learn about categories and their properties even when they are uncertain about which tokens are instances of the same object.

Our second and third experiments suggest that humans can infer how many objects they have seen and can learn about categories and their properties even when they are uncertain about which tokens are instances of the same object.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object again and deciding how many distinct objects have been encountered are closely related problems. A new observation might be another appearance of a familiar object or an encounter with a different one. This paper presents a simple statistical model to help explain how people make those judgments.

The authors evaluate the model in three behavioral experiments. The first suggests that prior knowledge influences whether people judge an observed object token to have been encountered before. Here, the important distinction is between an individual observation and the underlying object that may account for several observations.

The second and third experiments suggest that people can estimate how many objects they have seen and learn categories and their properties despite uncertainty about object identity. This means that category learning and object counting can proceed even while some observations remain ambiguously matched. The findings support a statistical account in which uncertainty about repeated encounters coexists with broader learning about the objects in an environment.
summary.tldr: A statistical model and three behavioral experiments examine how people recognize repeated objects and learn despite uncertainty about identity.

title: Individuation, Identification and Object Discovery

abstract: Learning linear combinations of multiple kernels is an appealing strategy when the right choice of features is unknown. Previous approaches to multiple kernel learning (MKL) promote sparse kernel combinations and hence support interpretability. Unfortunately, L1-norm MKL is hardly observed to outperform trivial baselines in practical applications. To allow for robust kernel mixtures, we generalize MKL to arbitrary Lp-norms. We devise new insights on the connection between several existing MKL formulations and develop two efficient interleaved optimization strategies for arbitrary p>1. Empirically, we demonstrate that the interleaved optimization strategies are much faster compared to the traditionally used wrapper approaches. Finally, we apply Lp-norm MKL to real-world problems from computational biology, showing that non-sparse MKL achieves accuracies that go beyond the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines several kernels when the most suitable feature representation is unclear. Earlier approaches encourage sparse combinations, which make the selected kernels easier to interpret. The paper points out that L1-based multiple kernel learning has rarely surpassed simple baselines in practical applications, motivating a broader family of ways to combine kernels.

The authors generalize the formulation to arbitrary Lp norms, allowing mixtures that need not be sparse. They also clarify connections among existing formulations and develop two interleaved optimization strategies for p greater than one. These strategies address the computational side of learning a kernel mixture, making the broader formulation practical to optimize.

Experiments show that the interleaved strategies are much faster than the wrapper approaches traditionally used for this task. On real computational biology problems, the authors report that non-sparse mixtures exceed the state-of-the-art accuracy. These findings support retaining contributions from multiple kernels in the evaluated settings and show that the choice of sparsity preference and optimization strategy both matter for practical multiple kernel learning.
summary.tldr: Lp-norm multiple kernel learning enables non-sparse mixtures, with faster reported optimization and improved accuracy on computational biology tasks.

title: Efficient and Accurate Lp-Norm Multiple Kernel Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of cardinality penalized optimization of a convex function over the probability simplex with additional convex constraints. It's well-known that the classical L1 regularizer fails to promote sparsity on the probability simplex since L1 norm on the probability simplex is trivially constant. We propose a direct relaxation of the minimum cardinality problem and show that it can be efficiently solved using convex programming. As a first application we consider recovering a sparse probability measure given moment constraints, in which our formulation becomes linear programming, hence can be solved very efficiently. A sufficient condition for exact recovery of the minimum cardinality solution is derived for arbitrary affine constraints. We then develop a penalized version for the noisy setting which can be solved using second order cone programs. The proposed method outperforms known heuristics based on L1 norm. As a second application we consider convex clustering using a sparse Gaussian mixture and compare our results with the well known soft k-means algorithm.

As a first application we consider recovering a sparse probability measure given moment constraints, in which our formulation becomes linear programming, hence can be solved very efficiently. paragraphs: The paper seeks sparse solutions among probability vectors, potentially subject to additional convex constraints. Sparsity means placing positive probability on relatively few entries. The usual L1 penalty cannot encourage this on the probability simplex because every feasible vector has the same L1 norm: its nonnegative entries already sum to one.

The authors instead relax the minimum-cardinality problem directly into a convex optimization problem. For recovering a sparse probability measure from moment constraints, the formulation becomes a linear program. They also derive a sufficient condition for exact recovery of a minimum-cardinality solution under arbitrary affine constraints. That condition establishes when exact recovery is guaranteed without claiming it is necessary.

For noisy observations, the paper introduces a penalized formulation solvable through second-order cone programming. The proposed method outperforms the discussed L1-based heuristics. A second application uses sparse Gaussian mixtures for convex clustering and compares results with soft k-means. Together, these applications show how the formulation addresses sparsity when ordinary L1 regularization is uninformative.
summary.tldr: A convex relaxation promotes sparse probability measures where L1 regularization is constant, with a sufficient condition for exact recovery.

title: Recovery of Sparse Probability Measures via Convex Programming

abstract: Monte-Carlo tree search is drawing great interest in the domain of planning under uncertainty, particularly when little or no domain knowledge is available. One of the central problems is the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. In this paper we present a novel Bayesian mixture modelling and inference based Thompson sampling approach to addressing this dilemma. The proposed Dirichlet-NormalGamma MCTS (DNG-MCTS) algorithm represents the uncertainty of the accumulated reward for actions in the MCTS search tree as a mixture of Normal distributions and inferences on it in Bayesian settings by choosing conjugate priors in the form of combinations of Dirichlet and NormalGamma distributions. Thompson sampling is used to select the best action at each decision node. Experimental results show that our proposed algorithm has achieved the state-of-the-art comparing with popular UCT algorithm in the context of online planning for general Markov decision processes.

paragraphs: Monte-Carlo tree search supports planning under uncertainty, including situations with little domain knowledge. A central challenge is deciding how much effort to spend investigating uncertain actions versus pursuing actions that already look promising. This paper introduces a Bayesian approach to that exploration and exploitation trade-off.

The proposed DNG-MCTS algorithm represents uncertainty about an action's accumulated reward using a mixture of Normal distributions. Bayesian inference uses conjugate priors combining Dirichlet and NormalGamma distributions. This construction gives the algorithm a structured representation of reward uncertainty, which is then used by Thompson sampling to select actions at decision nodes in the search tree.

The authors evaluate the algorithm for online planning in general Markov decision processes and report state-of-the-art performance in comparisons with the popular UCT algorithm. The result supports using richer reward-uncertainty models to guide search. Its reported advantage is empirical: the abstract establishes the approach through the planning experiments rather than asserting that it always selects better actions.
summary.tldr: DNG-MCTS combines Bayesian reward mixtures with Thompson sampling to guide exploration and exploitation in tree search.

title: Bayesian Mixture Modelling and Inference based Thompson Sampling in Monte-Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), posit that documents are drawn from admixtures of distributions over words, known as topics. The inference problem of recovering topics from such a collection of documents drawn from admixtures, is NP-hard. Making a strong assumption called separability, [4] gave the first provable algorithm for inference. For the widely used LDA model, [6] gave a provable algorithm using clever tensor-methods. But [4, 6] do not learn topic vectors with bounded $l_1$ error (a natural measure for probability vectors). Our aim is to develop a model which makes intuitive and empirically supported assumptions and to design an algorithm with natural, simple components such as SVD, which provably solves the inference problem for the model with bounded $l_1$ error. A topic in LDA and other models is essentially characterized by a group of co-occurring words. Motivated by this, we introduce topic specific Catchwords, a group of words which occur with strictly greater frequency in a topic than any other topic individually and are required to have high frequency together rather than individually. A major contribution of the paper is to show that under this more realistic assumption, which is empirically verified on real corpora, a singular value decomposition (SVD) based algorithm with a crucial pre-processing step of thresholding, can provably recover the topics from a collection of documents drawn from Dominant admixtures. Dominant admixtures are convex combination of distributions in which one distribution has a significantly higher contribution than the others. Apart from the simplicity of the algorithm, the sample complexity has near optimal dependence on $w_0$, the lowest probability that a topic is dominant, and is better than [4]. Empirical evidence shows that on several real world corpora, both Catchwords and Dominant admixture assumptions hold and the proposed algorithm substantially outperforms the state of the art [5].

paragraphs: Topic models describe documents as mixtures of topics, with each topic represented by a distribution over words. Recovering those distributions is computationally difficult in general. This paper develops an approach based on singular value decomposition, or SVD, that provides a recovery guarantee under assumptions about topic vocabulary and the mixtures appearing in documents.

The vocabulary assumption uses groups of topic-specific catchwords. These words occur more frequently in their associated topic than in any other individual topic, and their combined frequency matters more than each word being common alone. The document assumption requires dominant admixtures: one topic contributes substantially more than the others. A crucial thresholding step prepares the data before SVD.

Under these assumptions, the algorithm recovers topics with bounded total absolute error in their word probabilities. Its sample requirement has nearly optimal dependence on how rarely a topic is dominant. Evidence from several real corpora supports the assumptions, and the reported experiments substantially outperform the compared state of the art. The guarantee is therefore tied to a specified corpus structure, while the experiments support its practical relevance.
summary.tldr: An SVD-based topic learner provides bounded-error recovery when documents have dominant topics and topic-specific groups of catchwords.

title: A provable SVD-based algorithm for learning topics in dominant admixture corpus

abstract: We introduce principal differences analysis for analyzing differences between high-dimensional distributions. The method operates by finding the projection that maximizes the Wasserstein divergence between the resulting univariate populations. Relying on the Cramer-Wold device, it requires no assumptions about the form of the underlying distributions, nor the nature of their inter-class differences. A sparse variant of the method is introduced to identify features responsible for the differences. We provide algorithms for both the original minimax formulation as well as its semidefinite relaxation. In addition to deriving some convergence results, we illustrate how the approach may be applied to identify differences between cell populations in the somatosensory cortex and hippocampus as manifested by single cell RNA-seq. Our broader framework extends beyond the specific choice of Wasserstein divergence.

The method operates by finding the projection that maximizes the Wasserstein divergence between the resulting univariate populations. Relying on the Cramer-Wold device, it requires no assumptions about the form of the underlying distributions, nor the nature of their inter-class differences. A sparse variant of the method is introduced to identify features responsible for the differences. We provide algorithms for both the original minimax formulation as well as its semidefinite relaxation. In addition to deriving some convergence results, we illustrate how the approach may be applied to identify differences between cell populations in the somatosensory cortex and hippocampus as manifested by single cell RNA-seq. paragraphs: Principal differences analysis seeks an interpretable description of how two high-dimensional distributions differ. It searches for a projection that makes their resulting one-dimensional populations as different as possible, measured using Wasserstein divergence. The output therefore identifies a direction along which the distributions’ differences become especially visible.

The framework relies on the Cramér–Wold device and does not require assumptions about the distributions’ forms or the nature of their differences. A sparse version identifies features responsible for the separation, making the projection easier to interpret. The authors provide algorithms for the original minimax problem and a semidefinite relaxation, along with some convergence results.

An application uses single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize differences between cell populations in the somatosensory cortex and hippocampus. This illustrates how the method can connect distributional comparison with feature-level interpretation in complex data. The broader framework also permits choices beyond Wasserstein divergence, so its organizing idea is the search for informative projected differences rather than dependence on only one comparison measure.
summary.tldr: Principal differences analysis finds projections that expose distributional differences, with a sparse variant highlighting the features involved.

title: Principal Differences Analysis: Interpretable Characterization of Differences between Distributions

abstract: We propose and study a new model for reinforcement learning with rich observations, generalizing contextual bandits to sequential decision making. These models require an agent to take actions based on observations (features) with the goal of achieving long-term performance competitive with a large set of policies. To avoid barriers to sample-efficient learning associated with large observation spaces and general POMDPs, we focus on problems that can be summarized by a small number of hidden states and have long-term rewards that are predictable by a reactive function class. In this setting, we design and analyze a new reinforcement learning algorithm, Least Squares Value Elimination by Exploration. We prove that the algorithm learns near optimal behavior after a number of episodes that is polynomial in all relevant parameters, logarithmic in the number of policies, and independent of the size of the observation space. Our result provides theoretical justification for reinforcement learning with function approximation.

In this setting, we design and analyze a new reinforcement learning algorithm, Least Squares Value Elimination by Exploration. We prove that the algorithm learns near optimal behavior after a number of episodes that is polynomial in all relevant parameters, logarithmic in the number of policies, and independent of the size of the observation space. Our result provides theoretical justification for reinforcement learning with function approximation.

paragraphs: An agent may receive complicated observations while the underlying decision problem has a much smaller structure. This paper formalizes a reinforcement-learning setting that extends contextual bandits to sequential decisions. The objective is long-term performance competitive with a large collection of policies, despite the potentially enormous observation space.

The analysis focuses on problems summarized by a small number of hidden states, with long-term rewards predictable using a reactive function class. These assumptions provide the structure needed to avoid sample-efficiency barriers associated with unrestricted partially observed problems. Within this setting, the authors introduce Least Squares Value Elimination by Exploration.

They prove that the algorithm learns near-optimal behavior using a number of episodes polynomial in the relevant parameters, logarithmic in the policy count, and independent of observation-space size. The result separates the complexity of what the agent observes from the amount of experience needed to learn. Under the stated structural assumptions, it provides theoretical support for using function approximation in reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Under hidden-state and reward-predictability assumptions, a reinforcement-learning algorithm learns near-optimal behavior with episode complexity independent of observation-space size.

title: PAC Reinforcement Learning with Rich Observations

abstract: Many online communities present user-contributed responses, such as reviews of products and answers to questions. User-provided helpfulness votes can highlight the most useful responses, but voting is a social process that can gain momentum based on the popularity of responses and the polarity of existing votes. We propose the Chinese Voting Process (CVP) which models the evolution of helpfulness votes as a self-reinforcing process dependent on position and presentation biases. We evaluate this model on Amazon product reviews and more than 80 StackExchange forums, measuring the intrinsic quality of individual responses and behavioral coefficients of different communities.
originalAbstract: Many online communities present user-contributed responses, such as reviews of products and answers to questions. User-provided helpfulness votes can highlight the most useful responses, but voting is a social process that can gain momentum based on the popularity of responses and the polarity of existing votes. We propose the Chinese Voting Process (CVP) which models the evolution of helpfulness votes as a self-reinforcing process dependent on position and presentation biases. We evaluate this model on Amazon product reviews and more than 80 StackExchange forums, measuring the intrinsic quality of individual responses and behavioral coefficients of different communities.

paragraphs: Helpfulness votes are intended to identify useful reviews and answers, but they are also part of a social process. Existing popularity and the direction of previous votes can influence subsequent voting. A response's accumulated votes therefore reflect both its quality and the circumstances under which people encounter and judge it.

The paper introduces the Chinese Voting Process to model how these votes evolve. Voting is represented as self-reinforcing, with position and presentation biases affecting the process. This makes the history and display of responses relevant to the model, allowing it to represent momentum rather than treating all votes as interchangeable observations.

The authors evaluate the model using Amazon product reviews and more than 80 StackExchange forums. They use it to measure the intrinsic quality of individual responses and behavioral coefficients for different communities. The contribution is a framework for interpreting helpfulness votes through an explicit model of social influence, with response quality and community voting behavior represented as distinct aspects of the observed process.
summary.tldr: The Chinese Voting Process models helpfulness votes as a socially reinforced process shaped by response position and presentation.

title: Beyond Exchangeability: The Chinese Voting Process

abstract: We demonstrate how quantum computation can provide non-trivial improvements in the computational and statistical complexity of the perceptron model. We develop two quantum algorithms for perceptron learning. The first algorithm exploits quantum information processing to determine a separating hyperplane using a number of steps sublinear in the number of data points $N$, namely $O(\sqrt{N})$. The second algorithm illustrates how the classical mistake bound of $O(\frac{1}{\gamma^2})$ can be further improved to $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}})$ through quantum means, where $\gamma$ denotes the margin. Such improvements are achieved through the application of quantum amplitude amplification to the version space interpretation of the perceptron model.
originalAbstract: We demonstrate how quantum computation can provide non-trivial improvements in the computational and statistical complexity of the perceptron model. We develop two quantum algorithms for perceptron learning. The first algorithm exploits quantum information processing to determine a separating hyperplane using a number of steps sublinear in the number of data points $N$, namely $O(\sqrt{N})$. The second algorithm illustrates how the classical mistake bound of $O(\frac{1}{\gamma^2})$ can be further improved to $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}})$ through quantum means, where $\gamma$ denotes the margin. Such improvements are achieved through the application of quantum amplitude amplification to the version space interpretation of the perceptron model.

paragraphs: The perceptron is a model for learning a separating hyperplane. This paper develops two quantum algorithms for perceptron learning and analyzes improvements in computational and statistical complexity. The algorithms target different quantities: the dependence on the number of training points and the dependence of the mistake bound on the margin.

The first algorithm determines a separating hyperplane in O(sqrt(N)) steps, where N is the number of data points. This is sublinear in dataset size. The second changes the stated classical mistake bound from O(1/gamma²) to O(1/sqrt(gamma)), where gamma denotes the margin. These are distinct guarantees, describing dataset-size scaling and margin-dependent prediction complexity respectively.

Both improvements use quantum amplitude amplification applied to a version-space interpretation of the perceptron. That interpretation organizes learning around candidate separators consistent with the learning problem. The paper’s contribution is to show how this viewpoint supports quantum improvements in the stated complexity measures, giving two algorithmic routes for enhancing perceptron learning through quantum computation.
summary.tldr: Two quantum perceptron algorithms improve dataset-size scaling and margin-dependent mistake bounds using amplitude amplification.

title: Quantum Perceptron Models

abstract: A core challenge for an agent learning to interact with the world is to predict how its actions affect objects in its environment. Many existing methods for learning the dynamics of physical interactions require labeled object information. However, to scale real-world interaction learning to a variety of scenes and objects, acquiring labeled data becomes increasingly impractical. To learn about physical object motion without labels, we develop an action-conditioned video prediction model that explicitly models pixel motion, by predicting a distribution over pixel motion from previous frames. Because our model explicitly predicts motion, it is partially invariant to object appearance, enabling it to generalize to previously unseen objects. To explore video prediction for real-world interactive agents, we also introduce a dataset of 59,000 robot interactions involving pushing motions, including a test set with novel objects. In this dataset, accurate prediction of videos conditioned on the robot's future actions amounts to learning a "visual imagination" of different futures based on different courses of action. Our experiments show that our proposed method produces more accurate video predictions both quantitatively and qualitatively, when compared to prior methods.

paragraphs: An agent interacting with objects needs to anticipate how its actions will change what it sees. Learning these dynamics from labeled object information becomes difficult as the variety of scenes and objects grows. This paper develops a video prediction model that learns about physical motion without requiring those object labels.

The model conditions predictions on actions and explicitly predicts a distribution over pixel motion from earlier frames. Modeling motion gives it partial invariance to object appearance, supporting generalization to objects it has not previously seen. The approach therefore connects future visual observations to proposed actions through how image content moves.

The authors introduce a dataset of 59,000 robot pushing interactions, including a test set containing novel objects. Predicting videos for different future actions provides a form of visual imagination: the model generates different anticipated futures for different courses of action. Experiments report more accurate video predictions than prior methods in both quantitative and qualitative comparisons, supporting the usefulness of explicit motion modeling for this task.
summary.tldr: An action-conditioned pixel-motion model learns video prediction without object labels and improves predictions for robot interactions, including unseen objects.

title: Unsupervised Learning for Physical Interaction through Video Prediction

abstract: Count-based exploration algorithms are known to perform near-optimally when used in conjunction with tabular reinforcement learning (RL) methods for solving small discrete Markov decision processes (MDPs). It is generally thought that count-based methods cannot be applied in high-dimensional state spaces, since most states will only occur once. Recent deep RL exploration strategies are able to deal with high-dimensional continuous state spaces through complex heuristics, often relying on optimism in the face of uncertainty or intrinsic motivation. In this work, we describe a surprising finding: a simple generalization of the classic count-based approach can reach near state-of-the-art performance on various high-dimensional and/or continuous deep RL benchmarks. States are mapped to hash codes, which allows to count their occurrences with a hash table. These counts are then used to compute a reward bonus according to the classic count-based exploration theory. We find that simple hash functions can achieve surprisingly good results on many challenging tasks. Furthermore, we show that a domain-dependent learned hash code may further improve these results. Detailed analysis reveals important aspects of a good hash function: 1) having appropriate granularity and 2) encoding information relevant to solving the MDP. This exploration strategy achieves near state-of-the-art performance on both continuous control tasks and Atari 2600 games, hence providing a simple yet powerful baseline for solving MDPs that require considerable exploration.

paragraphs: Count-based exploration encourages a reinforcement learning agent to visit unfamiliar states. It works well in small discrete settings, but counting exact states becomes problematic in high-dimensional or continuous environments, where observations may rarely repeat. This paper investigates whether a simple generalization can retain the approach's practical value in deep reinforcement learning.

The method maps states to hash codes and counts those codes in a hash table. It then computes an exploration reward bonus from the counts using the classic count-based approach. Sharing a code lets observations contribute to the same count. The authors find that even simple hash functions can produce strong results, with learned, domain-dependent codes potentially improving performance further.

Their analysis identifies two important properties of a useful hash function: appropriate granularity and preservation of information relevant to the task. Experiments achieve near state-of-the-art performance on continuous control tasks and Atari games. These findings support hashing as a simple, effective exploration baseline; they do not transfer the small-state theoretical guarantees automatically to every high-dimensional setting.
summary.tldr: Counting hashed states provides a simple exploration strategy with strong empirical results in high-dimensional and continuous reinforcement learning.

title: #Exploration: A Study of Count-Based Exploration for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce TrustVI, a fast second-order algorithm for black-box variational inference based on trust-region optimization and the reparameterization trick. At each iteration, TrustVI proposes and assesses a step based on minibatches of draws from the variational distribution. The algorithm provably converges to a stationary point. We implemented TrustVI in the Stan framework and compared it to two alternatives: Automatic Differentiation Variational Inference (ADVI) and Hessian-free Stochastic Gradient Variational Inference (HFSGVI). The former is based on stochastic first-order optimization. The latter uses second-order information, but lacks convergence guarantees. TrustVI typically converged at least one order of magnitude faster than ADVI, demonstrating the value of stochastic second-order information. TrustVI often found substantially better variational distributions than HFSGVI, demonstrating that our convergence theory can matter in practice.

paragraphs: Variational inference learns a probability distribution that approximates a target distribution through optimization. This paper introduces TrustVI, a second-order method for black-box variational inference. It combines trust-region optimization with the reparameterization trick, using information about the objective's curvature to guide updates rather than relying only on first-order information.

At each iteration, TrustVI uses minibatches of samples from the variational distribution to propose a step and assess it. The authors prove convergence to a stationary point. That guarantee is specific: it establishes convergence to a point satisfying a local stationarity condition, rather than claiming that the algorithm always finds the globally best variational approximation.

Implemented in Stan, TrustVI is compared with ADVI and HFSGVI. It typically converges at least an order of magnitude faster than the first-order ADVI method. It also often finds substantially better variational distributions than HFSGVI, which uses second-order information without convergence guarantees. Together, these results support both the practical value of curvature information and the importance of controlling stochastic optimization steps.
summary.tldr: TrustVI uses stochastic second-order trust-region updates to accelerate variational inference with a stationary-point convergence guarantee.

title: Fast Black-box Variational Inference through Stochastic Trust-Region Optimization

abstract: We show that accelerated optimization methods can be seen as particular instances of multi-step integration schemes from numerical analysis, applied to the gradient flow equation. Compared with recent advances in this vein, the differential equation considered here is the basic gradient flow, and we derive a class of multi-step schemes which includes accelerated algorithms, using classical conditions from numerical analysis. Multi-step schemes integrate the differential equation using larger step sizes, which intuitively explains the acceleration phenomenon.
originalAbstract: We show that accelerated optimization methods can be seen as particular instances of multi-step integration schemes from numerical analysis, applied to the gradient flow equation. Multi-step schemes integrate the differential equation using larger step sizes, which intuitively explains the acceleration phenomenon.

paragraphs: The paper connects accelerated optimization with numerical methods for solving differential equations. Its starting point is gradient flow, the continuous-time equation describing motion along the negative gradient of an objective. An optimization algorithm can be understood as a sequence of discrete updates that approximates such continuous motion.

The authors show that accelerated methods arise as particular multistep integration schemes applied to this basic gradient-flow equation. Multistep schemes use information from multiple steps when constructing an update. Using classical conditions from numerical analysis, the paper derives a class of such schemes that includes accelerated optimization algorithms.

This viewpoint places the explanation for acceleration in the integration method. The schemes can advance the differential equation with larger step sizes, which the authors offer as an intuitive explanation of faster optimization. The contribution is a mathematical connection and a derivation of a family of methods. It also provides a way to study acceleration using established numerical-analysis ideas while keeping the underlying differential equation as ordinary gradient flow.
summary.tldr: Accelerated optimization can be derived as multistep numerical integration of basic gradient flow, with larger integration steps offering intuition for acceleration.

title: Integration Methods and Optimization Algorithms

abstract: We present extensive experimental and theoretical support for the efficacy of recurrent highway networks (RHNs) and recurrent hypernetworks complimentary to the original works. Where the original RHN work primarily provides theoretical treatment of the subject, we demonstrate experimentally that RHNs benefit from far better gradient flow than LSTMs in addition to their improved task accuracy. The original hypernetworks work presents detailed experimental results but leaves several theoretical issues unresolved--we consider these in depth and frame several feasible solutions that we believe will yield further gains in the future. We demonstrate that these approaches are complementary: by combining RHNs and hypernetworks, we make a significant improvement over current state-of-the-art character-level language modeling performance on Penn Treebank while relying on much simpler regularization. Finally, we argue for RHNs as a drop-in replacement for LSTMs (analogous to LSTMs for vanilla RNNs) and for hypernetworks as a de-facto augmentation (analogous to attention) for recurrent architectures.

paragraphs: This paper investigates recurrent highway networks and recurrent hypernetworks as complementary approaches to language modeling. It adds experimental evidence where prior treatment emphasized theory and examines theoretical questions where prior work emphasized experiments. The aim is both to explain these architectures more fully and to test what combining them achieves.

For recurrent highway networks, the authors report substantially better gradient flow than LSTMs alongside improved task accuracy. For hypernetworks, they analyze unresolved theoretical issues and propose feasible solutions that they believe could yield future gains. Those proposed gains remain a forward-looking expectation, distinct from the results demonstrated by the combined model.

Combining the two approaches significantly improves reported state-of-the-art character-level language modeling on Penn Treebank while using much simpler regularization. This supports their compatibility in the evaluated task. The authors also advocate recurrent highway networks as replacements for LSTMs and hypernetworks as a standard augmentation for recurrent architectures. Those broader recommendations extend the interpretation of the evidence beyond the specific benchmark result.
summary.tldr: Combining recurrent highway networks and hypernetworks improves reported Penn Treebank character modeling while using simpler regularization.

title: Language Modeling with Recurrent Highway Hypernetworks

abstract: When observing task demonstrations, human apprentices are able to identify whether a given task is executed correctly long before they gain expertise in actually performing that task. Prior research into learning from demonstrations (LfD) has failed to capture this notion of the acceptability of an execution; meanwhile, temporal logics provide a flexible language for expressing task specifications. Inspired by this, we present Bayesian specification inference, a probabilistic model for inferring task specification as a temporal logic formula. We incorporate methods from probabilistic programming to define our priors, along with a domain-independent likelihood function to enable sampling-based inference. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model for inferring true specifications with over 90% similarity between the inferred specification and the ground truth, both within a synthetic domain and a real-world table setting task.

paragraphs: Recognizing a correctly performed task can be easier than performing it yourself. This paper applies that distinction to learning from demonstrations: the aim is to infer what makes an execution acceptable. The output is a task specification expressed in temporal logic, a language suited to describing requirements about how events unfold over time.

The authors introduce Bayesian specification inference, which treats possible specifications as uncertain hypotheses. They use probabilistic programming to express prior beliefs about those hypotheses and a domain-independent likelihood to connect candidate specifications with observed demonstrations. Sampling-based inference then provides a way to explore specifications supported by the evidence.

The model is evaluated in a synthetic domain and a real table-setting task. In both, the authors report more than 90% similarity between inferred specifications and ground truth. This supports the approach as a way to recover task requirements from examples; the reported similarity concerns the inferred specifications, rather than a learner's ability to execute the task.
summary.tldr: Bayesian specification inference learns temporal-logic descriptions of acceptable task executions from demonstrations.

title: Bayesian Inference of Temporal Task Specifications from Demonstrations

abstract: Neuroscience studies of human decision-making abilities commonly involve subjects completing a decision-making task while BOLD signals are recorded using fMRI. Hypotheses are tested about which brain regions mediate the effect of past experience, such as rewards, on future actions. One standard approach to this is model-based fMRI data analysis, in which a model is fitted to the behavioral data, i.e., a subject's choices, and then the neural data are parsed to find brain regions whose BOLD signals are related to the model's internal signals. However, the internal mechanics of such purely behavioral models are not constrained by the neural data, and therefore might miss or mischaracterize aspects of the brain. To address this limitation, we introduce a new method using recurrent neural network models that are flexible enough to be jointly fitted to the behavioral and neural data. We trained a model so that its internal states were suitably related to neural activity during the task, while at the same time its output predicted the next action a subject would execute. We then used the fitted model to create a novel visualization of the relationship between the activity in brain regions at different times following a reward and the choices the subject subsequently made. Finally, we validated our method using a previously published dataset. We found that the model was able to recover the underlying neural substrates that were discovered by explicit model engineering in the previous work, and also derived new results regarding the temporal pattern of brain activity.
