The paper identifies a weakness in this sequence: a model fitted only to behavior has internal mechanisms unconstrained by neural measurements. Those mechanisms may therefore miss or mischaracterize relevant brain activity.

The authors introduce recurrent neural network models fitted jointly to behavioral and fMRI data. Training encourages internal states to relate appropriately to neural activity while the network predicts the subject's next action. This makes both the observed choices and the recorded brain signals contribute to the learned account of decision-making.

The fitted model also supports a visualization linking activity in different brain regions after a reward to subsequent choices. Using a previously published dataset, the method recovers neural substrates identified through explicit model engineering in earlier work and produces additional findings about temporal activity patterns. The results support joint fitting as a way to connect flexible behavioral prediction with measured neural dynamics, including how those relationships unfold over time.
summary.tldr: Jointly fitting recurrent networks to choices and fMRI signals connects behavioral prediction with the timing of measured brain activity.

title: Integrated accounts of behavioral and neuroimaging data using flexible recurrent neural network models

abstract: One of the most striking aspects of early visual processing in the retina is the immediate parcellation of visual information into multiple parallel pathways, formed by different retinal ganglion cell types each tiling the entire visual field. Existing theories of efficient coding have been unable to account for the functional advantages of such cell-type diversity in encoding natural scenes. Here we go beyond previous theories to analyze how a simple linear retinal encoding model with different convolutional cell types efficiently encodes naturalistic spatiotemporal movies given a fixed firing rate budget. We find that optimizing the receptive fields and cell densities of two cell types makes them match the properties of the two main cell types in the primate retina, midget and parasol cells, in terms of spatial and temporal sensitivity, cell spacing, and their relative ratio. Moreover, our theory gives a precise account of how the ratio of midget to parasol cells decreases with retinal eccentricity. Also, we train a nonlinear encoding model with a rectifying nonlinearity to efficiently encode naturalistic movies, and again find emergent receptive fields resembling those of midget and parasol cells that are now further subdivided into ON and OFF types. Thus our work provides a theoretical justification, based on the efficient coding of natural movies, for the existence of the four most dominant cell types in the primate retina that together comprise 70% of all ganglion cells.

paragraphs: The retina divides visual information into parallel pathways carried by different ganglion-cell types. This paper asks why such diversity might be useful for efficient encoding of natural visual input. It studies naturalistic movies, so the information being encoded includes both spatial structure and changes over time, under a fixed firing-rate budget.

In a linear encoding model, the authors optimize the receptive fields and densities of two convolutional cell types. The resulting types match properties of primate midget and parasol cells, including spatial and temporal sensitivity, spacing, and relative abundance. The findings offer an efficient-coding justification for four dominant primate retinal cell types, together comprising 70% of ganglion cells. This is a theoretical explanation supported by optimized encoding models, connecting the diversity of visual pathways to the demands of representing natural movies efficiently.
summary.tldr: Optimizing movie encoding under a firing-rate budget produces model cell types resembling the retina's dominant midget and parasol pathways.

title: The emergence of multiple retinal cell types through efficient coding of natural movies

abstract: This paper introduces a new approach for the scalable Tucker decomposition problem. Given a tensor X , the method proposed allows to infer the latent factors by processing one subtensor drawn from X at a time. The key principle of our approach is based on the recursive computations of gradient and on cyclic update of factors involving only one single step of gradient descent. We further improve the computational efficiency of this algorithm by proposing an inexact gradient version. These two algorithms are backed with theoretical guarantees of convergence and convergence rate under mild conditions. The scalabilty of the proposed approaches which can be easily extended to handle some common constraints encountered in tensor decomposition (e.g non-negativity), is proven via numerical experiments on both synthetic and real data sets.

paragraphs: Tucker decomposition represents a multidimensional data array through latent factors. This paper develops a scalable way to infer those factors by processing one smaller subtensor at a time. The approach makes the update process operate on pieces of the data rather than requiring each update to handle the entire tensor.

Its main mechanism combines recursive gradient calculations with cyclic updates of the factors. Each factor update uses only one gradient-descent step. The authors also introduce a version using inexact gradients to improve computational efficiency further, giving two related algorithms for the same decomposition problem.

Both algorithms have theoretical guarantees for convergence and convergence rate under conditions described as mild. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the claimed scalability. The authors additionally state that the methods can readily accommodate common constraints such as non-negativity. The work therefore connects small incremental updates with convergence analysis and practical decomposition settings, including cases where the latent factors must satisfy additional requirements.
summary.tldr: Singleshot scales Tucker decomposition through subtensor processing and single-step factor updates, with conditional convergence guarantees.

title: Singleshot : a scalable Tucker tensor decomposition

abstract: Equilibrium Propagation (EP) is a biologically inspired learning algorithm for convergent recurrent neural networks, i.e. RNNs that are fed by a static input x and settle to a steady state. Training convergent RNNs consists in adjusting the weights until the steady state of output neurons coincides with a target y. Convergent RNNs can also be trained with the more conventional Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) algorithm. In its original formulation EP was described in the case of real-time neuronal dynamics, which is computationally costly. In this work, we introduce a discrete-time version of EP with simplified equations and with reduced simulation time, bringing EP closer to practical machine learning tasks. We first prove theoretically, as well as numerically that the neural and weight updates of EP, computed by forward-time dynamics, are step-by-step equal to the ones obtained by BPTT, with gradients computed backward in time. The equality is strict when the transition function of the dynamics derives from a primitive function and the steady state is maintained long enough. We then show for more standard discrete-time neural network dynamics that the same property is approximately respected and we subsequently demonstrate training with EP with equivalent performance to BPTT. In particular, we define the first convolutional architecture trained with EP achieving ∼ 1% test error on MNIST, which is the lowest error reported with EP. These results can guide the development of deep neural networks trained with EP.

paragraphs: Equilibrium Propagation trains recurrent networks that receive a fixed input and settle into a steady state. Learning adjusts the weights so that the settled outputs match a target. This paper introduces a discrete-time formulation with simpler equations and shorter simulation time, making the method more practical than its original real-time formulation.

The central result connects forward-time Equilibrium Propagation updates with gradients computed backward through time. The authors establish step-by-step equality theoretically and numerically when the transition dynamics derive from a primitive function and the steady state is maintained sufficiently long. These conditions are essential to the strict equality claim.

summary.tldr: Discrete-time Equilibrium Propagation matches backpropagation-through-time updates under stated conditions and approximates them in more standard dynamics.

title: Updates of Equilibrium Prop Match Gradients of Backprop Through Time in an RNN with Static Input

abstract: Bilinear feature transformation has shown the state-of-the-art performance in learning fine-grained image representations. However, the computational cost to learn pairwise interactions between deep feature channels is prohibitively expensive, which restricts this powerful transformation to be used in deep neural networks. In this paper, we propose a deep bilinear transformation (DBT) block, which can be deeply stacked in convolutional neural networks to learn fine-grained image representations. The DBT block can uniformly divide input channels into several semantic groups. As bilinear transformation can be represented by calculating pairwise interactions within each group, the computational cost can be heavily relieved. The output of each block is further obtained by aggregating intra-group bilinear features, with residuals from the entire input features. We found that the proposed network achieves new state-of-the-art in several fine-grained image recognition benchmarks, including CUB-Bird, Stanford-Car, and FGVC-Aircraft.

paragraphs: Fine-grained image recognition requires representations that distinguish closely related visual categories. Bilinear transformations capture pairwise interactions between deep feature channels and have shown strong performance for this purpose. Their expense, however, makes them difficult to use repeatedly inside deep networks. This paper proposes a block designed to make that repeated use practical.

The deep bilinear transformation block divides input channels uniformly into several semantic groups. It computes pairwise interactions within each group, substantially reducing the computational burden. The block then aggregates the resulting bilinear features and includes residual information from the entire input. This arrangement combines grouped interaction modeling with a path for the full input representation.

Because these blocks can be stacked deeply in convolutional networks, bilinear processing becomes a repeated component of representation learning. The authors report new state-of-the-art results on CUB-Bird, Stanford-Car, and FGVC-Aircraft. The findings support the grouped design as an effective way to use feature interactions throughout a network for the tested fine-grained recognition problems.
summary.tldr: Grouped bilinear blocks reduce interaction costs enough to stack them deeply, improving fine-grained image recognition benchmarks.

title: Learning Deep Bilinear Transformation for Fine-grained Image Representation

abstract: A recent trend in optimizing maps such as dense correspondences between objects or neural networks between pairs of domains is to optimize them jointly. In this context, there is a natural \textsl{cycle-consistency} constraint, which regularizes composite maps associated with cycles, i.e., they are forced to be identity maps. However, as there is an exponential number of cycles in a graph, how to sample a subset of cycles becomes critical for efficient and effective enforcement of the cycle-consistency constraint. This paper presents an algorithm that select a subset of weighted cycles to minimize a condition number of the induced joint optimization problem. Experimental results on benchmark datasets justify the effectiveness of our approach for optimizing dense correspondences between 3D shapes and neural networks for predicting dense image flows.
originalAbstract: A recent trend in optimizing maps such as dense correspondences between objects or neural networks between pairs of domains is to optimize them jointly. In this context, there is a natural \textsl{cycle-consistency} constraint, which regularizes composite maps associated with cycles, i.e., they are forced to be identity maps. However, as there is an exponential number of cycles in a graph, how to sample a subset of cycles becomes critical for efficient and effective enforcement of the cycle-consistency constraint. This paper presents an algorithm that select a subset of weighted cycles to minimize a condition number of the induced joint optimization problem. Experimental results on benchmark datasets justify the effectiveness of our approach for optimizing dense correspondences between 3D shapes and neural networks for predicting dense image flows.

paragraphs: When maps connect several objects or domains, optimizing each map separately can leave their predictions inconsistent. Cycle consistency provides a shared constraint: following a sequence of maps around a loop should return to the starting point. Joint optimization uses these relationships to coordinate maps, including shape correspondences and neural networks connecting image domains.

The difficulty is deciding which loops to enforce. A graph can contain exponentially many cycles, making the choice of a manageable subset important for both efficiency and effectiveness. The paper introduces an algorithm that selects cycles and assigns them weights, with the objective of minimizing a condition number of the resulting joint optimization problem.

This turns cycle selection into a question about the numerical properties of the optimization problem. The selected constraints are intended to support effective joint fitting, rather than merely increase the number of enforced loops. Benchmark experiments support the approach for dense correspondences between 3D shapes and neural networks that predict dense image flows.
summary.tldr: The paper selects and weights consistency cycles by an optimization condition number, with demonstrated benefits for shape matching and image-flow prediction.

title: A Condition Number for Joint Optimization of Cycle-Consistent Networks

abstract: Extracting and predicting object structure and dynamics from videos without supervision is a major challenge in machine learning. To address this challenge, we adopt a keypoint-based image representation and learn a stochastic dynamics model of the keypoints. Future frames are reconstructed from the keypoints and a reference frame. By modeling dynamics in the keypoint coordinate space, we achieve stable learning and avoid compounding of errors in pixel space. Our method improves upon unstructured representations both for pixel-level video prediction and for downstream tasks requiring object-level understanding of motion dynamics. We evaluate our model on diverse datasets: a multi-agent sports dataset, the Human3.6M dataset, and datasets based on continuous control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite. The spatially structured representation outperforms unstructured representations on a range of motion-related tasks such as object tracking, action recognition and reward prediction.

This paper tackles that problem without supervision by representing images through keypoints and learning a stochastic model of how those keypoints evolve. The representation gives motion an explicit spatial form that can support prediction and object-level understanding.

Future frames are reconstructed from predicted keypoints together with a reference frame. Modeling the dynamics in keypoint coordinates produces stable learning and avoids compounding errors in pixel space, according to the authors. This separates the representation of motion from the reconstruction of detailed images while retaining a path back to pixel-level video predictions.

These results indicate that the learned spatial structure is useful beyond reconstructing frames: it also captures motion information relevant to several forms of subsequent analysis.
summary.tldr: Learning stochastic keypoint dynamics from unlabeled video improves frame prediction and motion-related tasks over unstructured representations.

title: Unsupervised learning of object structure and dynamics from videos

abstract: We study the problem of how to repeatedly sell to a buyer running a no-regret, mean-based algorithm. Previous work [Braverman et al., 2018] shows that it is possible to design effective mechanisms in such a setting that extract almost all of the economic surplus, but these mechanisms require the buyer's values each round to be drawn independently and identically from a fixed distribution. In this work, we do away with this assumption and consider the prior-free setting where the buyer's value each round is chosen adversarially (possibly adaptively). We show that even in this prior-free setting, it is possible to extract a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of the full economic surplus for any $\varepsilon > 0$. The number of options offered to a buyer in any round scales independently of the number of rounds $T$ and polynomially in $\varepsilon$. We show that this is optimal up to a polynomial factor; any mechanism achieving this approximation factor, even when values are drawn stochastically, requires at least $\Omega(1/\varepsilon)$ options. Finally, we examine what is possible when we constrain our mechanism to a natural auction format where overbidding is dominated. Braverman et al. [2018] show that even when values are drawn from a known stochastic distribution supported on $[1/H, 1]$, it is impossible in general to extract more than $O(\log\log H / \log H)$ of the economic surplus. We show how to achieve the same approximation factor in the prior-independent setting (where the distribution is unknown to the seller), and an approximation factor of $O(1 / \log H)$ in the prior-free setting (where the values are chosen adversarially).

title: Prior-Free Dynamic Auctions with Low Regret Buyers

abstract: Few-shot or one-shot learning of classifiers requires a significant inductive bias towards the type of task to be learned. One way to acquire this is by meta-learning on tasks similar to the target task. In this paper, we propose UMTRA, an algorithm that performs unsupervised, model-agnostic meta-learning for classification tasks. The meta-learning step of UMTRA is performed on a flat collection of unlabeled images. While we assume that these images can be grouped into a diverse set of classes and are relevant to the target task, no explicit information about the classes or any labels are needed. UMTRA uses random sampling and augmentation to create synthetic training tasks for meta-learning phase. Labels are only needed at the final target task learning step, and they can be as little as one sample per class. On the Omniglot and Mini-Imagenet few-shot learning benchmarks, UMTRA outperforms every tested approach based on unsupervised learning of representations, while alternating for the best performance with the recent CACTUs algorithm. Compared to supervised model-agnostic meta-learning approaches, UMTRA trades off some classification accuracy for a reduction in the required labels of several orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Learning a classifier from one or a few labeled examples requires useful prior bias about the task. Meta-learning can acquire that bias from related tasks, but those tasks often require labels. This paper introduces UMTRA, a model-agnostic approach that performs the meta-learning stage using a flat collection of unlabeled images.

UMTRA constructs synthetic training tasks through random sampling and augmentation. It assumes that the unlabeled images contain a diverse set of classes relevant to the target task, even though their labels and explicit class organization are unavailable. Labels are needed only when learning the final target task, potentially with just one labeled example per class.

On Omniglot and Mini-Imagenet, UMTRA outperforms every tested method based on unsupervised representation learning and alternates with CACTUs for best performance. Relative to supervised model-agnostic meta-learning, it sacrifices some classification accuracy while reducing label requirements by several orders of magnitude. The result demonstrates a substantial label-efficiency trade-off under the stated assumptions about diversity and relevance of the unlabeled images.
summary.tldr: UMTRA creates meta-learning tasks from unlabeled images, enabling few-shot classification with far fewer labels at some cost to accuracy.

title: Unsupervised Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification

abstract: Design of experiments and estimation of treatment effects in large-scale networks, in the presence of strong interference, is a challenging and important problem. Most existing methods' performance deteriorates as the density of the network increases. In this paper, we present a novel strategy for accurately estimating the causal effects of a class of treatments in a dense large-scale network. First, we design an approximate randomized controlled experiment by solving an optimization problem to allocate treatments in the presence of competition among neighboring nodes. Then we apply an importance sampling adjustment to correct for any leftover bias (from the approximation) in estimating average treatment effects. We provide theoretical guarantees, verify robustness in a simulation study, and validate the scalability and usefulness of our procedure in a real-world experiment on a large social network.

paragraphs: A/B testing becomes difficult when changing one participant’s treatment also affects neighboring participants. In densely connected networks, these spillovers can be strong, and the abstract reports that many existing methods become less effective as connections increase. This paper addresses estimating causal effects for a particular class of treatments under those conditions.

The procedure combines experiment design with a correction during analysis. First, it solves an optimization problem to allocate treatments while accounting for competition among neighboring nodes. This produces an approximation to a randomized controlled experiment. It then uses importance sampling to adjust the estimated average treatment effect for bias left by that approximation.

These two stages address complementary parts of the problem: treatment allocation manages interference before outcomes are analyzed, while the adjustment addresses remaining estimation bias. The authors provide theoretical guarantees, examine robustness through simulation, and test the procedure in an experiment on a large social network. That real-world experiment supports the method’s scalability and usefulness within the treatment setting studied.
summary.tldr: An optimized treatment allocation and importance-sampling correction support causal effect estimation in dense networks with interference.

title: A/B Testing in Dense Large-Scale Networks: Design and Inference

abstract: Unsupervised learning methods based on contrastive learning have drawn increasing attention and achieved promising results. Most of them aim to learn representations invariant to instance-level variations, which are provided by different views of the same instance. In this paper, we propose Invariance Propagation to focus on learning representations invariant to category-level variations, which are provided by different instances from the same category. Our method recursively discovers semantically consistent samples residing in the same high-density regions in representation space. We demonstrate a hard sampling strategy to concentrate on maximizing the agreement between the anchor sample and its hard positive samples, which provide more intra-class variations to help capture more abstract invariance. As a result, with a ResNet-50 as the backbone, our method achieves 71.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet linear classification and 78.2% top-5 accuracy fine-tuning on only 1% labels, surpassing previous results. We also achieve state-of-the-art performance on other downstream tasks, including linear classification on Places205 and Pascal VOC, and transfer learning on small scale datasets.

paragraphs: Many contrastive learning methods teach representations to agree across different views of the same instance. Invariance Propagation instead targets variation between different instances of the same category. The goal is to learn features that capture shared category information despite differences between individual examples, extending the scope of the invariance being learned.

The method recursively discovers semantically consistent samples within the same high-density regions of representation space. It then emphasizes hard positive samples when maximizing agreement with an anchor. These positives provide more variation within a class, encouraging the representation to capture more abstract commonalities than agreement between closely related views alone.

With a ResNet-50 backbone, the method achieves 71.3% top-1 accuracy for ImageNet linear classification and 78.2% top-5 accuracy when fine-tuned using only 1% of labels, surpassing previous results. It also reports state-of-the-art results on Places205 and Pascal VOC linear classification and transfer to small datasets. These findings support the usefulness of discovering cross-instance relationships without supervised category labels.
summary.tldr: Invariance Propagation discovers related instances and emphasizes hard positives to learn category-level invariances without supervision.

title: Unsupervised Representation Learning by Invariance Propagation

abstract: It is often difficult to hand-specify what the correct reward function is for a task, so researchers have instead aimed to learn reward functions from human behavior or feedback. The types of behavior interpreted as evidence of the reward function have expanded greatly in recent years. We've gone from demonstrations, to comparisons, to reading into the information leaked when the human is pushing the robot away or turning it off. And surely, there is more to come. How will a robot make sense of all these diverse types of behavior? Our key observation is that different types of behavior can be interpreted in a single unifying formalism - as a reward-rational choice that the human is making, often implicitly. We use this formalism to survey prior work through a unifying lens, and discuss its potential use as a recipe for interpreting new sources of information that are yet to be uncovered.

paragraphs: Writing down the right reward function for a robot can be difficult, so reward learning uses human behavior and feedback as evidence. That evidence takes many forms, including demonstrations, comparisons, physical interventions, and shutting a robot down. This paper asks how a robot can interpret these different signals within one conceptual framework.

The proposed formalism treats behavior as a reward-rational choice, including choices the person makes implicitly. Under this interpretation, an action provides information about what the person values because it expresses a choice related to reward. Different feedback formats can therefore be examined through a common account of how behavior supplies evidence.

The authors use this framework to survey earlier reward-learning research and discuss how it could guide interpretation of new information sources. Its contribution is a unifying lens and a possible recipe for extending reward learning. The reward-rational interpretation is the modeling premise connecting the signals; the abstract presents the framework's potential for future sources of feedback rather than an experimental guarantee that every human action can be interpreted correctly.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies diverse human feedback as implicit or explicit reward-rational choices that provide evidence for learning rewards.

title: Reward-rational (implicit) choice: A unifying formalism for reward learning

abstract: Multi-task learning is a very challenging problem in reinforcement learning. While training multiple tasks jointly allow the policies to share parameters across different tasks, the optimization problem becomes non-trivial: It remains unclear what parameters in the network should be reused across tasks, and how the gradients from different tasks may interfere with each other. Thus, instead of naively sharing parameters across tasks, we introduce an explicit modularization technique on policy representation to alleviate this optimization issue. Given a base policy network, we design a routing network which estimates different routing strategies to reconfigure the base network for each task. Instead of directly selecting routes for each task, our task-specific policy uses a method called soft modularization to softly combine all the possible routes, which makes it suitable for sequential tasks. We experiment with various robotics manipulation tasks in simulation and show our method improves both sample efficiency and performance over strong baselines by a large margin.

paragraphs: Training one reinforcement-learning system across several tasks offers opportunities to share useful policy parameters. It also creates an optimization problem: tasks may need different computations, and their training gradients can interfere. This paper addresses that tension by explicitly organizing the policy representation into modules whose use can vary across tasks.

A routing network estimates how to reconfigure a base policy network for each task. The task-specific policy softly combines possible routes through the network, producing a flexible combination of computations. The authors call this soft modularization and present it as suitable for sequential tasks, where policy behavior must support a sequence of decisions.

The method is evaluated on simulated robotic manipulation tasks. The authors report large improvements in both sample efficiency and performance over strong baselines. In this setting, the results suggest that learning how tasks share and combine policy components can ease the optimization difficulties of joint training. The empirical claim is grounded in simulation, where the modular routing approach is compared with the stated baselines.
summary.tldr: Soft modularization learns task-dependent combinations of policy-network routes, improving sample efficiency and performance on simulated manipulation tasks.

title: Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Soft Modularization

abstract: We study the fixed-support Wasserstein barycenter problem (FS-WBP), which consists in computing the Wasserstein barycenter of $m$ discrete probability measures supported on a finite metric space of size $n$. We show first that the constraint matrix arising from the standard linear programming (LP) representation of the FS-WBP is \textit{not totally unimodular} when $m \geq 3$ and $n \geq 3$. This result resolves an open question pertaining to the relationship between the FS-WBP and the minimum-cost flow (MCF) problem since it proves that the FS-WBP in the standard LP form is not an MCF problem when $m \geq 3$ and $n \geq 3$. We also develop a provably fast \textit{deterministic} variant of the celebrated iterative Bregman projection (IBP) algorithm, named \textsc{FastIBP}, with a complexity bound of $\tilde{O}(mn^{7/3}\varepsilon^{-4/3})$, where $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$ is the desired tolerance. This complexity bound is better than the best known complexity bound of $\tilde{O}(mn^2\varepsilon^{-2})$ for the IBP algorithm in terms of $\varepsilon$, and that of $\tilde{O}(mn^{5/2}\varepsilon^{-1})$ from accelerated alternating minimization algorithm or accelerated primal-dual adaptive gradient algorithm in terms of $n$. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments with both synthetic data and real images and demonstrate the favorable performance of the \textsc{FastIBP} algorithm in practice.

paragraphs: A fixed-support Wasserstein barycenter summarizes several discrete probability distributions using transport-based distance, with the possible support locations specified in advance. This paper studies both the structure of its standard linear-programming formulation and the speed of algorithms for solving it. The problem involves m distributions on a finite metric space containing n points.

The authors prove that the standard formulation's constraint matrix is not totally unimodular when both m and n are at least three. This resolves a question about whether that formulation is a minimum-cost flow problem: in this regime, it is not. The result identifies a structural distinction between two optimization formulations that might otherwise appear closely related.

The paper also introduces FastIBP, a deterministic variant of iterative Bregman projection. Its complexity bound is approximately O(m n^(7/3) epsilon^(-4/3)), suppressing logarithmic factors. This improves the tolerance dependence over the cited IBP bound and the support-size dependence over two cited accelerated methods, rather than improving every factor simultaneously. Experiments on synthetic data and real images show favorable practical performance.
summary.tldr: The paper clarifies the structure of fixed-support Wasserstein barycenters and introduces FastIBP with improved complexity tradeoffs.

title: Fixed-Support Wasserstein Barycenters: Computational Hardness and Fast Algorithm

abstract: We study a regret minimization problem with the existence of multiple best/near-optimal arms in the multi-armed bandit setting. We consider the case when the number of arms/actions is comparable or much larger than the time horizon, and make \emph{no} assumptions about the structure of the bandit instance. Our goal is to design algorithms that can automatically adapt to the \emph{unknown} hardness of the problem, i.e., the number of best arms. Our setting captures many modern applications of bandit algorithms where the action space is enormous and the information about the underlying instance/structure is unavailable. We first propose an adaptive algorithm that is agnostic to the hardness level and theoretically derive its regret bound. We then prove a lower bound for our problem setting, which indicates: (1) no algorithm can be minimax optimal simultaneously over all hardness levels; and (2) our algorithm achieves a rate function that is Pareto optimal. With additional knowledge of the expected reward of the best arm, we propose another adaptive algorithm that is minimax optimal, up to polylog factors, over \emph{all} hardness levels. Experimental results confirm our theoretical guarantees and show advantages of our algorithms over the previous state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: The paper studies bandit problems with so many possible actions that their number is comparable to, or much larger than, the number of available rounds. Multiple actions may be optimal or nearly optimal. The learner is not given structural information about the actions and does not know how many best actions exist, which determines the problem's hardness.

The authors first develop an algorithm that adapts without knowing this hardness level and prove a regret bound. They also establish an impossibility result: no algorithm can be minimax optimal at every hardness level simultaneously in this setting. Their algorithm achieves a Pareto-optimal rate function, expressing an optimal tradeoff across those levels rather than uniform optimality everywhere.

The situation improves when the expected reward of a best action is supplied as additional information. With that knowledge, a second adaptive algorithm is minimax optimal across all hardness levels up to polylogarithmic factors. Experiments support the theoretical guarantees and show advantages over prior leading methods. The results identify both the value and the limits of adapting to an unknown abundance of good actions.
summary.tldr: Adaptive bandit algorithms exploit multiple good actions, with provable tradeoffs that improve when the best action's expected reward is known.

title: On Regret with Multiple Best Arms

abstract: Implicit-depth models such as Deep Equilibrium Networks have recently been shown to match or exceed the performance of traditional deep networks while being much more memory efficient. However, these models suffer from unstable convergence to a solution and lack guarantees that a solution exists. On the other hand, Neural ODEs, another class of implicit-depth models, do guarantee existence of a unique solution but perform poorly compared with traditional networks. In this paper, we develop a new class of implicit-depth model based on the theory of monotone operators, the Monotone Operator Equilibrium Network (monDEQ). We show the close connection between finding the equilibrium point of an implicit network and solving a form of monotone operator splitting problem, which admits efficient solvers with guaranteed, stable convergence. We then develop a parameterization of the network which ensures that all operators remain monotone, which guarantees the existence of a unique equilibrium point. Finally, we show how to instantiate several versions of these models, and implement the resulting iterative solvers, for structured linear operators such as multi-scale convolutions. The resulting models vastly outperform the Neural ODE-based models while also being more computationally efficient. Code is available at http://github.com/locuslab/monotone_op_net.

paragraphs: Implicit-depth networks define their output through a solution or equilibrium rather than a fixed sequence of layers. They can be memory efficient, but finding an equilibrium can be unstable, and a solution may lack an existence guarantee. This paper introduces Monotone Operator Equilibrium Networks, or monDEQ, to give that computation a firmer mathematical foundation.

The authors connect equilibrium computation to a monotone operator splitting problem, for which efficient solvers offer stable, guaranteed convergence. They then parameterize the network so that the relevant operators remain monotone, with their construction guaranteeing a unique equilibrium. The model design and solution procedure are therefore developed together.

The paper instantiates several versions and implements iterative solvers for structured linear operators, including multiscale convolutions. The resulting models substantially outperform the Neural ODE-based models in the reported comparison while also being more computationally efficient. The contribution joins an equilibrium existence guarantee with a convergent computational approach, showing how mathematical structure can support practical implicit-depth architectures.
summary.tldr: monDEQ builds implicit-depth networks with unique equilibria and stable solvers, outperforming the compared Neural ODE models in performance and computational efficiency.

title: Monotone operator equilibrium networks

abstract: Contrastive learning (CL) is a popular technique for self-supervised learning (SSL) of visual representations. It uses pairs of augmentations of unlabeled training examples to define a classification task for pretext learning of a deep embedding. Despite extensive works in augmentation procedures, prior works do not address the selection of challenging negative pairs, as images within a sampled batch are treated independently. This paper addresses the problem, by introducing a new family of adversarial examples for constrastive learning and using these examples to define a new adversarial training algorithm for SSL, denoted as CLAE. When compared to standard CL, the use of adversarial examples creates more challenging positive pairs and adversarial training produces harder negative pairs by accounting for all images in a batch during the optimization. CLAE is compatible with many CL methods in the literature. Experiments show that it improves the performance of several existing CL baselines on multiple datasets.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds visual representations from unlabeled images by comparing augmented examples. Positive pairs come from different augmentations of the same example, while negative pairs provide contrasts with other examples. The paper focuses on how to make these comparisons more challenging, particularly the negative pairs that earlier approaches did not explicitly select jointly across a batch.

The proposed method, CLAE, introduces adversarial examples designed for contrastive learning and uses them in a self-supervised adversarial training algorithm. The adversarial examples create more difficult positive pairs. By considering all images in the batch during optimization, the training procedure also produces harder negative pairs, making the relationships among examples part of the challenge construction.

This approach matters because it changes how demanding the learning task is without requiring labeled training examples. CLAE is compatible with many existing contrastive learning methods, allowing it to augment several established approaches. Experiments on multiple datasets show performance improvements over several standard contrastive learning baselines, providing empirical support for constructing challenging pairs through adversarial optimization.
summary.tldr: CLAE improves self-supervised contrastive learning by constructing harder positive and negative pairs through adversarial optimization.

title: Contrastive Learning with Adversarial Examples

abstract: Standard Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) designed for computer vision tasks tend to have large intermediate activation maps. These require large working memory and are thus unsuitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices typically used for inference on the edge. Aggressively downsampling the images via pooling or strided convolutions can address the problem but leads to a significant decrease in accuracy due to gross aggregation of the feature map by standard pooling operators. In this paper, we introduce RNNPool, a novel pooling operator based on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), that efficiently aggregates features over large patches of an image and rapidly downsamples activation maps. Empirical evaluation indicates that an RNNPool layer can effectively replace multiple blocks in a variety of architectures such as MobileNets, DenseNet when applied to standard vision tasks like image classification and face detection. That is, RNNPool can significantly decrease computational complexity and peak memory usage for inference while retaining comparable accuracy. We use RNNPool with the standard S3FD architecture to construct a face detection method that achieves state-of-the-art MAP for tiny ARM Cortex-M4 class microcontrollers with under 256 KB of RAM. Code is released at https://github.com/Microsoft/EdgeML.

Rapidly shrinking those maps helps memory usage, but ordinary pooling or strided convolutions can lose accuracy when they aggregate too coarsely. RNNPool addresses this tradeoff with a pooling operator based on recurrent neural networks.

The operator aggregates features over large image patches and quickly downsamples activation maps. Experiments indicate that a single RNNPool layer can replace multiple blocks in architectures including MobileNets and DenseNet. The evaluated tasks include image classification and face detection.

summary.tldr: RNNPool uses recurrent networks to downsample image features efficiently, reducing inference memory and computation while retaining comparable accuracy.

title: RNNPool: Efficient Non-linear Pooling for RAM Constrained Inference

abstract: We introduce Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL), a new approach to self-supervised image representation learning. BYOL relies on two neural networks, referred to as online and target networks, that interact and learn from each other. From an augmented view of an image, we train the online network to predict the target network representation of the same image under a different augmented view. At the same time, we update the target network with a slow-moving average of the online network. While state-of-the art methods intrinsically rely on negative pairs, BYOL achieves a new state of the art without them. BYOL reaches 74.3% top-1 classification accuracy on ImageNet using the standard linear evaluation protocol with a standard ResNet-50 architecture and 79.6% with a larger ResNet. We also show that BYOL performs on par or better than the current state of the art on both transfer and semi-supervised benchmarks.

paragraphs: Bootstrap Your Own Latent, or BYOL, learns image representations through two interacting neural networks. Its training signal comes from different augmented views of the same image. The online network learns to predict the representation produced by a target network when that target receives another view.

The target network changes through a slow-moving average of the online network's parameters. This couples the two networks while making their updates different. The approach matters because it achieves strong representation learning without negative pairs, which the state-of-the-art methods discussed in the abstract rely on.

Under the standard linear evaluation protocol on ImageNet, BYOL reports 74.3% top-1 accuracy with a standard ResNet-50 and 79.6% with a larger ResNet. It also matches or exceeds the compared state of the art on transfer and semi-supervised benchmarks. These results demonstrate that predicting a slowly updated target across augmented views can produce useful representations without requiring the negative-pair mechanism used by those earlier methods.
summary.tldr: BYOL learns strong image representations without negative pairs by predicting a slowly updated target network's representation of another augmented view.

title: Bootstrap Your Own Latent - A New Approach to Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Models recently used in the literature proving residual networks (ResNets) are better than linear predictors are actually different from standard ResNets that have been widely used in computer vision. In addition to the assumptions such as scalar-valued output or single residual block, the models fundamentally considered in the literature have no nonlinearities at the final residual representation that feeds into the final affine layer. To codify such a difference in nonlinearities and reveal a linear estimation property, we define ResNEsts, i.e., Residual Nonlinear Estimators, by simply dropping nonlinearities at the last residual representation from standard ResNets. We show that wide ResNEsts with bottleneck blocks can always guarantee a very desirable training property that standard ResNets aim to achieve, i.e., adding more blocks does not decrease performance given the same set of basis elements. To prove that, we first recognize ResNEsts are basis function models that are limited by a coupling problem in basis learning and linear prediction. Then, to decouple prediction weights from basis learning, we construct a special architecture termed augmented ResNEst (A-ResNEst) that always guarantees no worse performance with the addition of a block. As a result, such an A-ResNEst establishes empirical risk lower bounds for a ResNEst using corresponding bases. Our results demonstrate ResNEsts indeed have a problem of diminishing feature reuse; however, it can be avoided by sufficiently expanding or widening the input space, leading to the above-mentioned desirable property. Inspired by the densely connected networks (DenseNets) that have been shown to outperform ResNets, we also propose a corresponding new model called Densely connected Nonlinear Estimator (DenseNEst). We show that any DenseNEst can be represented as a wide ResNEst with bottleneck blocks. Unlike ResNEsts, DenseNEsts exhibit the desirable property without any special architectural re-design.

title: ResNEsts and DenseNEsts: Block-based DNN Models with Improved Representation Guarantees

abstract: Neural networks have achieved success in a wide array of perceptual tasks but often fail at tasks involving both perception and higher-level reasoning. On these more challenging tasks, bespoke approaches (such as modular symbolic components, independent dynamics models or semantic parsers) targeted towards that specific type of task have typically performed better. The downside to these targeted approaches, however, is that they can be more brittle than general-purpose neural networks, requiring significant modification or even redesign according to the particular task at hand. Here, we propose a more general neural-network-based approach to dynamic visual reasoning problems that obtains state-of-the-art performance on three different domains, in each case outperforming bespoke modular approaches tailored specifically to the task. Our method relies on learned object-centric representations, self-attention and self-supervised dynamics learning, and all three elements together are required for strong performance to emerge. The success of this combination suggests that there may be no need to trade off flexibility for performance on problems involving spatio-temporal or causal-style reasoning. With the right soft biases and learning objectives in a neural network we may be able to attain the best of both worlds.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning requires more than recognizing what appears in an image: a model may also need to reason about objects, their relationships, and changes over time. Specialized systems have often handled these tasks well, but their task-specific components can require substantial redesign when the problem changes. This paper investigates a more general neural approach.

The method combines learned representations organized around objects, self-attention, and self-supervised learning of dynamics. These components bring object structure, interactions, and temporal behavior into the same approach. The authors report that all three are needed together for strong performance in their study, making their combination central to the result.

Across three domains, the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance and surpasses modular systems specifically designed for those tasks. This provides evidence that flexible neural architectures can perform well on demanding visual reasoning problems. The broader conclusion remains a possibility supported by these results: suitable structural biases and learning objectives may reduce the need to sacrifice flexibility for spatial, temporal, or causal-style reasoning performance.
summary.tldr: Combining learned object representations, attention, and self-supervised dynamics achieves strong visual reasoning performance across three domains.

title: Attention over Learned Object Embeddings Enables Complex Visual Reasoning

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViT) have achieved remarkable success in large-scale image recognition. They split every 2D image into a fixed number of patches, each of which is treated as a token. Generally, representing an image with more tokens would lead to higher prediction accuracy, while it also results in drastically increased computational cost. To achieve a decent trade-off between accuracy and speed, the number of tokens is empirically set to 16x16 or 14x14. In this paper, we argue that every image has its own characteristics, and ideally the token number should be conditioned on each individual input. In fact, we have observed that there exist a considerable number of “easy” images which can be accurately predicted with a mere number of 4x4 tokens, while only a small fraction of “hard” ones need a finer representation. Inspired by this phenomenon, we propose a Dynamic Transformer to automatically configure a proper number of tokens for each input image. This is achieved by cascading multiple Transformers with increasing numbers of tokens, which are sequentially activated in an adaptive fashion at test time, i.e., the inference is terminated once a sufficiently confident prediction is produced. We further design efficient feature reuse and relationship reuse mechanisms across different components of the Dynamic Transformer to reduce redundant computations. Extensive empirical results on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the competitive baselines in terms of both theoretical computational efficiency and practical inference speed. Code and pre-trained models (based on PyTorch and MindSpore) are available at https://github.com/blackfeather-wang/Dynamic-Vision-Transformer and https://github.com/blackfeather-wang/Dynamic-Vision-Transformer-MindSpore.

The central idea is to allocate image-processing effort according to the individual input. Confidence-based early termination supplies the operational decision rule, while the reuse mechanisms address the cost of processing an image at multiple levels of detail.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Transformers adapt token counts to each image and reuse computation, improving reported efficiency and inference speed.

title: Not All Images are Worth 16x16 Words: Dynamic Transformers for Efficient Image Recognition

abstract: Data efficiency is a key challenge for deep reinforcement learning. We address this problem by using unlabeled data to pretrain an encoder which is then finetuned on a small amount of task-specific data. To encourage learning representations which capture diverse aspects of the underlying MDP, we employ a combination of latent dynamics modelling and unsupervised goal-conditioned RL. When limited to 100k steps of interaction on Atari games (equivalent to two hours of human experience), our approach significantly surpasses prior work combining offline representation pretraining with task-specific finetuning, and compares favourably with other pretraining methods that require orders of magnitude more data. Our approach shows particular promise when combined with larger models as well as more diverse, task-aligned observational data -- approaching human-level performance and data-efficiency on Atari in our best setting.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can require substantial task-specific experience. This paper studies whether an encoder can first learn useful representations from unlabeled data and then be fine-tuned using a small amount of experience for a particular task. The goal is to make the later learning stage more data efficient.

Pretraining combines latent dynamics modeling with unsupervised goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. These components encourage the representation to capture diverse aspects of the underlying decision process. The encoder is therefore trained through both modeling changes in its latent space and learning behavior conditioned on goals, before task-specific fine-tuning begins.

With task interaction limited to 100,000 steps on Atari games, the approach significantly outperforms earlier work combining offline representation pretraining and fine-tuning. It also compares favorably with other pretraining approaches that use orders of magnitude more data. Larger models and more diverse observations aligned with the task show particular promise. In the authors' best setting, performance and data efficiency approach human levels on Atari; that qualification matters to the reported result.
summary.tldr: Unlabeled pretraining that combines latent dynamics and goal-conditioned learning improves Atari reinforcement learning with limited task-specific interaction.

title: Pretraining Representations for Data-Efficient Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Selective rationalization explains the prediction of complex neural networks by finding a small subset of the input that is sufficient to predict the neural model output. The selection mechanism is commonly integrated into the model itself by specifying a two-component cascaded system consisting of a rationale generator, which makes a binary selection of the input features (which is the rationale), and a predictor, which predicts the output based only on the selected features. The components are trained jointly to optimize prediction performance. In this paper, we reveal a major problem with such cooperative rationalization paradigm --- model interlocking. Inter-locking arises when the predictor overfits to the features selected by the generator thus reinforcing the generator's selection even if the selected rationales are sub-optimal. The fundamental cause of the interlocking problem is that the rationalization objective to be minimized is concave with respect to the generator’s selection policy. We propose a new rationalization framework, called A2R, which introduces a third component into the architecture, a predictor driven by soft attention as opposed to selection. The generator now realizes both soft and hard attention over the features and these are fed into the two different predictors. While the generator still seeks to support the original predictor performance, it also minimizes a gap between the two predictors. As we will show theoretically, since the attention-based predictor exhibits a better convexity property, A2R can overcome the concavity barrier. Our experiments on two synthetic benchmarks and two real datasets demonstrate that A2R can significantly alleviate the interlock problem and find explanations that better align with human judgments.

A common design jointly trains a rationale generator and a predictor that sees only the selected features. This paper identifies a failure mode called interlocking: the predictor adapts to poor selections and reinforces them.

The authors trace this problem to concavity of the training objective with respect to the generator's selection policy. Their A2R framework adds another predictor driven by soft attention. The generator now supplies hard selections to the original predictor and soft attention to the added predictor, while also minimizing a gap between their predictions.

The additional predictor has a more favorable convexity property, and the theoretical analysis shows how A2R can overcome the concavity barrier. Experiments on two synthetic benchmarks and two real datasets show substantial alleviation of interlocking and explanations that agree better with human judgments. The result targets a specific feedback problem in joint training, helping rationale generation escape selections that the original predictor has learned to accommodate.
summary.tldr: A2R adds a soft-attention predictor to reduce self-reinforcing poor rationale selections and improve agreement with human judgments.

title: Understanding Interlocking Dynamics of Cooperative Rationalization

abstract: We introduce ViSER, a method for recovering articulated 3D shapes and dense3D trajectories from monocular videos. Previous work on high-quality reconstruction of dynamic 3D shapes typically relies on multiple camera views, strong category-specific priors, or 2D keypoint supervision. We show that none of these are required if one can reliably estimate long-range correspondences in a video, making use of only 2D object masks and two-frame optical flow as inputs. ViSER infers correspondences by matching 2D pixels to a canonical, deformable 3D mesh via video-specific surface embeddings that capture the pixel appearance of each surface point. These embeddings behave as a continuous set of keypoint descriptors defined over the mesh surface, which can be used to establish dense long-range correspondences across pixels. The surface embeddings are implemented as coordinate-based MLPs that are fit to each video via self-supervised losses.Experimental results show that ViSER compares favorably against prior work on challenging videos of humans with loose clothing and unusual poses as well as animals videos from DAVIS and YTVOS. Project page: viser-shape.github.io.

paragraphs: ViSER reconstructs articulated 3D shapes and dense 3D motion trajectories from a single-camera video. The paper shows that multiple views, strong category-specific priors, and annotated 2D keypoints are unnecessary if reliable long-range correspondences can be estimated. Its inputs use 2D object masks and optical flow between pairs of frames to support that reconstruction.

The method matches image pixels to a shared deformable 3D mesh through surface embeddings tailored to each video. These embeddings capture the appearance associated with points on the mesh and act like a continuous collection of keypoint descriptors. They enable dense matches across frames, connecting observations separated in time through a common surface representation.

Coordinate-based multilayer perceptrons implement the embeddings and are fitted to each video using self-supervised losses. Experiments compare favorably with prior work on challenging human videos involving loose clothing and unusual poses, as well as animal videos from DAVIS and YTVOS. The findings support reliable correspondence estimation as a route to reconstructing complex motion with reduced supervision, with that correspondence requirement central to the stated result.
summary.tldr: ViSER learns video-specific surface embeddings to recover articulated 3D shapes and motion from monocular video using masks and optical flow.

title: ViSER: Video-Specific Surface Embeddings for Articulated 3D Shape Reconstruction

abstract: Recent evidence has shown the existence of a so-called double-descent and even triple-descent behavior for the generalization error of deep-learning models. This important phenomenon commonly appears in implemented neural network architectures, and also seems to emerge in epoch-wise curves during the training process. A recent line of research has highlighted that random matrix tools can be used to obtain precise analytical asymptotics of the generalization (and training) errors of the random feature model. In this contribution, we analyze the whole temporal behavior of the generalization and training errors under gradient flow for the random feature model. We show that in the asymptotic limit of large system size the full time-evolution path of both errors can be calculated analytically. This allows us to observe how the double and triple descents develop over time, if and when early stopping is an option, and also observe time-wise descent structures. Our techniques are based on Cauchy complex integral representations of the errors together with recent random matrix methods based on linear pencils.

paragraphs: Generalization error can exhibit double or triple descent, producing more complicated behavior than a single improvement followed by deterioration. Such patterns can also appear as training progresses. This paper investigates those dynamics in the random feature model, studying the entire evolution of training and generalization errors under gradient flow.

The authors derive an analytical description of both errors over time in the limit of large system size. Their techniques combine complex integral representations with random matrix methods based on linear pencils. The result extends the analysis beyond a final trained model to the full trajectory through which its errors develop.

Having that trajectory makes it possible to examine how double and triple descents emerge, whether and when early stopping is useful, and what descent structures occur along the time axis. The scope is the asymptotic random feature setting analyzed in the paper. Within that setting, the work offers a precise mathematical view of how training duration interacts with error behavior.
summary.tldr: An analytical solution tracks random-feature training and generalization errors over time, revealing descent patterns and possible opportunities for early stopping.

title: Model, sample, and epoch-wise descents: exact solution of gradient flow in the random feature model

abstract: Continual learning aims to learn a sequence of tasks from dynamic data distributions. Without accessing to the old training samples, knowledge transfer from the old tasks to each new task is difficult to determine, which might be either positive or negative. If the old knowledge interferes with the learning of a new task, i.e., the forward knowledge transfer is negative, then precisely remembering the old tasks will further aggravate the interference, thus decreasing the performance of continual learning. By contrast, biological neural networks can actively forget the old knowledge that conflicts with the learning of a new experience, through regulating the learning-triggered synaptic expansion and synaptic convergence. Inspired by the biological active forgetting, we propose to actively forget the old knowledge that limits the learning of new tasks to benefit continual learning. Under the framework of Bayesian continual learning, we develop a novel approach named Active Forgetting with synaptic Expansion-Convergence (AFEC). Our method dynamically expands parameters to learn each new task and then selectively combines them, which is formally consistent with the underlying mechanism of biological active forgetting. We extensively evaluate AFEC on a variety of continual learning benchmarks, including CIFAR-10 regression tasks, visual classification tasks and Atari reinforcement tasks, where AFEC effectively improves the learning of new tasks and achieves the state-of-the-art performance in a plug-and-play way.

title: AFEC: Active Forgetting of Negative Transfer in Continual Learning

abstract: In causal bandit problems the action set consists of interventions on variables of a causal graph. Several researchers have recently studied such bandit problems and pointed out their practical applications. However, all existing works rely on a restrictive and impractical assumption that the learner is given full knowledge of the causal graph structure upfront. In this paper, we develop novel causal bandit algorithms without knowing the causal graph. Our algorithms work well for causal trees, causal forests and a general class of causal graphs. The regret guarantees of our algorithms greatly improve upon those of standard multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms under mild conditions. Lastly, we prove our mild conditions are necessary: without them one cannot do better than standard MAB algorithms.

paragraphs: In a causal bandit problem, an action changes a variable in a causal system, and the learner seeks interventions that yield good rewards. Relationships between variables can provide useful structure for learning. Earlier approaches discussed in the paper assume that the learner already knows the entire causal graph, an assumption the authors seek to remove.

The paper develops algorithms that operate without advance knowledge of that graph. They cover causal trees, causal forests, and a broader class of causal graphs. Under conditions described as mild, their regret guarantees substantially improve on those of standard multi-armed bandit algorithms. Regret measures the reward lost through learning and choosing actions instead of consistently selecting an optimal action.

The authors also prove that their conditions are necessary for the stated advantage: without them, one cannot improve over standard bandit algorithms. Together, the positive and negative results explain when causal structure can help even though it is initially unknown. The benefit is conditional on properties of the problem, rather than following merely from calling the actions causal interventions.
summary.tldr: Causal bandit algorithms can outperform standard bandit guarantees without knowing the graph, under conditions also shown to be necessary.

title: Causal Bandits with Unknown Graph Structure

abstract: A widely used algorithm for transfer learning is fine-tuning, where a pre-trained model is fine-tuned on a target task with a small amount of labeled data. When the capacity of the pre-trained model is much larger than the size of the target data set, fine-tuning is prone to overfitting and "memorizing" the training labels. Hence, an important question is to regularize fine-tuning and ensure its robustness to noise. To address this question, we begin by analyzing the generalization properties of fine-tuning. We present a PAC-Bayes generalization bound that depends on the distance traveled in each layer during fine-tuning and the noise stability of the fine-tuned model. We empirically measure these quantities. Based on the analysis, we propose regularized self-labeling---the interpolation between regularization and self-labeling methods, including (i) layer-wise regularization to constrain the distance traveled in each layer; (ii) self label-correction and label-reweighting to correct mislabeled data points (that the model is confident) and reweight less confident data points. We validate our approach on an extensive collection of image and text data sets using multiple pre-trained model architectures. Our approach improves baseline methods by 1.76% (on average) for seven image classification tasks and 0.75% for a few-shot classification task. When the target data set includes noisy labels, our approach outperforms baseline methods by 3.56% on average in two noisy settings.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large pretrained model on a small labeled dataset can lead to memorization, especially when some labels are wrong. This paper examines how to constrain adaptation while handling unreliable supervision. Its theoretical starting point is a PAC-Bayes generalization bound that depends on how far each layer moves during fine-tuning and on the resulting model’s stability to noise.

The authors measure these quantities empirically and develop regularized self-labeling from the analysis. Layer-specific regularization restricts parameter movement. Label correction changes suspected mistakes when the model is confident, while label reweighting adjusts the influence of less confident examples. Together, these components address both changes to the pretrained model and the quality of the training signal.

Evaluation covers image and text datasets with multiple pretrained architectures. The method improves baselines by 1.76% on average across seven image-classification tasks and by 0.75% on a few-shot task. Across two noisy-label settings, the average improvement is 3.56%. These findings support combining controlled adaptation with confidence-based treatment of labels.
summary.tldr: Regularized self-labeling combines layer-specific fine-tuning constraints with label correction and reweighting to improve generalization and noise robustness.

title: Improved Regularization and Robustness for Fine-tuning in Neural Networks

abstract: We study a dynamic version of the implicit trace estimation problem. Given access to an oracle for computing matrix-vector multiplications with a dynamically changing matrix A, our goal is to maintain an accurate approximation to A's trace using as few multiplications as possible. We present a practical algorithm for solving this problem and prove that, in a natural setting, its complexity is quadratically better than the standard solution of repeatedly applying Hutchinson's stochastic trace estimator. We also provide an improved algorithm assuming additional common assumptions on A's dynamic updates. We support our theory with empirical results, showing significant computational improvements on three applications in machine learning and network science: tracking moments of the Hessian spectral density during neural network optimization, counting triangles and estimating natural connectivity in a dynamically changing graph.

paragraphs: The trace of a matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries, but accessing those entries directly may be impractical. This paper considers a setting where the available operation is multiplying the matrix by a vector. The additional challenge is that the matrix changes over time, so its trace estimate must be maintained as it evolves.

The authors propose a practical dynamic estimation algorithm designed to use few matrix-vector multiplications. In a natural setting studied by the paper, they prove a quadratic improvement in complexity over repeatedly running Hutchinson’s stochastic trace estimator. They also give another algorithm with improved performance under additional common assumptions about the matrix updates. These gains are therefore tied to the update settings covered by the analysis.

Experiments examine tracking moments of Hessian spectral density during neural network training, counting triangles in changing graphs, and estimating graph natural connectivity. The reported computational improvements support the value of treating trace estimation as a continuing task over a changing matrix, rather than repeatedly solving independent estimation problems.
summary.tldr: Dynamic trace estimation reduces matrix-vector computations for changing matrices, with a quadratic complexity improvement in the analyzed setting.

title: Dynamic Trace Estimation

abstract: This paper studies the problem of conducting self-supervised learning for node representation learning on graphs. Most existing self-supervised learning methods assume the graph is homophilous, where linked nodes often belong to the same class or have similar features. However, such assumptions of homophily do not always hold in real-world graphs. We address this problem by developing a decoupled self-supervised learning (DSSL) framework for graph neural networks. DSSL imitates a generative process of nodes and links from latent variable modeling of the semantic structure, which decouples different underlying semantics between different neighborhoods into the self-supervised learning process. Our DSSL framework is agnostic to the encoders and does not need prefabricated augmentations, thus is flexible to different graphs. To effectively optimize the framework, we derive the evidence lower bound of the self-supervised objective and develop a scalable training algorithm with variational inference. We provide a theoretical analysis to justify that DSSL enjoys the better downstream performance. Extensive experiments on various types of graph benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed framework can achieve better performance compared with competitive baselines.

paragraphs: Many self-supervised graph methods rely on homophily: connected nodes tend to have similar features or belong to the same class. Real graphs do not always follow that pattern. This paper asks how to learn useful node representations when different connections can carry different semantic meanings.

The proposed DSSL framework uses latent variables to model the semantic structure behind nodes and links. Its learning process separates the underlying meanings associated with different neighborhoods instead of treating them as interchangeable evidence of similarity. The framework can work with different encoders and does not require prefabricated graph augmentations, giving it flexibility across graph types.

To train the model, the authors derive an evidence lower bound for its self-supervised objective and develop a scalable variational-inference algorithm. They provide theoretical analysis supporting improved downstream performance, while experiments across different graph benchmarks show gains over competitive baselines. The central idea is to make neighborhood semantics part of the learning problem, rather than relying on homophily as a broadly applicable shortcut.
summary.tldr: DSSL learns node representations by separating neighborhood semantics, addressing graphs where connected nodes need not be similar.

title: Decoupled Self-supervised Learning for Graphs

abstract: No-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) aims to quantify how humans perceive visual distortions of digital images without access to their undistorted references. NR-IQA models are extensively studied in computational vision, and are widely used for performance evaluation and perceptual optimization of man-made vision systems. Here we make one of the first attempts to examine the perceptual robustness of NR-IQA models. Under a Lagrangian formulation, we identify insightful connections of the proposed perceptual attack to previous beautiful ideas in computer vision and machine learning. We test one knowledge-driven and three data-driven NR-IQA methods under four full-reference IQA models (as approximations to human perception of just-noticeable differences). Through carefully designed psychophysical experiments, we find that all four NR-IQA models are vulnerable to the proposed perceptual attack. More interestingly, we observe that the generated counterexamples are not transferable, manifesting themselves as distinct design flows of respective NR-IQA methods.

Such models are used to evaluate vision systems and guide perceptual optimization. This paper examines whether their judgments remain reliable under deliberately constructed perceptual attacks, placing human perception at the center of the robustness question.

The authors formulate their attack through a Lagrangian approach and relate it to earlier ideas in computer vision and machine learning. They test one knowledge-driven and three data-driven quality models. Four full-reference quality models serve as approximations to human sensitivity to just-noticeable image differences during the evaluation.

Psychophysical experiments with people find that all four tested no-reference models are vulnerable to the proposed attack. The generated counterexamples do not transfer across the tested models, suggesting distinct weaknesses in their respective designs. This finding matters because a quality estimator can appear useful in ordinary evaluation yet disagree with human perception on targeted examples; the observed vulnerability is established for the particular models studied.
summary.tldr: Human experiments reveal perceptual-attack vulnerabilities in four tested no-reference image quality models, with counterexamples exposing different weaknesses across models.

title: Perceptual Attacks of No-Reference Image Quality Models with Human-in-the-Loop

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are powerful frameworks for learning embeddings of graph-structured data. GCNs are traditionally studied through the lens of Euclidean geometry. Recent works find that non-Euclidean Riemannian manifolds provide specific inductive biases for embedding hierarchical or spherical data. However, they cannot align well with data of mixed graph topologies. We consider a larger class of pseudo-Riemannian manifolds that generalize hyperboloid and sphere. We develop new geodesic tools that allow for extending neural network operations into geodesically disconnected pseudo-Riemannian manifolds. As a consequence, we derive a pseudo-Riemannian GCN that models data in pseudo-Riemannian manifolds of constant nonzero curvature in the context of graph neural networks. Our method provides a geometric inductive bias that is sufficiently flexible to model mixed heterogeneous topologies like hierarchical graphs with cycles. We demonstrate the representational capabilities of this method by applying it to the tasks of graph reconstruction, node classification, and link prediction on a series of standard graphs with mixed topologies. Empirical results demonstrate that our method outperforms Riemannian counterparts when embedding graphs of complex topologies.
