paragraphs: AutoPSV creates automatic annotations for intermediate reasoning steps, with the aim of improving how language-model answers are checked. It starts by training a verifier using whether final answers are correct. The verifier then scores each intermediate step according to the estimated probability that reasoning from that point will reach a correct final answer.

The method examines relative changes in these confidence scores across a reasoning sequence. Those changes supply a signal for locating errors and annotating the process. This makes final-answer supervision useful for a more detailed task: assessing the path toward an answer. The approach can detect errors even when ground-truth answers are unavailable during that assessment, and reduces reliance on extensive manual annotation or computationally expensive model-generated annotation.

Experiments support the usefulness of the learned confidence changes for identifying reasoning errors. Training a verifier on AutoPSV's process annotations also improves its ability to choose correct answers from multiple language-model outputs. The authors report substantial improvements across five mathematics and commonsense reasoning datasets, connecting automatic step annotation to better answer selection.
summary.tldr: AutoPSV turns changes in a verifier's stepwise confidence into automatic reasoning annotations that improve answer selection.

title: AutoPSV: Automated Process-Supervised Verifier

abstract: Training agents in multi-agent games presents significant challenges due to their intricate nature. These challenges are exacerbated by dynamics influenced not only by the environment but also by strategies of opponents. Existing methods often struggle with slow convergence and instability.To address these challenges, we harness the potential of imitation learning (IL) to comprehend and anticipate actions of the opponents, aiming to mitigate uncertainties with respect to the game dynamics.Our key contributions include:(i) a new multi-agent IL model for predicting next moves of the opponents - our model works with hidden actions of opponents and local observations;(ii) a new multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithm that combines our IL model and policy training into one single training process;and (iii) extensive experiments in three challenging game environments, including an advanced version of the Star-Craft multi-agent challenge (i.e., SMACv2).Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art MARL algorithms.

paragraphs: Learning in a multi-agent game is difficult because outcomes depend on both the environment and the strategies of other players. Uncertainty about opponents can contribute to slow or unstable training. This paper uses imitation learning to predict opponents' next moves, aiming to reduce that uncertainty during the learning process.

The proposed imitation model works with local observations even when opponents' actions are hidden. This is central to its intended use: anticipating other players must be possible from the information available to the agent. The authors then integrate the prediction model with policy learning in a single multi-agent reinforcement-learning training process.

Combining opponent prediction and policy training makes anticipating other agents part of learning how to act. The authors evaluate the approach in three challenging game environments, including SMACv2, an advanced StarCraft multi-agent challenge. Their experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement-learning methods. These findings support the usefulness of the integrated approach in the evaluated games, particularly the idea that learning about opponents can help agents handle the uncertainty created by their strategies.
summary.tldr: The method jointly trains opponent-action prediction and agent policies to improve performance in the evaluated multi-agent games.

title: Mimicking To Dominate: Imitation Learning Strategies for Success in Multiagent Games

abstract: 3D GAN inversion aims to project a single image into the latent space of a 3D Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), thereby achieving 3D geometry reconstruction. While there exist encoders that achieve good results in 3D GAN inversion, they are predominantly built on EG3D, which specializes in synthesizing near-frontal views and is limiting in synthesizing comprehensive 3D scenes from diverse viewpoints. In contrast to existing approaches, we propose a novel framework built on PanoHead, which excels in synthesizing images from a 360-degree perspective. To achieve realistic 3D modeling of the input image, we introduce a dual encoder system tailored for high-fidelity reconstruction and realistic generation from different viewpoints. Accompanying this, we propose a stitching framework on the triplane domain to get the best predictions from both. To achieve seamless stitching, both encoders must output consistent results despite being specialized for different tasks. For this reason, we carefully train these encoders using specialized losses, including an adversarial loss based on our novel occlusion-aware triplane discriminator. Experiments reveal that our approach surpasses the existing encoder training methods qualitatively and quantitatively.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a three-dimensional head from one image requires matching the visible appearance while producing realistic views from other directions. GAN inversion approaches this by mapping the image into a generative model's latent space. Existing encoders are largely built on EG3D, whose emphasis on near-frontal images limits its ability to synthesize comprehensive views.

This paper instead builds on PanoHead, which supports synthesis around a full 360-degree perspective. It introduces two encoders specialized for faithful reconstruction and realistic generation from different viewpoints. A stitching framework combines their predictions in the triplane representation. The aim is to retain the strengths of both encoders within a single reconstructed head.

Combining specialized predictions requires consistency where they are stitched together. The authors train the encoders with tailored losses, including an adversarial loss from an occlusion-aware triplane discriminator. Experiments report qualitative and quantitative improvements over existing encoder training methods. The results support coordinating reconstruction fidelity and viewpoint realism through specialized encoders whose internal representations are trained to fit together.
summary.tldr: Two coordinated encoders and triplane stitching improve single-image head reconstruction and realistic synthesis across viewpoints.

title: Dual Encoder GAN Inversion for High-Fidelity 3D Head Reconstruction from Single Images

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) inevitably memorize sensitive, copyrighted, and harmful knowledge from the training corpus; therefore, it is crucial to erase this knowledge from the models. Machine unlearning is a promising solution for efficiently removing specific knowledge by post hoc modifying models. In this paper, we propose a Real-World Knowledge Unlearning benchmark (RWKU) for LLM unlearning. RWKU is designed based on the following three key factors: (1) For the task setting, we consider a more practical and challenging unlearning setting, where neither the forget corpus nor the retain corpus is accessible. (2) For the knowledge source, we choose 200 real-world famous people as the unlearning targets and show that such popular knowledge is widely present in various LLMs. (3) For the evaluation framework, we design the forget set and the retain set to evaluate the model’s capabilities across various real-world applications. Regarding the forget set, we provide four four membership inference attack (MIA) methods and nine kinds of adversarial attack probes to rigorously test unlearning efficacy. Regarding the retain set, we assess locality and utility in terms of neighbor perturbation, general ability, reasoning ability, truthfulness, factuality, and fluency. We conduct extensive experiments across two unlearning scenarios, two models and six baseline methods and obtain some meaningful findings. We release our benchmark and code publicly at http://rwku-bench.github.io for future work.
originalAbstract: Large language models (LLMs) inevitably memorize sensitive, copyrighted, and harmful knowledge from the training corpus; therefore, it is crucial to erase this knowledge from the models. Machine unlearning is a promising solution for efficiently removing specific knowledge by post hoc modifying models. In this paper, we propose a Real-World Knowledge Unlearning benchmark (RWKU) for LLM unlearning. RWKU is designed based on the following three key factors: (1) For the task setting, we consider a more practical and challenging unlearning setting, where neither the forget corpus nor the retain corpus is accessible. (2) For the knowledge source, we choose 200 real-world famous people as the unlearning targets and show that such popular knowledge is widely present in various LLMs. (3) For the evaluation framework, we design the forget set and the retain set to evaluate the model’s capabilities across various real-world applications. Regarding the forget set, we provide four four membership inference attack (MIA) methods and nine kinds of adversarial attack probes to rigorously test unlearning efficacy. Regarding the retain set, we assess locality and utility in terms of neighbor perturbation, general ability, reasoning ability, truthfulness, factuality, and fluency. We conduct extensive experiments across two unlearning scenarios, two models and six baseline methods and obtain some meaningful findings. We release our benchmark and code publicly at http://rwku-bench.github.io for future work.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove particular knowledge from an already trained model. RWKU creates a benchmark for evaluating this process in language models under a demanding setting: neither the corpus to forget nor the corpus to retain is accessible. It uses 200 famous people as targets and establishes that knowledge about them is widespread across various models.

The benchmark evaluates both targeted forgetting and preservation of other capabilities. Its forget set includes four membership-inference attack methods and nine kinds of adversarial probes to test unlearning efficacy. These assessments examine forgetting through multiple forms of probing, making the evaluation broader than a single way of asking about the target.

The retain set measures effects on neighboring knowledge alongside general ability, reasoning, truthfulness, factuality, and fluency. Experiments cover two unlearning scenarios, two models, and six baseline methods. The contribution is an evaluation framework that considers removal and preservation together, so unlearning can be assessed in relation to the model's remaining usefulness across real-world applications.
summary.tldr: RWKU evaluates language-model unlearning without access to forget or retain corpora, testing targeted removal alongside preserved capabilities.

title: RWKU: Benchmarking Real-World Knowledge Unlearning for Large Language Models

abstract: Understanding the power of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) in accomplishing machine learning tasks is one of the most important questions in quantum machine learning. In this paper, we focus on the PQC expressivity for general multivariate function classes. Previously established Universal Approximation Theorems for PQCs are either nonconstructive or assisted with parameterized classical data processing, making it hard to justify whether the expressive power comes from the classical or quantum parts. We explicitly construct data re-uploading PQCs for approximating multivariate polynomials and smooth functions and establish the first non-asymptotic approximation error bounds for such functions in terms of the number of qubits, the quantum circuit depth and the number of trainable parameters of the PQCs. Notably, we show that for multivariate polynomials and multivariate smooth functions, the quantum circuit size and the number of trainable parameters of our proposed PQCs can be smaller than the deep ReLU neural networks. We further demonstrate the approximation capability of PQCs via numerical experiments. Our results pave the way for designing practical PQCs that can be implemented on near-term quantum devices with limited resources.

paragraphs: Knowing that a quantum circuit can approximate a function eventually does not establish what it can achieve with limited resources. This paper studies parameterized quantum circuits through explicit constructions and finite-resource error bounds. It focuses on multivariate polynomials and smooth functions, connecting approximation quality to concrete circuit requirements.

The authors construct data re-uploading circuits and bound their error in terms of qubit count, circuit depth, and number of trainable parameters. This addresses weaknesses in earlier universal approximation results that were either nonconstructive or relied on trainable classical processing. Explicit quantum constructions help clarify which approximation capability is attributable to the quantum circuit itself.

They also demonstrate approximation capability numerically. This is a qualified resource comparison for the proposed constructions, rather than a universal advantage for quantum machine learning. The bounds provide a basis for designing circuits around the limited resources available on near-term quantum devices.
summary.tldr: Explicit quantum-circuit constructions yield finite-resource approximation bounds and can use fewer resources than deep ReLU networks for the studied function classes.

title: Non-asymptotic Approximation Error Bounds of Parameterized Quantum Circuits

abstract: It is vital to infer a signed distance function (SDF) for multi-view based surface reconstruction. 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) provides a novel perspective for volume rendering, and shows advantages in rendering efficiency and quality. Although 3DGS provides a promising neural rendering option, it is still hard to infer SDFs for surface reconstruction with 3DGS due to the discreteness, the sparseness, and the off-surface drift of 3D Gaussians. To resolve these issues, we propose a method that seamlessly merge 3DGS with the learning of neural SDFs. Our key idea is to more effectively constrain the SDF inference with the multi-view consistency. To this end, we dynamically align 3D Gaussians on the zero-level set of the neural SDF, and then render the aligned 3D Gaussians through the differentiable rasterization. Meanwhile, we update the neural SDF by pulling neighboring space to the pulled 3D Gaussians, which progressively refine the signed distance field near the surface. With both differentiable pulling and splatting, we jointly optimize 3D Gaussians and the neural SDF with both RGB and geometry constraints, which recovers more accurate, smooth, and complete surfaces with more geometry details. Our numerical and visual comparisons show our superiority over the state-of-the-art results on the widely used benchmarks.

paragraphs: A signed distance function represents a surface through the locations where its value is zero. Learning such a function from multiple views is difficult when using 3D Gaussian Splatting because the Gaussian elements are discrete, sparse, and can drift away from the surface. This paper couples Gaussian rendering with a learned distance field to address those problems.

The method dynamically pulls the Gaussians onto the neural field's zero-level surface and renders them through differentiable rasterization. In the other direction, it updates the distance field by pulling neighboring space toward the aligned Gaussians. These linked operations progressively refine the field near the surface while making use of consistency across views.

Both the Gaussians and the neural distance function are jointly optimized using image-color and geometric constraints. The authors report more accurate, smoother, and more complete surfaces with finer geometric detail. Numerical and visual comparisons on widely used benchmarks show improvements over state-of-the-art results, supporting the benefit of keeping the rendered elements and inferred surface closely aligned.
summary.tldr: Jointly aligning Gaussian elements with a neural distance field improves multi-view surface reconstruction in the reported comparisons.

title: Neural Signed Distance Function Inference through Splatting 3D Gaussians Pulled on Zero-Level Set

abstract: Generating realistic and diverse layouts of furnished indoor 3D scenes unlocks multiple interactive applications impacting a wide range of industries. The inherent complexity of object interactions, the limited amount of available data and the requirement to fulfill spatial constraints all make generative modeling for 3D scene synthesis and arrangement challenging. Current methods address these challenges autoregressively or by using off-the-shelf diffusion objectives by simultaneously predicting all attributes without 3D reasoning considerations. In this paper, we introduce DeBaRA, a score-based model specifically tailored for precise, controllable and flexible arrangement generation in a bounded environment. We argue that the most critical component of a scene synthesis system is to accurately establish the size and position of various objects within a restricted area. Based on this insight, we propose a lightweight conditional score-based model designed with 3D spatial awareness at its core. We demonstrate that by focusing on spatial attributes of objects, a single trained DeBaRA model can be leveraged at test time to perform several downstream applications such as scene synthesis, completion and re-arrangement. Further, we introduce a novel Self Score Evaluation procedure so it can be optimally employed alongside external LLM models. We evaluate our approach through extensive experiments and demonstrate significant improvement upon state-of-the-art approaches in a range of scenarios.

This makes the same learned arrangement capability available across different ways of specifying a room-generation task.

Extensive experiments report significant improvements over leading approaches in a range of scenarios. The broader finding is that a model tailored to the geometry of arrangement can provide both strong results and flexibility across related scene-editing applications.
summary.tldr: DeBaRA uses a spatially aware denoising model to generate, complete, and rearrange furnished 3D rooms with one trained system.

title: DeBaRA: Denoising-Based 3D Room Arrangement Generation

abstract: Image diffusion distillation achieves high-fidelity generation with very few sampling steps. However, directly applying these techniques to video models results in unsatisfied frame quality. This issue arises from the limited frame appearance quality in public video datasets, affecting the performance of both teacher and student video diffusion models. Our study aims to improve video diffusion distillation and meanwhile enabling the student model to improve frame appearance using the abundant high-quality image data. To this end, we propose motion consistency models (MCM), a single-stage video diffusion distillation method that disentangles motion and appearance learning. Specifically, MCM involves a video consistency model that distills motion from the video teacher model, and an image discriminator that boosts frame appearance to match high-quality image data. However, directly combining these components leads to two significant challenges: a conflict in frame learning objectives, where video distillation learns from low-quality video frames while the image discriminator targets high-quality images, and training-inference discrepancies due to the differing quality of video samples used during training and inference. To address these challenges, we introduce disentangled motion distillation and mixed trajectory distillation. The former applies the distillation objective solely to the motion representation, while the latter mitigates training-inference discrepancies by mixing distillation trajectories from both the low- and high-quality video domains. Extensive experiments show that our MCM achieves state-of-the-art video diffusion distillation performance. Additionally, our method can enhance frame quality in video diffusion models, producing frames with high aesthetic value or specific styles.

paragraphs: Diffusion distillation can reduce the number of sampling steps needed for generation, but transferring image-focused techniques directly to video can produce disappointing frames. This paper links that problem to limited appearance quality in public video datasets, which affects both the teacher model and the student trained from it.

The method therefore applies its distillation objective specifically to motion representations.

A second component mixes distillation trajectories from lower- and higher-quality video domains to reduce differences between training and inference. Experiments report state-of-the-art video diffusion distillation performance. They also show that the method can improve frame appearance, including aesthetic quality or particular styles. The approach lets video and image data contribute different kinds of supervision within one training stage.
summary.tldr: Motion Consistency Models separate motion distillation from appearance learning to accelerate video diffusion while improving frame quality.

title: Motion Consistency Model: Accelerating Video Diffusion with Disentangled Motion-Appearance Distillation

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) faces significant challenges due to data heterogeneity across distributed clients. To address this, we propose FedGMKD, a novel framework that combines knowledge distillation and differential aggregation for efficient prototype-based personalized FL without the need for public datasets or server-side generative models. FedGMKD introduces Cluster Knowledge Fusion, utilizing Gaussian Mixture Models to generate prototype features and soft predictions on the client side, enabling effective knowledge distillation while preserving data privacy. Additionally, we implement a Discrepancy-Aware Aggregation Technique that weights client contributions based on data quality and quantity, enhancing the global model's generalization across diverse client distributions. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence of FedGMKD. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, demonstrate that FedGMKD outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly improving both local and global accuracy in non-IID data settings.

paragraphs: Federated learning brings together training contributions from clients whose data can differ substantially. Those differences complicate both learning a useful shared model and producing models that work well locally. FedGMKD addresses this problem with a prototype-based personalized learning framework that combines knowledge distillation with an aggregation rule sensitive to differences among clients.

Its Cluster Knowledge Fusion component uses Gaussian mixture models on each client to generate prototype features and soft predictions. These summaries support knowledge distillation while preserving data privacy. A second component, discrepancy-aware aggregation, weights client contributions according to both data quality and quantity, aiming to improve generalization across the clients’ different distributions.

The framework operates without public datasets or generative models on the server. The authors provide a theoretical convergence analysis and evaluate FedGMKD on benchmarks including SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. They report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both local and global accuracy under non-IID data. These findings support combining client-side knowledge summaries with aggregation that accounts for heterogeneous contributions.
summary.tldr: FedGMKD combines client-side prototype distillation with quality- and quantity-aware aggregation to improve federated learning on heterogeneous data.

title: FedGMKD: An Efficient Prototype Federated Learning Framework through Knowledge Distillation and Discrepancy-Aware Aggregation

abstract: Canonical work handling distribution shifts typically necessitates an entire target distribution that lands inside the training distribution.However, practical scenarios often involve only a handful target samples, potentially lying outside the training support, which requires the capability of extrapolation.In this work, we aim to provide a theoretical understanding of when extrapolation is possible and offer principled methods to achieve it without requiring an on-support target distribution.To this end, we formulate the extrapolation problem with a latent-variable model that embodies the minimal change principle in causal mechanisms.Under this formulation, we cast the extrapolation problem into a latent-variable identification problem.We provide realistic conditions on shift properties and the estimation objectives that lead to identification even when only one off-support target sample is available, tackling the most challenging scenarios.Our theory reveals the intricate interplay between the underlying manifold's smoothness and the shift properties.We showcase how our theoretical results inform the design of practical adaptation algorithms. Through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, we validate our theoretical findings and their practical implications.

paragraphs: Adapting to a new distribution becomes especially difficult when only a few target examples are available and they fall outside the training data's support. This paper develops a theoretical account of when extrapolation is possible in that setting, without requiring an entire target distribution contained within the training distribution.

The authors use a latent-variable model built around minimal changes in causal mechanisms. This turns extrapolation into a question of identifying hidden variables. They establish conditions on the distribution shift and estimation objectives that permit identification even with a single target sample outside the training support. The result is conditional on those properties, rather than a general guarantee from one observation.

The theory also reveals how the smoothness of the underlying manifold interacts with the nature of the shift. These relationships inform the design of practical adaptation algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the theoretical findings and their practical implications, connecting a causal account of limited change to methods for adapting beyond previously observed data.
summary.tldr: A causal latent-variable framework identifies conditions that make extrapolation possible even from one off-support target sample.

title: Towards Understanding Extrapolation: a Causal Lens

abstract: Personalized retrieval and segmentation aim to locate specific instances within a dataset based on an input image and a short description of the reference instance. While supervised methods are effective, they require extensive labeled data for training. Recently, self-supervised foundation models have been introduced to these tasks showing comparable results to supervised methods. However, a significant flaw in these models is evident: they struggle to locate a desired instance when other instances within the same class are presented. In this paper, we explore text-to-image diffusion models for these tasks. Specifically, we propose a novel approach called PDM for Personalized Diffusion Features Matching, that leverages intermediate features of pre-trained text-to-image models for personalization tasks without any additional training. PDM demonstrates superior performance on popular retrieval and segmentation benchmarks, outperforming even supervised methods. We also highlight notable shortcomings in current instance and segmentation datasets and propose new benchmarks for these tasks.

paragraphs: Personalized retrieval and segmentation aim to find a particular instance from a reference image and short description. Recognizing the right category is insufficient when several instances of that category are present. The paper identifies this distinction as a weakness of self-supervised foundation models, even when their overall results are comparable to supervised approaches.

Personalized Diffusion Features Matching, or PDM, uses intermediate features from pretrained text-to-image diffusion models to perform these personalization tasks. It requires no additional training. The approach examines whether representations already learned by a generative model can distinguish the requested instance well enough to support both finding relevant images and locating the instance within them.

PDM outperforms methods on popular retrieval and segmentation benchmarks, including supervised approaches. The authors also identify shortcomings in existing instance and segmentation datasets and propose new benchmarks. These contributions address both representation choice and evaluation: strong personalization requires measuring whether a system finds the particular reference instance, especially when category-level recognition alone cannot resolve the task.
summary.tldr: PDM uses pretrained diffusion-model features without additional training to improve retrieval and segmentation of specific instances.

title: Where's Waldo: Diffusion Features For Personalized Segmentation and Retrieval

abstract: Large vision language models (LVLMs) integrate large language models (LLMs) with pre-trained vision encoders, thereby activating the perception capability of the model to understand image inputs for different queries and conduct subsequent reasoning. Improving this capability requires high-quality vision-language data, which is costly and labor-intensive to acquire. Self-training approaches have been effective in single-modal settings to alleviate the need for labeled data by leveraging model's own generation. However, effective self-training remains a challenge regarding the unique visual perception and reasoning capability of LVLMs. To address this, we introduce **S**elf-**T**raining on **I**mage **C**omprehension (**STIC**), which emphasizes a self-training approach specifically for image comprehension. First, the model self-constructs a preference dataset for image descriptions using unlabeled images. Preferred responses are generated through a step-by-step prompt, while dis-preferred responses are generated from either corrupted images or misleading prompts. To further self-improve reasoning on the extracted visual information, we let the model reuse a small portion of existing instruction-tuning data and append its self-generated image descriptions to the prompts. We validate the effectiveness of STIC across seven different benchmarks, demonstrating substantial performance gains of 4.0% on average while using 70% less supervised fine-tuning data than the current method. Further studies dive into various components of STIC and highlight its potential to leverage vast quantities of unlabeled images for self-training.

The paper designs a self-training procedure around these two needs, using the model’s own descriptions of unlabeled images as a source of training material.

This supports further reasoning over the extracted visual information. Across seven benchmarks, STIC reports average performance gains of 4.0% while using 70% less supervised fine-tuning data than the comparison method. Component studies further support its potential to make productive use of large collections of unlabeled images.
summary.tldr: STIC uses self-generated image-description preferences and reasoning prompts to improve vision-language models with substantially less supervised fine-tuning data.

title: Enhancing Large Vision Language Models with Self-Training on Image Comprehension

abstract: Drug-target interaction (DTI) prediction is crucial for identifying new therapeutics and detecting mechanisms of action. While structure-based methods accurately model physical interactions between a drug and its protein target, cell-based assays such as Cell Painting can better capture complex DTI interactions. This paper introduces MOTIVE, a Morphological cOmpound Target Interaction Graph dataset comprising Cell Painting features for 11,000 genes and 3,600 compounds, along with their relationships extracted from seven publicly available databases. We provide random, cold-source (new drugs), and cold-target (new genes) data splits to enable rigorous evaluation under realistic use cases. Our benchmark results show that graph neural networks that use Cell Painting features consistently outperform those that learn from graph structure alone, feature-based models, and topological heuristics. MOTIVE accelerates both graph ML research and drug discovery by promoting the development of more reliable DTI prediction models. MOTIVE resources are available at https://github.com/carpenter-singh-lab/motive.

MOTIVE provides a graph dataset for this task that combines recorded relationships with Cell Painting features. The motivation is that cell-based measurements can capture complex interaction effects that complement the physical interactions modeled by structure-based approaches.

The dataset contains Cell Painting features for 11,000 genes and 3,600 compounds, together with relationships drawn from seven public databases. It supplies random splits as well as cold-source and cold-target splits. The latter settings test predictions involving new drugs or new genes, making generalization to previously unseen entities an explicit part of evaluation.

This supports combining cellular features with relational information for the evaluated prediction tasks. MOTIVE’s contribution is both a biological graph resource and an evaluation setup for developing more reliable models of interactions involving unfamiliar compounds or genes.
summary.tldr: MOTIVE combines Cell Painting features and drug-target relationships to benchmark predictions, including interactions involving new drugs or genes.

title: MOTIVE: A Drug-Target Interaction Graph For Inductive Link Prediction

abstract: Designing efficient algorithms for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is fundamentally challenging because the size of the joint state and action spaces grows exponentially in the number of agents. These difficulties are exacerbated when balancing sequential global decision-making with local agent interactions. In this work, we propose a new algorithm $\texttt{SUBSAMPLE-MFQ}$ ($\textbf{Subsample}$-$\textbf{M}$ean-$\textbf{F}$ield-$\textbf{Q}$-learning) and a decentralized randomized policy for a system with $n$ agents. For any $k\leq n$, our algorithm learns a policy for the system in time polynomial in $k$. We prove that this learned policy converges to the optimal policy on the order of $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{k})$ as the number of subsampled agents $k$ increases. In particular, this bound is independent of the number of agents $n$.

These difficulties are exacerbated when balancing sequential global decision-making with local agent interactions. In this work, we propose a new algorithm $\texttt{SUBSAMPLE-MFQ}$ ($\textbf{Subsample}$-$\textbf{M}$ean-$\textbf{F}$ield-$\textbf{Q}$-learning) and a decentralized randomized policy for a system with $n$ agents. For any $k\leq n$, our algorithm learns a policy for the system in time polynomial in $k$. We prove that this learned policy converges to the optimal policy on the order of $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{k})$ as the number of subsampled agents $k$ increases. In particular, this bound is independent of the number of agents $n$.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning becomes difficult as the number of agents grows because their combined states and actions create exponentially large spaces. The problem also requires connecting global decisions over time with interactions among individual agents. This paper proposes SUBSAMPLE-MFQ and a decentralized randomized policy to address that scaling challenge.

For a system containing n agents, the algorithm uses a subsample of k agents, where k can be any value up to n. Its learning time is polynomial in k. The subsample size therefore provides a way to control the computational scale of learning while still obtaining a policy for the larger system.

The paper proves convergence toward the optimal policy at a rate of approximately one over the square root of k, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Crucially, this bound does not depend on the total agent count n. The result establishes a theoretical trade-off: increasing the sampled population improves the guarantee, while the stated learning cost depends polynomially on that sample size.
summary.tldr: SUBSAMPLE-MFQ learns cooperative policies with a convergence bound controlled by the sampled agent count rather than total population size.

title: Mean-Field Sampling for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A challenge in human-AI decision-making is to balance three factors: the *correctness* of predictions, the *cost* of knowledge and reasoning complexity, and the confidence about whether to *abstain* from automated answers or escalate to human experts. In this work, we present a cascaded LLM decision framework that adaptively delegates tasks across multiple tiers of expertise -- a base model for initial candidate answers, a more capable and knowledgeable (but costlier) large model, and a human expert for when the model cascade abstains. Our method proceeds in two stages. First, a deferral policy determines whether to accept the base model’s answer or regenerate it with the large model based on the confidence score. Second, an abstention policy decides whether the cascade model response is sufficiently certain or requires human intervention. Moreover, to overcome static policies and accommodate changing task difficulty, we incorporate an online learning mechanism which uses human feedback. We demonstrate this approach to general question-answering (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU) and medical question-answering (MedQA and MedMCQA). Our results demonstrate that our cascaded strategy outperforms single-model baselines in most cases, achieving higher accuracy while reducing costs and providing a principled approach to handling abstentions.

Then an abstention policy determines whether the cascade’s response is sufficiently certain to use or should be referred to a human. The findings support treating model escalation and human referral as coordinated but separate decisions, allowing the system to allocate more expertise when its confidence warrants it.
summary.tldr: A confidence-guided cascade routes questions between two language models and human experts to balance accuracy, cost, and abstention.

title: Cascaded Language Models for Cost-Effective Human–AI Decision-Making

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive generalization abilities, yet adapting them effectively across multiple heterogeneous domains remains challenging due to inter-domain interference. To overcome this challenge, we propose a partition-based multi-stage fine-tuning framework designed to exploit inter-domain synergies while minimizing negative transfer. Our approach strategically partitions domains into subsets (stages) by balancing domain discrepancy, synergy, and model capacity constraints. We theoretically analyze the proposed framework and derive novel generalization bounds that justify our partitioning strategy. Extensive empirical evaluations on various language understanding tasks show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Adapting one language model to several different domains can create interference: learning from one domain can hinder performance on another. This paper treats the organization of multi-domain fine-tuning as a way to manage that problem. It seeks to preserve beneficial relationships between domains while reducing negative transfer.

The proposed framework partitions domains into subsets used as stages of fine-tuning. The partitioning balances three considerations: differences between domains, opportunities for mutual benefit, and the model’s capacity constraints. This makes the grouping decision central to adaptation. A useful partition must account for what domains can contribute to one another as well as how different they are.

The authors derive generalization bounds that support their partitioning strategy and evaluate the framework on multiple language-understanding tasks. They report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in those evaluations. The contribution combines a theoretically motivated way to organize training domains with empirical evidence that staged grouping can improve multi-domain adaptation, rather than treating domain differences alone as the deciding factor.
summary.tldr: Partitioning domains into fine-tuning stages balances synergy, discrepancy, and model capacity to reduce interference and improve evaluated language-understanding performance.

title: Synergy over Discrepancy: A Partition-Based Approach to Multi-Domain LLM Fine-Tuning

abstract: Learning effective multi-modal 3D representations of objects is essential for numerous applications, such as augmented reality and robotics. Existing methods often rely on task-specific embeddings that are tailored either for semantic understanding or geometric reconstruction. As a result, these embeddings typically cannot be decoded into explicit geometry and simultaneously reused across tasks. In this paper, we propose Object-X, a versatile multi-modal object representation framework capable of encoding rich object embeddings (e.g., images, point cloud, text) and decoding them back into detailed geometric and visual reconstructions. Object-X operates by geometrically grounding the captured modalities in a 3D voxel grid and learning an unstructured embedding fusing the information from the voxels with the object attributes. The learned embedding enables 3D Gaussian Splatting-based object reconstruction, while also supporting a range of downstream tasks, including scene alignment, single-image 3D object reconstruction, and localization. Evaluations on two challenging real-world datasets demonstrate that Object-X produces high-fidelity novel-view synthesis comparable to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, while significantly improving geometric accuracy. Moreover, Object-X achieves competitive performance with specialized methods in scene alignment and localization. Critically, our object-centric descriptors require 3-4 orders of magnitude less storage compared to traditional image- or point cloud-based approaches, establishing Object-X as a scalable and highly practical solution for multi-modal 3D scene representation.

summary.tldr: Object-X compresses multimodal object information into reusable embeddings that support detailed 3D reconstruction, alignment, and localization.

title: Object-X: Learning to Reconstruct Multi-Modal 3D Object Representations

abstract: Large-scale vision foundation models such as DINOv2 boast impressive performances by leveraging massive architectures and training datasets. The expense of large-scale pre-training puts such research out of reach for many, hence limiting scientific advancements. We thus propose a novel pretraining strategy for DINOv2 that simultaneously accelerates convergence–and strengthens robustness to common corruptions as a by-product. Our approach involves a frequency filtering curriculum–low-frequency being seen first–and the Gaussian noise patching augmentation. Applied to a ViT-B/16 backbone trained on ImageNet-1K, while pre-training time is reduced by 1.6×–from 16.64 to 10.32 NVIDIA L40S days–and FLOPs by 2.25×, our method still achieves matching robustness in corruption benchmarks (ImageNet-C) and maintains competitive linear probing performance compared with the DINOv2 baseline. This dual benefit of efficiency and robustness makes large-scale self-supervised foundation modeling more attainable, while opening the door to novel exploration around data curriculum and augmentation as a means to improve self-supervised learning models robustness.

paragraphs: Training large vision models demands substantial computation, limiting who can study and develop them. FastDINOv2 investigates whether changing the presentation of training images can make DINOv2 pretraining more efficient while retaining useful representations and robustness. Its focus is the training procedure rather than simply increasing model or dataset size.

The approach combines a frequency-based curriculum with Gaussian noise patching. The curriculum presents low-frequency image information first, organizing learning around the order in which visual frequencies become available. Noise patching provides an additional augmentation. Together, these changes are intended to accelerate convergence and strengthen resistance to common image corruptions.

For a ViT-B/16 trained on ImageNet-1K, pretraining falls from 16.64 to 10.32 NVIDIA L40S days, a reported 1.6-fold reduction, while FLOPs decrease by a factor of 2.25. In that configuration, corruption robustness on ImageNet-C matches the DINOv2 baseline and linear-probing performance remains competitive. The concrete result is therefore reduced training cost while preserving these capabilities, supporting curriculum and augmentation as useful efficiency tools.
summary.tldr: FastDINOv2 reduces pretraining cost through frequency ordering and noise augmentation while matching corruption robustness in the reported configuration.

title: FastDINOv2: Frequency Based Curriculum Learning Improves Robustness and Training Speed

abstract: Recent years have seen a surge in interest in digital content watermarking techniques, driven by the proliferation of generative models and increased legal pressure. With an ever-growing percentage of AI-generated content available online, watermarking plays an increasingly important role in ensuring content authenticity and attribution at scale. There have been many works assessing the robustness of watermarking to removal attacks, yet, watermark forging, the scenario when a watermark is stolen from genuine content and applied to malicious content, remains underexplored. In this work, we investigate watermark forging in the context of widely used post-hoc image watermarking. Our contributions are as follows. First, we introduce a preference model to assess whether an image is watermarked. The model is trained using a ranking loss on purely procedurally generated images without any need for real watermarks. Second, we demonstrate the model's capability to remove and forge watermarks by optimizing the input image through backpropagation. This technique requires only a single watermarked image and works without knowledge of the watermarking model, making our attack much simpler and more practical than attacks introduced in related work. Third, we evaluate our proposed method on a variety of post-hoc image watermarking models, demonstrating that our approach can effectively forge watermarks, questioning the security of current watermarking approaches. Our code and further resources are publicly available.

This paper examines forging: transferring a watermark from genuine content to other content. That threat matters because a watermark can be misleading even when it remains detectable, if its presence no longer reliably indicates the claimed origin.

The authors introduce an image preference model that estimates whether an image is watermarked. It is trained with a ranking loss using procedurally generated images, without requiring real watermarks for training. They then demonstrate watermark removal and forgery through image optimization guided by the model. The attack uses a single watermarked reference image and does not require knowledge of the watermarking model.

Evaluation spans multiple post-hoc image watermarking models and demonstrates effective forgery. These findings identify an attribution weakness in the tested approaches and broaden the security question beyond resistance to removal. The contribution is especially relevant to practical evaluation because the demonstrated attack needs limited access: one marked image and no internal knowledge of the target watermarking system.
summary.tldr: A preference model trained without real watermarks enables black-box watermark forgery from one marked image across multiple tested watermarking systems.

title: Transferable Black-Box One-Shot Forging of Watermarks via Image Preference Models

abstract: Although COLMAP has long remained the predominant method for camera parameter optimization in static scenes, it is constrained by its lengthy runtime and reliance on ground truth (GT) motion masks for application to dynamic scenes. Many efforts attempted to improve it by incorporating more priors as supervision such as GT focal length, motion masks, 3D point clouds, camera poses, and metric depth, which, however, are typically unavailable in casually captured RGB videos. In this paper, we propose a novel method for more accurate and efficient camera parameter optimization in dynamic scenes solely supervised by a single RGB video, dubbed $\textbf{\textit{ROS-Cam}}$. Our method consists of three key components: (1) Patch-wise Tracking Filters, to establish robust and maximally sparse hinge-like relations across the RGB video. (2) Outlier-aware Joint Optimization, for efficient camera parameter optimization by adaptive down-weighting of moving outliers, without reliance on motion priors. (3) A Two-stage Optimization Strategy, to enhance stability and optimization speed by a trade-off between the Softplus limits and convex minima in losses. We visually and numerically evaluate our camera estimates. To further validate accuracy, we feed the camera estimates into a 4D reconstruction method and assess the resulting 3D scenes, and rendered 2D RGB and depth maps. We perform experiments on 4 real-world datasets (NeRF-DS, DAVIS, iPhone, and TUM-dynamics) and 1 synthetic dataset (MPI-Sintel), demonstrating that our method estimates camera parameters more efficiently and accurately with a single RGB video as the only supervision.

Existing approaches often use additional supervision, such as motion masks, known poses, or depth, that casually captured videos do not provide. ROS-Cam estimates camera parameters using a single RGB video as its only supervision, aiming to improve both accuracy and efficiency in dynamic scenes.

The authors assess camera estimates directly, then use them in a 4D reconstruction method and examine the resulting scenes and rendered color and depth maps. These checks connect camera estimation to the reconstruction it supports. The reported results show more accurate and efficient estimation with RGB video alone as supervision.
summary.tldr: ROS-Cam improves camera estimation in dynamic scenes using only RGB-video supervision and adaptively reducing the influence of moving outliers.

title: RGB-Only Supervised Camera Parameter Optimization in Dynamic Scenes

abstract: Despite the remarkable advances of Large Language Models (LLMs) across diverse cognitive tasks, the rapid enhancement of these capabilities also introduces emergent deception behaviors that may induce severe risks in high-stakes deployments. More critically, the characterization of deception across realistic real-world scenarios remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we establish **DeceptionBench**, the first benchmark that systematically evaluates how deceptive tendencies manifest across different societal domains, what their intrinsic behavioral patterns are, and how extrinsic factors affect them. Specifically, on the static count, the benchmark encompasses 150 meticulously designed scenarios in five domains, *i.e.*, *Economy, Healthcare, Education, Social Interaction, and Entertainment*, with over 1,000 samples, providing sufficient empirical foundations for deception analysis. On the intrinsic dimension, we explore whether models exhibit self-interested egoistic tendencies or sycophantic behaviors that prioritize user appeasement. On the extrinsic dimension, we investigate how contextual factors modulate deceptive outputs under neutral conditions, reward-based incentivization, and coercive pressures. Moreover, we incorporate sustained multi-turn interaction loops to construct a more realistic simulation of real-world feedback dynamics. Extensive experiments across LLMs and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) reveal critical vulnerabilities, particularly amplified deception under reinforcement dynamics, demonstrating that current models lack robust resistance to manipulative contextual cues and the urgent need for advanced safeguards against various deception behaviors. Code and resources are publicly available at https://github.com/Aries-iai/DeceptionBench.

Its focus is broader than whether a model produces a false statement: it examines patterns of deception and the circumstances that influence them. The benchmark contains 150 scenarios and more than 1,000 samples across economy, healthcare, education, social interaction, and entertainment.

It also varies external conditions, comparing neutral contexts with reward incentives and coercive pressure. Sustained interactions across multiple turns add feedback dynamics, allowing the benchmark to examine how behavior develops as a conversation continues rather than only testing isolated responses.

Experiments with language models and reasoning models reveal vulnerabilities, including stronger deception under reinforcing feedback. The findings indicate that the tested models do not reliably resist manipulative contextual cues. By connecting behavioral tendencies with incentives and conversational feedback, the benchmark provides a structured way to investigate when deceptive outputs become more likely and motivates safeguards that account for the surrounding interaction.
summary.tldr: DeceptionBench tests deception across five societal domains and finds that incentives and reinforcing interactions can amplify deceptive model behavior.

title: DeceptionBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for AI Deception Behaviors in Real-world Scenarios

abstract: In Bayesian persuasion, an informed sender strategically discloses information to a receiver so as to persuade them to undertake desirable actions. Recently, Markov persuasion processes (MPPs) have been introduced to capture sequential scenarios where a sender faces a stream of myopic receivers in a Markovian environment. The MPPs studied so far in the literature suffer from issues that prevent them from being fully operational in practice, e.g., they assume that the sender knows receivers' rewards. We fix such issues by addressing MPPs where the sender has no knowledge about the environment. We design a learning algorithm for the sender, working with partial feedback. We prove that its regret with respect to an optimal information-disclosure policy grows sublinearly in the number of episodes, as it is the case for the loss in persuasiveness cumulated while learning. Moreover, we provide lower bounds for our setting matching the guarantees of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender chooses what information to reveal in order to influence a receiver’s actions. Markov persuasion processes extend this to sequential environments with a stream of receivers focused on immediate outcomes. Earlier formulations assume knowledge, such as receivers’ rewards, that may be unavailable to a sender trying to learn in practice.

This paper studies a sender who begins without knowledge of the environment and receives only partial feedback. The authors design a learning algorithm for choosing information-disclosure policies under those conditions. Its analysis tracks both regret relative to an optimal disclosure policy and the accumulated loss in persuasiveness incurred while the sender is still learning.

Both quantities are proved to grow sublinearly with the number of episodes. This means their per-episode averages diminish as learning proceeds, rather than requiring perfect persuasion from the outset. The authors also establish matching lower bounds for the setting. Those bounds indicate that the algorithm’s guarantees match the fundamental difficulty of the problem as formulated.
summary.tldr: A sender can learn sequential information-disclosure policies from partial feedback with provably sublinear regret and accumulated loss of persuasiveness.

title: Markov Persuasion Processes: Learning to Persuade From Scratch

abstract: We propose Shallow Flow Matching (SFM), a novel mechanism that enhances flow matching (FM)-based text-to-speech (TTS) models within a coarse-to-fine generation paradigm. Unlike conventional FM modules, which use the coarse representations from the weak generator as conditions, SFM constructs intermediate states along the FM paths from these representations. During training, we introduce an orthogonal projection method to adaptively determine the temporal position of these states, and apply a principled construction strategy based on a single-segment piecewise flow. The SFM inference starts from the intermediate state rather than pure noise, thereby focusing computation on the latter stages of the FM paths. We integrate SFM into multiple TTS models with a lightweight SFM head. Experiments demonstrate that SFM yields consistent gains in speech naturalness across both objective and subjective evaluations, and significantly accelerates inference when using adaptive-step ODE solvers. Demo and codes are available at https://ydqmkkx.github.io/SFMDemo/.

paragraphs: Coarse-to-fine speech synthesis first produces a rough representation and then improves it. In conventional flow-matching systems, the rough representation conditions a generation process that begins from noise. Shallow Flow Matching changes how that initial output is used: it constructs a state partway along the flow path, giving refinement a more advanced starting point.

During training, an orthogonal projection method adaptively determines where that intermediate state should sit along the path. A construction based on a single-segment piecewise flow supports this formulation. At inference, generation begins from the constructed intermediate state, concentrating computation on the later part of the transformation instead of traversing the full path from pure noise.

The authors integrate this mechanism into multiple text-to-speech systems using a lightweight prediction head. Experiments show consistent improvements in speech naturalness under both objective measurements and subjective evaluation. They also report substantial inference acceleration when adaptive-step ODE solvers are used. The findings suggest that a coarse generator can contribute more directly to refinement by providing its starting state, improving speech quality while reducing computation in the evaluated solver setting.
summary.tldr: Shallow Flow Matching starts speech refinement partway along a generation path, improving naturalness and accelerating inference with adaptive-step solvers.

title: Shallow Flow Matching for Coarse-to-Fine Text-to-Speech Synthesis

abstract: Most work on adaptive data analysis assumes that samples in the dataset are independent. When correlations are allowed, even the non-adaptive setting can become intractable, unless some structural constraints are imposed. To address this, Bassily and Freund [2016] introduced the elegant framework of *concentrated queries*, which requires the analyst to restrict itself to queries that are concentrated around their expected value. While this assumption makes the problem trivial in the non-adaptive setting, in the adaptive setting it remains quite challenging. In fact, all known algorithms in this framework support significantly fewer queries than in the independent case: At most $O(n)$ queries for a sample of size $n$, compared to $O(n^2)$ in the independent setting. In this work, we prove that this utility gap is inherent under the current formulation of the concentrated queries framework, assuming some natural conditions on the algorithm. Additionally, we present a simplified version of the best-known algorithms that match our impossibility result.

To address this, Bassily and Freund [2016] introduced the elegant framework of *concentrated queries*, which requires the analyst to restrict itself to queries that are concentrated around their expected value. While this assumption makes the problem trivial in the non-adaptive setting, in the adaptive setting it remains quite challenging. In fact, all known algorithms in this framework support significantly fewer queries than in the independent case: At most $O(n)$ queries for a sample of size $n$, compared to $O(n^2)$ in the independent setting. In this work, we prove that this utility gap is inherent under the current formulation of the concentrated queries framework, assuming some natural conditions on the algorithm. Additionally, we present a simplified version of the best-known algorithms that match our impossibility result.

paragraphs: Adaptive data analysis lets an analyst choose later questions using answers to earlier ones. Most theory assumes independent data samples, but correlations can make accurate analysis difficult even when questions are fixed in advance. The concentrated-query framework addresses this by restricting attention to queries whose values stay close to their expectations.

That restriction makes the non-adaptive problem straightforward, yet adaptive querying remains harder. Previously known methods in this framework support at most O(n) queries from n samples, compared with O(n²) in the independent setting. The paper asks whether this difference reflects inadequate algorithms or a genuine constraint imposed by the framework.

The authors prove that the gap is inherent under the current concentrated-query formulation, assuming certain natural conditions on the algorithm. They also present a simpler version of the best known algorithms that matches the impossibility result. Together, the lower and upper bounds identify what is achievable within the stated setting, explaining why concentration alone does not recover the adaptive-query capacity associated with independent samples.
summary.tldr: Under stated algorithmic conditions, the paper proves that concentrated queries retain an inherent adaptive-query gap from the independent-data setting.

title: Tight Bounds for Answering Adaptively Chosen Concentrated Queries

abstract: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) plays a foundational role in modern manufacturing and product development, often requiring designers to modify or build upon existing models. Converting 3D scans into parametric CAD representations—a process known as CAD reverse engineering—remains a significant challenge due to the high precision and structural complexity of CAD models. Existing deep learning-based approaches typically fall into two categories: bottom-up, geometry-driven methods, which often fail to produce fully parametric outputs, and top-down strategies, which tend to overlook fine-grained geometric details. Moreover, current methods neglect an essential aspect of CAD modeling: sketch-level constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to CAD reverse engineering inspired by how human designers manually perform the task. Our method leverages multi-plane cross-sections to extract 2D patterns and capture fine parametric details more effectively. It enables the reconstruction of detailed and editable CAD models, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and, for the first time, incorporating sketch constraints directly into the reconstruction process.

paragraphs: Turning a 3D scan into a useful CAD model requires recovering more than visible shape. Designers need a precise representation they can modify through parameters, together with the structural relationships that make those edits meaningful. Existing learning-based reconstruction methods can struggle either to produce fully parametric models or to preserve fine geometric details.

MiCADangelo takes inspiration from how human designers approach reverse engineering. It extracts cross-sections on multiple planes and uses the resulting 2D patterns to recover detailed parametric structure. This gives the reconstruction process a way to examine fine shape information through sectional views rather than relying only on a broad representation of the whole object.

They report detailed, editable CAD outputs and performance exceeding existing leading methods. The contribution brings geometric detail and constrained parametric structure into the same reconstruction process, addressing the practical requirement that a recovered model should remain useful for subsequent design changes.
summary.tldr: MiCADangelo reconstructs detailed, editable CAD models from 3D scans using multiple cross-sections and explicit sketch constraints.

title: MiCADangelo: Fine-Grained Reconstruction of Constrained CAD Models from 3D Scans

abstract: Foundation models have enabled rapid progress across many specialized domains by leveraging large-scale pre-training on unlabeled data, demonstrating strong generalization to a variety of downstream tasks. While such models have gained significant attention in fields like Earth Observation, their application to Mars science remains limited. A key enabler of progress in other domains has been the availability of standardized benchmarks that support systematic evaluation. In contrast, Mars science lacks such benchmarks and standardized evaluation frameworks, which have limited progress toward developing foundation models for Martian tasks. To address this gap, we introduce Mars-Bench, the first benchmark designed to systematically evaluate models across a broad range of Mars-related tasks using both orbital and surface imagery. Mars-Bench comprises 20 datasets spanning classification, segmentation, and object detection, focused on key geologic features such as craters, cones, boulders, and frost. We provide standardized, ready-to-use datasets and baseline evaluations using models pre-trained on natural images, Earth satellite data, and state-of-the-art vision-language models. Results from all analyses suggest that Mars-specific foundation models may offer advantages over general-domain counterparts, motivating further exploration of domain-adapted pre-training. Mars-Bench aims to establish a standardized foundation for developing and comparing machine learning models for Mars science. Our data, models, and code are available at: https://mars-bench.github.io/.

Without standardized tasks and datasets, it is harder to compare approaches systematically or assess whether existing pretrained models transfer effectively. Mars-Bench provides a shared evaluation resource for this setting.

The benchmark contains 20 datasets covering both orbital and surface imagery. These tasks examine different capabilities: recognizing image content, identifying regions, and locating objects. The authors provide ready-to-use datasets and baseline evaluations.

Across the analyses, the results suggest that Mars-specific foundation models may have advantages over general-domain models. That finding motivates further investigation of pretraining adapted to Martian data; it does not establish that specialization will always win. The benchmark's broader contribution is a consistent basis for developing and comparing models across multiple Mars-science tasks.
summary.tldr: Mars-Bench standardizes evaluation across 20 Mars-imagery datasets and motivates further study of Mars-specific pretraining.

title: Mars-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models for Mars Science Tasks

abstract: We consider the problem of detecting a community of densely connected vertices in a high-dimensional bipartite graph of size $n_1 \times n_2$. Under the null hypothesis, the observed graph is drawn from a bipartite Erdos-Renyi distribution with connection probability $p_0$. Under the alternative hypothesis, there exists an unknown bipartite subgraph of size $k_1 \times k_2$ in which edges appear with probability $p_1 = p_0 + \delta$ for some $\delta > 0$, while all other edges outside the subgraph appear with probability $p_0$. Specifically, we provide non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the smallest signal strength $\delta^*$ that is both necessary and sufficient to ensure the existence of a test with small enough type one and type two errors. We also derive novel minimax-optimal tests achieving these fundamental limits when the underlying graph is sufficiently dense. Our proposed tests involve a combination of hard-thresholded nonlinear statistics of the adjacency matrix, the analysis of which may be of independent interest. In contrast with previous work, our non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds match for any configuration of $n_1,n_2, k_1,k_2$.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a densely connected community can be detected inside a bipartite graph. Under the no-community hypothesis, every possible edge has probability p0. Under the alternative, an unknown subgraph has a higher edge probability, p0 plus a positive increase, while the remaining edges retain the background probability.

The main goal is to characterize how large that increase must be for a test to keep both false alarms and missed detections sufficiently small. The authors derive non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on this detection threshold. These bounds match across all configurations of the two graph dimensions and the two community dimensions considered in the model.

For sufficiently dense graphs, the paper also constructs minimax-optimal tests that reach the fundamental detection limits. The tests combine hard-thresholded nonlinear statistics of the adjacency matrix. The contribution therefore connects an information-theoretic question about detectability with concrete statistical tests, while retaining the stated density condition for the optimality result.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes matching detection thresholds for bipartite communities and develops optimal tests when the graph is sufficiently dense.

title: Optimal community detection in dense bipartite graphs

abstract: Diffusion models produce realistic images and videos but require substantial computational resources, necessitating multi-accelerator parallelism for real-time deployment. However, parallel inference introduces significant communication overhead from exchanging large activations between devices, limiting efficiency and scalability. We present CompactFusion, a compression framework that significantly reduces communication while preserving generation quality. Our key observation is that diffusion activations exhibit strong temporal redundancy—adjacent steps produce highly similar activations, saturating bandwidth with near-duplicate data carrying little new information. To address this inefficiency, we seek a more compact representation that encodes only the essential information. CompactFusion achieves this via Residual Compression that transmits only compressed residuals (step-wise activation differences). Based on empirical analysis and theoretical justification, we show that it effectively removes redundant data, enabling substantial data reduction while maintaining high fidelity. We also integrate lightweight error feedback to prevent error accumulation. CompactFusion establishes a new paradigm for parallel diffusion inference, delivering lower latency and significantly higher generation quality than prior methods. On 4$\times$L20, it achieves $3.0\times$ speedup while greatly improving fidelity. It also uniquely supports communication-heavy strategies like sequence parallelism on slow networks, achieving $6.7\times$ speedup over prior overlap-based method. CompactFusion applies broadly across diffusion models and parallel settings, and integrates easily without requiring pipeline rework. Portable implementation demonstrated on xDiT is publicly available at https://github.com/Cobalt-27/CompactFusion

paragraphs: Running diffusion generation across several accelerators creates a communication problem: devices repeatedly exchange large intermediate activations. CompactFusion starts from the observation that activations at neighboring diffusion steps are highly similar. Sending them in full therefore consumes bandwidth on information that has largely already been communicated, limiting the benefit of distributing computation.

The framework instead transmits compressed residuals, meaning the differences between activations at successive steps. This targets the new information introduced at each step. Lightweight error feedback addresses the accumulation of compression errors. The paper supports this design with empirical analysis and theoretical justification, reporting substantial reductions in transmitted data while maintaining generation fidelity.

On four L20 accelerators, CompactFusion reports a threefold speedup alongside improved fidelity. For communication-heavy sequence parallelism on slow networks, it reports a 6.7-fold speedup over a prior overlap-based method. These results show how exploiting redundancy across diffusion steps can improve distributed serving. The framework is presented as applicable across models and parallel configurations, with integration that does not require redesigning the serving pipeline.
summary.tldr: CompactFusion accelerates distributed diffusion inference by communicating compressed changes between steps instead of repeatedly sending similar activations.

title: Accelerating Parallel Diffusion Model Serving with Residual Compression

abstract: The statistical consistency of surrogate losses for discrete prediction tasks is often checked using the condition of calibration. However, directly verifying calibration can be arduous. Recent work shows that for polyhedral surrogates, a less arduous condition, indirect elicitation (IE), is still equivalent to calibration. We give the first results of this type for non-polyhedral surrogates, specifically the class of convex differentiable losses. We first prove that under mild conditions, IE and calibration are equivalent for one-dimensional losses in this class. We construct a counter-example that shows that this equivalence fails in higher dimensions. This motivates the introduction of strong IE, a strengthened form of IE that is equally easy to verify. We establish that strong IE implies calibration for differentiable surrogates and is both necessary and sufficient for strongly convex, differentiable surrogates. Finally, we apply these results to a range of problems to demonstrate the power of IE and strong IE for designing and analyzing consistent differentiable surrogates.

paragraphs: Discrete prediction tasks are often trained using a smoother substitute objective, called a surrogate loss. A central question is whether optimizing that substitute leads to the right predictions for the original task. Calibration is a standard way to establish this connection, but checking it directly can be difficult. The paper investigates simpler conditions for convex, differentiable losses.

The first result concerns indirect elicitation, or IE. Under mild conditions, IE is equivalent to calibration for one-dimensional losses in this class. However, the authors construct a counterexample showing that the equivalence does not extend generally to higher dimensions. This makes dimensionality a substantive boundary for the simpler test.

The authors then introduce strong IE, a strengthened condition described as equally easy to verify. They prove that it implies calibration for differentiable surrogates. For strongly convex, differentiable surrogates, it is both necessary and sufficient. Applications across several problems demonstrate how these conditions can help researchers design and analyze consistent training objectives without always checking calibration directly.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes simpler calibration tests for differentiable surrogate losses, with guarantees that depend on dimension and convexity.

title: Consistency Conditions for Differentiable Surrogate Losses

abstract: Leveraging multimodal large models for image segmentation has become a prominent research direction. However, existing approaches typically rely heavily on manually annotated datasets that include explicit reasoning processes, which are costly and time-consuming to produce. Recent advances suggest that reinforcement learning (RL) can endow large models with reasoning capabilities without requiring such reasoning-annotated data. In this paper, we propose SAM-R1, a novel framework that enables multimodal large models to perform fine-grained reasoning in image understanding tasks. Our approach is the first to incorporate fine-grained segmentation settings during the training of multimodal reasoning models. By integrating task-specific, fine-grained rewards with a tailored optimization objective, we further enhance the model's reasoning and segmentation alignment. We also leverage the Segment Anything Model (SAM) as a strong and flexible reward provider to guide the learning process. With only 3k training samples, SAM-R1 achieves strong performance across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in equipping multimodal models with segmentation-oriented reasoning capabilities.
