paragraphs: Training multimodal models for segmentation often depends on manually prepared data that include explicit reasoning processes. Producing such annotations is costly and time-consuming. SAM-R1 explores reinforcement learning as a way to develop fine-grained image understanding and segmentation-oriented reasoning without depending on that form of reasoning annotation.

The framework incorporates fine-grained segmentation into multimodal reasoning training. It combines task-specific rewards with an optimization objective designed to align reasoning and segmentation. The Segment Anything Model, or SAM, acts as a flexible reward provider, supplying feedback that guides the learning process toward the segmentation task.

Using only 3,000 training samples, SAM-R1 achieves strong performance across multiple benchmarks. The reported result supports the effectiveness of reinforcement learning for teaching segmentation-oriented reasoning with a relatively small training set. Its main contribution is the connection between a segmentation model that provides rewards and a multimodal model learning to reason: the feedback is tied directly to the fine-grained visual task the model is intended to perform.
summary.tldr: SAM-R1 uses SAM-provided rewards to train segmentation-oriented multimodal reasoning, achieving strong benchmark performance with 3,000 training samples.

title: SAM-R1: Leveraging SAM for Reward Feedback in Multimodal Segmentation via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Neural network architectures have a large impact in machine learning. However, in the specific case of reinforcement learning, network architectures have remained notably simple, as changes often lead to small gains in performance. This work introduces a novel encoder architecture for pixel-based model-free reinforcement learning. The Hadamax (\textbf{Hada}mard \textbf{max}-pooling) encoder achieves state-of-the-art performance by max-pooling Hadamard products between GELU-activated parallel hidden layers. Based on the recent PQN algorithm, the Hadamax encoder achieves state-of-the-art model-free performance in the Atari-57 benchmark. Specifically, without applying any algorithmic hyperparameter modifications, Hadamax-PQN achieves an 80\% performance gain over vanilla PQN and significantly surpasses Rainbow-DQN. For reproducibility, the full code is available on GitHub.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how much a change in neural-network architecture can improve reinforcement learning from pixels. Although architecture choices strongly influence many learning systems, reinforcement-learning networks have often remained simple because modifications produce only modest gains. The authors introduce Hadamax, an encoder intended to improve the representation learned from visual input in model-free reinforcement learning.

Hadamax combines parallel hidden layers after applying GELU activations. It forms Hadamard products, meaning element-by-element multiplication of their outputs, and applies max pooling to those products. These operations define the encoder’s distinctive way of combining features. The researchers integrate the encoder with the existing PQN learning algorithm to form Hadamax-PQN.

On Atari-57, the combined system achieves reported state-of-the-art model-free performance. The abstract reports an 80% performance improvement over standard PQN and a substantial advantage over Rainbow-DQN, without modifying the algorithm’s hyperparameters. This comparison makes the encoder change central to the reported improvement. The findings show that architecture can deliver substantial gains in this evaluated setting, and the authors release their implementation for reproducibility.
summary.tldr: Hadamax combines multiplicative features and max pooling to improve PQN’s reported Atari-57 performance by 80% without algorithmic hyperparameter changes.

title: Hadamax Encoding: Elevating Performance in Model-Free Atari

abstract: Conventional video outpainting methods primarily focus on maintaining coherent textures and visual consistency across frames. However, they often fail at handling dynamic scenes due to the complex motion of objects or camera movement, leading to temporal incoherence and visible flickering artifacts across frames. This is primarily because they lack instance-aware modeling to accurately separate and track individual object motions throughout the video. In this paper, we propose a novel video outpainting framework that explicitly takes shadow-object pairs into consideration to enhance the temporal and spatial consistency of instances, even when they are temporarily invisible. Specifically, we first track the shadow-object pairs across frames and predict the instances in the scene to unveil the spatial regions of invisible instances. Then, these prediction results are fed to guide the instance-aware optical flow completion to unveil the temporal motion of invisible instances. Next, these spatiotemporal guidances of instances are used to guide the video outpainting process. Finally, a video-aware discriminator is implemented to enhance alignment among dynamic shadows and the extended semantics in the scene. Comprehensive experiments underscore the superiority of our approach, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in widely recognized benchmarks.

paragraphs: Video outpainting extends a video beyond its original visible region. Keeping textures plausible is only part of the problem: objects and cameras move, and generated content must remain consistent across frames. This paper attributes common flickering and temporal inconsistencies to insufficient modeling of individual objects and their motion.

The proposed framework tracks objects together with their shadows. These pairs provide information for predicting where an instance occupies space even when it is temporarily invisible. The predictions then guide instance-aware optical-flow completion, which estimates the missing motion information. Together, the predicted locations and movements guide the outpainting process across space and time.

A video-aware discriminator further encourages agreement between moving shadows and the generated scene content. The approach matters because a shadow can contribute evidence about an object beyond the currently visible object itself. Experiments on established benchmarks report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, supporting the use of explicit shadow-object relationships to improve spatial and temporal consistency in dynamic video extensions.
summary.tldr: Tracking objects with their shadows helps video outpainting preserve the locations and motion of temporarily invisible instances.

title: Dynamic Shadow Unveils Invisible Semantics for Video Outpainting

abstract: Benchmarks are essential for quantitatively tracking progress in AI. As AI agents become increasingly capable, researchers and practitioners have introduced agentic benchmarks to evaluate agents on complex, real-world tasks. These benchmarks typically measure agent capabilities by evaluating task outcomes via specific reward designs. However, we show that many agentic benchmarks have issues in task setup or reward design. For example, SWE-bench-Verified uses insufficient test cases, while $\tau$-bench counts empty responses as successes. Such issues can lead to under- or overestimation of agents’ performance by up to 100% in relative terms. To make agentic evaluation rigorous, we introduce the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC), a set of guidelines that we synthesized from our benchmark-building experience, a survey of best practices, and previously reported issues. When applied to CVE-Bench, a benchmark with a particularly complex evaluation design, ABC reduces performance overestimation by 33%.

paragraphs: Benchmarks for AI agents judge performance by checking task outcomes through reward rules. This paper shows that problems in the task setup or those rules can distort the resulting scores. The issue matters because an apparent change in agent capability may instead reflect what an evaluation mistakenly accepts or fails to recognize.

The authors identify concrete examples: SWE-bench-Verified has insufficient test cases, and τ-bench can count empty responses as successful. Across the issues examined, performance can be underestimated or overestimated by as much as 100% in relative terms. These findings connect evaluation validity to the specific checks used to decide whether an agent has completed its task.

To improve benchmark construction, the paper introduces the Agentic Benchmark Checklist. It combines the authors' benchmark-building experience, a survey of best practices, and previously reported problems into guidelines. Applying the checklist to CVE-Bench, which has a particularly complex evaluation design, reduces performance overestimation by 33%. The result demonstrates a practical use of the checklist for improving the reliability of reported agent performance.
summary.tldr: The Agentic Benchmark Checklist addresses task and reward-design flaws that can substantially distort reported AI-agent performance.

title: Establishing Best Practices in Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks

abstract: Understanding the predictions made by deep learning models remains a central challenge, especially in high-stakes applications. A promising approach is to equip models with the ability to answer counterfactual questions -- hypothetical ``what if?'' scenarios that go beyond the observed data and provide insight into a model reasoning. In this work, we introduce the notion of causal interpretability, which formalizes when counterfactual queries can be evaluated from a specific class of models and observational data. We analyze two common model classes -- blackbox and concept-based predictors -- and show that neither is causally interpretable in general. To address this gap, we develop a framework for building models that are causally interpretable by design. Specifically, we derive a complete graphical criterion that determines whether a given model architecture supports a given counterfactual query. This leads to a fundamental tradeoff between causal interpretability and predictive accuracy, which we characterize by identifying the unique maximal set of features that yields an interpretable model with maximal predictive expressiveness. Experiments corroborate the theoretical findings.

Representing predictions through concepts therefore does not by itself settle counterfactual questions. They develop a framework for designing causally interpretable models and derive a complete graphical criterion for deciding whether an architecture supports a given query.

The analysis exposes a tradeoff between causal interpretability and predictive accuracy. To characterize it, the authors identify a unique maximal feature set that preserves interpretability while providing maximal predictive expressiveness. Experiments corroborate the theory. The contribution is a principled way to connect architecture, available features, and the counterfactual questions a model can support, rather than treating interpretability as an undifferentiated property.
summary.tldr: A graphical criterion identifies which counterfactual questions a model architecture can support and characterizes the associated predictive tradeoff.

title: From Black-box to Causal-box: Towards Building More Interpretable Models

abstract: Designing efficient reward functions for low-level control tasks is a challenging problem. Recent research aims to reduce reliance on expert experience by using Large Language Models (LLMs) with task information to generate dense reward functions. These methods typically rely on training results as feedback, iteratively generating new reward functions with greedy or evolutionary algorithms. However, they suffer from poor utilization of historical feedback and inefficient search, resulting in limited improvements in complex control tasks. To address this challenge, we propose RF-Agent, a framework that treats LLMs as language agents and frames reward function design as a sequential decision-making process, enhancing optimization through better contextual reasoning. RF-Agent integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to manage the reward design and optimization process, leveraging the multi-stage contextual reasoning ability of LLM. This approach better utilizes historical information and improves search efficiency to identify promising reward functions. Outstanding experimental results in 17 diverse low-level control tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

Historical feedback becomes part of the reasoning used to identify promising reward functions, rather than simply prompting another isolated revision.

The authors evaluate the framework on 17 diverse low-level control tasks and report strong results supporting its effectiveness. By connecting successive design decisions with accumulated feedback, RF-Agent aims to make reward optimization more efficient and better suited to complex control tasks.
summary.tldr: RF-Agent combines language-model reasoning with Monte Carlo Tree Search to use historical feedback more effectively when designing control rewards.

title: RF-Agent: Automated Reward Function Design via Language Agent Tree Search

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are powerful models for node classification, but their performance is heavily reliant on manually labeled data, which is often costly and results in insufficient labeling. Recent studies have shown that message-passing neural networks struggle to propagate information in low-degree nodes, negatively affecting overall performance. To address the information bias caused by degree imbalance, we propose a Learnable Enhancement and Label Selection Dynamic Graph Convolutional Network (L2DGCN). L2DGCN consists of a teacher model and a student model. The teacher model employs an improved label propagation mechanism that enables remote label information dissemination among all nodes. The student model introduces a dynamically learnable graph enhancement strategy, perturbing edges to facilitate information exchange among low-degree nodes. This approach maintains the global graph structure while learning graph representations. Additionally, we have designed a label selector to mitigate the impact of unreliable pseudo-labels on model learning. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed model with limited labeled data, we conducted comprehensive evaluations of semi-supervised node classification across various scenarios with a limited number of annotated nodes. Experimental results demonstrate that our data enhancement model significantly contributes to node classification tasks under sparse labeling conditions.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks classify nodes partly by passing information along graph connections. Nodes with few connections can receive less useful information, creating a bias associated with node degree. This becomes especially challenging when only a small number of nodes have human-provided labels. L2DGCN addresses the combination of limited supervision and uneven access to information.

Its teacher model uses an improved label-propagation mechanism to distribute label information over longer distances among nodes. The student model learns how to perturb graph edges so that low-degree nodes can exchange information more effectively while preserving the global graph structure. The method brings together three connected interventions: spreading supervision farther, improving information exchange for poorly connected nodes, and filtering uncertain supervision. Their combination targets the mechanisms through which sparse labels and degree imbalance can undermine classification.
summary.tldr: L2DGCN combines label propagation, learned graph changes, and pseudo-label selection to improve node classification with sparse supervision.

title: L2DGCN: Learnable Enhancement and Label Selection Dynamic Graph Convolutional Networks for Mitigating Degree Bias

abstract: In this paper we introduce Maximum Variance Correction (MVC), which finds large-scale feasible solutions to Maximum Variance Unfolding (MVU) by post-processing embeddings from any manifold learning algorithm. It increases the scale of MVU embeddings by several orders of magnitude and is naturally parallel. This unprecedented scalability opens up new avenues of applications for manifold learning, in particular the use of MVU embeddings as effective heuristics to speed-up A* search (Rayner et al. 2011). We demonstrate that MVC embeddings lead to un-matched reductions in search time across several non-trivial A* benchmark search problems and bridge the gap between the manifold learning literature and one of its most promising high impact applications.

paragraphs: Maximum Variance Unfolding is a manifold-learning method whose embeddings have potential applications in search. This paper introduces Maximum Variance Correction, or MVC, to make feasible MVU solutions available at much larger scales. The method works by post-processing embeddings produced by any manifold-learning algorithm, making correction of an existing embedding the central computational step.

The authors report that MVC increases the scale of MVU embeddings by several orders of magnitude and is naturally parallel. This scalability matters for applications that require embeddings large enough to represent substantial search problems. The paper specifically explores using MVU embeddings as heuristics to accelerate A* search, connecting a geometric representation to a search procedure.

Experiments on several nontrivial A* benchmark problems report reductions in search time unmatched in the comparisons presented. The contribution links a scalable embedding procedure with a concrete downstream use. MVC’s large-scale feasible solutions make it possible to investigate manifold-learning embeddings as practical aids to search, and the reported benchmarks demonstrate substantial benefits for that application.
summary.tldr: MVC scales feasible Maximum Variance Unfolding embeddings through post-processing and uses them to substantially accelerate benchmark A* searches.

title: Maximum Variance Correction with Application to A* Search

abstract: During the last fifteen years, the lasso procedure has been the target of a substantial amount of theoretical and applied research. Correspondingly, many results are known about its behavior for a fixed or optimally chosen smoothing parameter (given up to unknown constants). Much less, however, is known about the lasso’s behavior when the smoothing parameter is chosen in a data dependent way. To this end, we give the first result about the risk consistency of lasso when the smoothing parameter is chosen via cross-validation. We consider the high-dimensional setting wherein the number of predictors p=n^α, α>0 grows with the number of observations.

paragraphs: The paper examines a gap between theoretical understanding of the lasso and the way its smoothing parameter is selected from data. Many existing results concern a fixed parameter or an optimally chosen one, sometimes specified only up to unknown constants. These results leave open the behavior of a procedure that uses cross-validation to choose that parameter.

The authors provide a risk-consistency result for the lasso with cross-validated parameter selection. This makes the data-dependent choice part of the object being analyzed. The contribution concerns prediction risk, placing the parameter-selection step within the theoretical account of the fitted procedure rather than treating the parameter as already given.

The analysis considers a high-dimensional regime where the number of predictors is the number of observations raised to a positive power. Model dimension therefore grows as more observations become available. Within this setting, the result connects cross-validation with risk consistency and extends lasso theory to an important form of data-dependent tuning.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes risk consistency for cross-validated lasso in a setting where the number of predictors grows polynomially with sample size.

title: The lasso, persistence, and cross-validation

abstract: We study the problem of exploration in stochastic Multi-Armed Bandits. Even in the simplest setting of identifying the best arm, there remains a logarithmic multiplicative gap between the known lower and upper bounds for the number of arm pulls required for the task. This extra logarithmic factor is quite meaningful in nowadays large-scale applications. We present two novel, parameter-free algorithms for identifying the best arm, in two different settings: given a target confidence and given a target budget of arm pulls, for which we prove upper bounds whose gap from the lower bound is only doubly-logarithmic in the problem parameters. We corroborate our theoretical results with experiments demonstrating that our algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art and scales better as the size of the problem increases.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best option in a stochastic multi-armed bandit, where trying an option produces uncertain evidence about its quality. The central resource is the number of arm pulls needed to make that identification. Existing upper and lower bounds differed by a multiplicative logarithmic factor, which can become consequential for large problems.

The authors introduce two parameter-free algorithms for two versions of the task. One starts with a desired confidence level; the other starts with a fixed budget of arm pulls. They prove upper bounds whose remaining gap from the lower bound is only doubly logarithmic in the problem parameters.

These results bring the theoretical cost of exploration closer to the known limits without claiming to close the gap completely. Experiments support the analysis: the proposed approach outperforms the state of the art in the reported comparisons and scales better as problem size increases. The contribution combines stronger guarantees with empirical evidence that the improvement matters as exploration problems grow.
summary.tldr: Two best-arm identification algorithms reduce the gap to known exploration lower bounds from logarithmic to doubly logarithmic factors.

title: Almost Optimal Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: We evaluate whether features extracted from the activation of a deep convolutional network trained in a fully supervised fashion on a large, fixed set of object recognition tasks can be re-purposed to novel generic tasks. Our generic tasks may differ significantly from the originally trained tasks and there may be insufficient labeled or unlabeled data to conventionally train or adapt a deep architecture to the new tasks. We investigate and visualize the semantic clustering of deep convolutional features with respect to a variety of such tasks, including scene recognition, domain adaptation, and fine-grained recognition challenges. We compare the efficacy of relying on various network levels to define a fixed feature, and report novel results that significantly outperform the state-of-the-art on several important vision challenges. We are releasing DeCAF, an open-source implementation of these deep convolutional activation features, along with all associated network parameters to enable vision researchers to be able to conduct experimentation with deep representations across a range of visual concept learning paradigms.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a deep convolutional network trained for one collection of object recognition tasks can provide useful features for substantially different visual tasks. The setting matters when the new task has too little labeled or unlabeled data to train or adapt a deep network conventionally.

The authors extract network activations and use them as fixed image representations. They compare features taken from different network levels and investigate how these features cluster images by semantic content. Their evaluation covers scene recognition, domain adaptation, and fine-grained recognition, examining transfer across several kinds of visual learning problems.

The reported results significantly outperform the existing state of the art on several evaluated vision challenges. This supports the idea that supervised training can produce representations useful beyond the original recognition tasks, including settings with limited data for adaptation. The authors also release DeCAF and the associated network parameters, making the extracted features available for further experiments with deep representations across different visual concept learning settings.
summary.tldr: DeCAF shows that fixed features from a supervised convolutional network can transfer effectively to diverse visual recognition tasks.

title: DeCAF: A Deep Convolutional Activation Feature for Generic Visual Recognition

abstract: We study the min-max problem in factor graphs, which seeks the assignment that minimizes the maximum value over all factors. We reduce this problem to both min-sum and sum-product inference, and focus on the later. This approach reduces the min-max inference problem to a sequence of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) which allows us to sample from a uniform distribution over the set of solutions. We demonstrate how this scheme provides a message passing solution to several NP-hard combinatorial problems, such as min-max clustering (a.k.a. K-clustering), the asymmetric K-center problem, K-packing and the bottleneck traveling salesman problem. Furthermore we theoretically relate the min-max reductions to several NP hard decision problems, such as clique cover, set cover, maximum clique and Hamiltonian cycle, therefore also providing message passing solutions for these problems. Experimental results suggest that message passing often provides near optimal min-max solutions for moderate size instances.

paragraphs: The paper studies factor-graph assignments that minimize the largest factor value. This min-max objective focuses on the worst contributing value rather than a total across factors. The authors reduce the problem to familiar forms of inference, including min-sum and sum-product, with their main attention on sum-product inference.

Their approach turns min-max inference into a sequence of constraint satisfaction problems. This construction permits uniform sampling over the set of solutions and supplies a message-passing approach to several difficult combinatorial tasks. Examples include min-max clustering, asymmetric K-center, K-packing, and the bottleneck traveling salesman problem.

The authors also establish theoretical connections to decision problems including clique cover, set cover, maximum clique, and Hamiltonian cycle, extending the message-passing treatment to those problems. Experiments suggest that message passing often finds nearly optimal min-max solutions for moderately sized instances. That empirical finding supports the method's usefulness in the evaluated regime without asserting efficient exact solutions for these NP-hard problems generally.
summary.tldr: Reductions from min-max inference to constraint satisfaction provide message-passing approaches to several NP-hard problems, often yielding near-optimal solutions in moderate-size experiments.

title: Min-Max Problems on Factor Graphs

abstract: We propose nested sequential Monte Carlo (NSMC), a methodology to sample from sequences of probability distributions, even where the random variables are high-dimensional. NSMC generalises the SMC framework by requiring only approximate, properly weighted, samples from the SMC proposal distribution, while still resulting in a correct SMC algorithm. Furthermore, NSMC can in itself be used to produce such properly weighted samples. Consequently, one NSMC sampler can be used to construct an efficient high-dimensional proposal distribution for another NSMC sampler, and this nesting of the algorithm can be done to an arbitrary degree. This allows us to consider complex and high-dimensional models using SMC. We show results that motivate the efficacy of our approach on several filtering problems with dimensions in the order of 100 to 1000.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo samples from a sequence of probability distributions. This paper extends that framework to support complex models with high-dimensional random variables through nested sequential Monte Carlo. The key change concerns how proposal samples are generated: they may be approximate, provided they carry the proper weights required by the method.

Under that weighting requirement, the outer procedure remains a correct SMC algorithm. An NSMC sampler can itself produce the properly weighted samples needed by another sampler, so the construction can be repeated through multiple levels. This recursive property lets an inner sampling procedure construct a high-dimensional proposal for an outer one.

The importance of the result is that approximate internal sampling can fit within a formally valid overall procedure when its weighting is handled correctly. The authors demonstrate results on filtering problems with dimensions on the order of 100 to 1000. Those examples motivate the approach's effectiveness for demanding filtering tasks, alongside the general framework permitting arbitrary nesting depth.
summary.tldr: Nested SMC uses properly weighted approximate proposals, allowing samplers to be composed recursively for high-dimensional inference.

title: Nested Sequential Monte Carlo Methods

abstract: Crowdsourcing has become a popular tool for labeling large datasets. This paper studies the optimal error rate for aggregating crowdsourced labels provided by a collection of amateur workers. Under the Dawid-Skene probabilistic model, we establish matching upper and lower bounds with an exact exponent mI(\pi), where m is the number of workers and I(\pi) is the average Chernoff information that characterizes the workers’ collective ability. Such an exact characterization of the error exponent allows us to state a precise sample size requirement m \ge \frac1I(\pi)\log\frac1ε in order to achieve an εmisclassification error. In addition, our results imply optimality of various forms of EM algorithms given accurate initializers of the model parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately labels can be recovered by combining judgments from amateur workers. It works under the Dawid-Skene probabilistic model and focuses on the optimal aggregation error. The goal is a precise characterization of how the number of workers and their collective ability determine achievable accuracy.

The authors establish matching upper and lower bounds with error exponent mI(pi). Here, m counts workers, and I(pi) is their average Chernoff information, which summarizes collective labeling ability. Matching bounds identify the same exponent from both achievable performance and fundamental impossibility arguments. This makes the result more precise than a broad statement that additional workers reduce error.

The characterization yields the stated worker requirement m ≥ log(1/epsilon)/I(pi) for achieving epsilon misclassification error. It also implies optimality for various expectation-maximization algorithms when they begin with accurate estimates of the model parameters. That initialization condition is essential to the stated algorithmic conclusion. Together, the results relate workforce quality, workforce size, and the performance of practical aggregation procedures.
summary.tldr: Matching error bounds precisely connect crowdsourcing accuracy to worker count and collective ability, with conditional optimality for EM algorithms.

title: Exact Exponent in Optimal Rates for Crowdsourcing

abstract: Performing exact posterior inference in complex generative models is often difficult or impossible due to an expensive to evaluate or intractable likelihood function. Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is an inference framework that constructs an approximation to the true likelihood based on the similarity between the observed and simulated data as measured by a predefined set of summary statistics. Although the choice of informative problem-specific summary statistics crucially influences the quality of the likelihood approximation and hence also the quality of the posterior sample in ABC, there are only few principled general-purpose approaches to the selection or construction of such summary statistics. In this paper, we develop a novel framework for solving this problem. We model the functional relationship between the data and the optimal choice (with respect to a loss function) of summary statistics using kernel-based distribution regression. Furthermore, we extend our approach to incorporate kernel-based regression from conditional distributions, thus appropriately taking into account the specific structure of the posited generative model. We show that our approach can be implemented in a computationally and statistically efficient way using the random Fourier features framework for large-scale kernel learning. In addition to that, our framework outperforms related methods by a large margin on toy and real-world data, including hierarchical and time series models.

It compares simulated and observed data through summary statistics. Choosing those summaries is crucial: the information they preserve affects the likelihood approximation and, consequently, the quality of the resulting posterior sample.

It uses kernel-based distribution regression, treating distributions as inputs to this learning problem. The framework uses random Fourier features for a computationally and statistically efficient implementation of large-scale kernel learning. In experiments on toy and real-world data, including hierarchical and time-series models, it substantially outperforms the related methods considered. The contribution is a principled route to constructing useful summaries, with optimality tied to the selected loss.
summary.tldr: DR-ABC learns loss-specific summary statistics through kernel distribution regression to improve approximate Bayesian computation.

title: DR-ABC: Approximate Bayesian Computation with Kernel-Based Distribution Regression

abstract: The standard Kernel Quadrature method for numerical integration with random point sets (also called Bayesian Monte Carlo) is known to converge in root mean square error at a rate determined by the ratio s/d, where s and d encode the smoothness and dimension of the integrand. However, an empirical investigation reveals that the rate constant C is highly sensitive to the distribution of the random points. In contrast to standard Monte Carlo integration, for which optimal importance sampling is well-understood, the sampling distribution that minimises C for Kernel Quadrature does not admit a closed form. This paper argues that the practical choice of sampling distribution is an important open problem. One solution is considered; a novel automatic approach based on adaptive tempering and sequential Monte Carlo. Empirical results demonstrate a dramatic reduction in integration error of up to 4 orders of magnitude can be achieved with the proposed method.

paragraphs: Kernel quadrature estimates integrals from function values at selected points. Its known root-mean-square convergence rate depends on the integrand's smoothness relative to its dimension. This paper focuses on another part of the error expression: the multiplying constant, which empirical investigation shows can be highly sensitive to how the random points are sampled.

That sensitivity makes the sampling distribution a practical design choice. Unlike optimal importance sampling for standard Monte Carlo integration, the distribution minimizing this constant for kernel quadrature has no closed-form expression. The authors identify choosing a useful sampling distribution as an important open problem and investigate one automatic approach.

Their proposed method combines adaptive tempering with sequential Monte Carlo to select the sampling distribution. Experiments show integration-error reductions of up to four orders of magnitude. The result illustrates how improving point selection can greatly improve practical accuracy even when attention to the convergence-rate exponent alone would miss the opportunity. It is an empirical improvement, rather than a closed-form solution to the optimal-sampling problem.
summary.tldr: Adaptive sampling for kernel quadrature produces reported integration-error reductions of up to four orders of magnitude.

title: On the Sampling Problem for Kernel Quadrature

abstract: Undirected graphical models or Markov random fields (MRFs) are widely used for modeling multivariate probability distributions. Much of the work on MRFs has focused on continuous variables, and nominal variables (that is, unordered categorical variables). However, data from many real world applications involve ordered categorical variables also known as ordinal variables, e.g., movie ratings on Netflix which can be ordered from 1 to 5 stars. With respect to univariate ordinal distributions, as we detail in the paper, there are two main categories of distributions; while there have been efforts to extend these to multivariate ordinal distributions, the resulting distributions are typically very complex, with either a large number of parameters, or with non-convex likelihoods. While there have been some work on tractable approximations, these do not come with strong statistical guarantees, and moreover are relatively computationally expensive. In this paper, we theoretically investigate two classes of graphical models for ordinal data, corresponding to the two main categories of univariate ordinal distributions. In contrast to previous work, our theoretical developments allow us to provide correspondingly two classes of estimators that are not only computationally efficient but also have strong statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: Ordinal variables are categories with a meaningful order, such as ratings from one to five stars. The paper studies graphical models for collections of these variables. Much earlier work on Markov random fields focused on continuous measurements or unordered categories, leaving the structure of ordinal data less directly addressed.

The authors organize their analysis around two main categories of univariate ordinal distributions and investigate corresponding classes of multivariate graphical models. Extending a model from one ordinal variable to many can create difficulties: earlier constructions may require many parameters or have non-convex likelihoods. Existing tractable approximations also lack strong statistical guarantees and can remain computationally expensive.

The paper develops theory supporting two corresponding classes of estimators that are computationally efficient and have strong statistical guarantees. The significance is the combination of appropriate ordinal modeling, manageable computation, and statistical justification. Rather than treating ordering as an incidental feature of categorical data, the work builds the multivariate models around the two established approaches to describing individual ordinal variables.
summary.tldr: The paper develops two classes of ordinal graphical-model estimators that combine computational efficiency with strong statistical guarantees.

title: Ordinal Graphical Models: A Tale of Two Approaches

abstract: This paper is about the study of B-FQI, an Approximated Value Iteration (AVI) algorithm that exploits a boosting procedure to estimate the action-value function in reinforcement learning problems. B-FQI is an iterative off-line algorithm that, given a dataset of transitions, builds an approximation of the optimal action-value function by summing the approximations of the Bellman residuals across all iterations. The advantage of such approach w.r.t. to other AVI methods is twofold: (1) while keeping the same function space at each iteration, B-FQI can represent more complex functions by considering an additive model; (2) since the Bellman residual decreases as the optimal value function is approached, regression problems become easier as iterations proceed. We study B-FQI both theoretically, providing also a finite-sample error upper bound for it, and empirically, by comparing its performance to the one of FQI in different domains and using different regression techniques.

paragraphs: Boosted Fitted Q-Iteration learns an approximation of the optimal action-value function from a fixed dataset of transitions. This function describes the value of actions in reinforcement learning. The method belongs to approximate value iteration, but uses boosting to build its estimate through a sequence of additive corrections.

At each iteration, the algorithm approximates a Bellman residual, which represents a discrepancy in the current value estimate. It sums these approximations across iterations. This additive construction can represent increasingly complex functions even while keeping the function space used for each individual approximation unchanged. The overall model gains expressive capacity through accumulated corrections.

A second stated advantage is that residuals decrease as the estimate approaches the optimal value function, making later regression problems easier. The authors provide a theoretical analysis that includes a finite-sample upper bound on error. They also compare the method empirically with Fitted Q-Iteration across different domains and regression techniques. The abstract establishes the rationale and evaluation approach without asserting a uniform empirical advantage over that comparison method.
summary.tldr: Boosted Fitted Q-Iteration builds action-value estimates by adding fitted Bellman-residual corrections, with a finite-sample error analysis.

title: Boosted Fitted Q-Iteration

abstract: Online learning to rank is a core problem in information retrieval and machine learning. Many provably efficient algorithms have been recently proposed for this problem in specific click models. The click model is a model of how the user interacts with a list of documents. Though these results are significant, their impact on practice is limited, because all proposed algorithms are designed for specific click models and lack convergence guarantees in other models. In this work, we propose BatchRank, the first online learning to rank algorithm for a broad class of click models. The class encompasses two most fundamental click models, the cascade and position-based models. We derive a gap-dependent upper bound on the T-step regret of BatchRank and evaluate it on a range of web search queries. We observe that BatchRank outperforms ranked bandits and is more robust than CascadeKL-UCB, an existing algorithm for the cascade model.

The difficulty is that clicks depend on how people inspect the list, not just on document quality. Algorithms designed around one particular model of clicking may lose their convergence guarantees when users behave according to another model.

The paper introduces BatchRank, an algorithm designed for a broader class of click models. That class includes both the cascade and position-based models, two fundamental ways of describing interactions with ranked results. Its contribution is therefore a shared learning approach across multiple models, rather than a separate algorithm tailored to each one.

The authors establish a gap-dependent upper bound on cumulative regret, measuring the cost of learning over successive rounds. In evaluations on web search queries, BatchRank outperforms ranked bandits and proves more robust than CascadeKL-UCB. These findings support the practical value of broader model coverage, while the theoretical guarantee remains tied to the specified class of click models.
summary.tldr: BatchRank learns document rankings with regret guarantees across a broad class of click models and shows improved robustness in web search evaluations.

title: Online Learning to Rank in Stochastic Click Models

abstract: Recent work has shown local convergence of GAN training for absolutely continuous data and generator distributions. In this paper, we show that the requirement of absolute continuity is necessary: we describe a simple yet prototypical counterexample showing that in the more realistic case of distributions that are not absolutely continuous, unregularized GAN training is not always convergent. Furthermore, we discuss regularization strategies that were recently proposed to stabilize GAN training. Our analysis shows that GAN training with instance noise or zero-centered gradient penalties converges. On the other hand, we show that Wasserstein-GANs and WGAN-GP with a finite number of discriminator updates per generator update do not always converge to the equilibrium point. We discuss these results, leading us to a new explanation for the stability problems of GAN training. Based on our analysis, we extend our convergence results to more general GANs and prove local convergence for simplified gradient penalties even if the generator and data distributions lie on lower dimensional manifolds. We find these penalties to work well in practice and use them to learn high-resolution generative image models for a variety of datasets with little hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: The paper examines when GAN training converges, particularly when data and generator distributions occupy lower-dimensional structures. It also shows that Wasserstein GANs and WGAN-GP do not always reach equilibrium when only finitely many discriminator updates are performed per generator update. summary.tldr: Counterexamples expose GAN convergence failures, while simplified gradient penalties provide local convergence guarantees even for distributions on lower-dimensional manifolds.

title: Which Training Methods for GANs do actually Converge?

abstract: In recent years, state-of-the-art methods in computer vision have utilized increasingly deep convolutional neural network architectures (CNNs), with some of the most successful models employing hundreds or even thousands of layers. A variety of pathologies such as vanishing/exploding gradients make training such deep networks challenging. While residual connections and batch normalization do enable training at these depths, it has remained unclear whether such specialized architecture designs are truly necessary to train deep CNNs. In this work, we demonstrate that it is possible to train vanilla CNNs with ten thousand layers or more simply by using an appropriate initialization scheme. We derive this initialization scheme theoretically by developing a mean field theory for signal propagation and by characterizing the conditions for dynamical isometry, the equilibration of singular values of the input-output Jacobian matrix. These conditions require that the convolution operator be an orthogonal transformation in the sense that it is norm-preserving. We present an algorithm for generating such random initial orthogonal convolution kernels and demonstrate empirically that they enable efficient training of extremely deep architectures.

paragraphs: Very deep convolutional networks can be difficult to train because gradients may shrink or grow excessively as they pass through many layers. Residual connections and batch normalization have helped make such networks trainable. This paper asks whether those architectural devices are necessary and demonstrates that suitable initialization can enable training of vanilla convolutional networks with ten thousand layers or more.

They characterize conditions for dynamical isometry, concerning the equalization of singular values of the matrix describing how inputs affect outputs. These conditions require the convolution operation to be orthogonal, meaning that it preserves the norm of the signal it transforms.

The paper supplies an algorithm for generating random convolution kernels with that orthogonality property. Experiments show that these initial kernels enable efficient training of extremely deep architectures. The result establishes that appropriate initialization can make such depth trainable; it does not make specialized architectural features a prerequisite for the demonstrated training capability.
summary.tldr: A theoretically derived orthogonal initialization enables efficient training of vanilla convolutional networks with ten thousand layers or more.

title: Dynamical Isometry and a Mean Field Theory of CNNs: How to Train 10,000-Layer Vanilla Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Training neural networks is traditionally done by providing a sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the entire training data. In this work, we analyze the effect of curriculum learning, which involves the non-uniform sampling of mini-batches, on the training of deep networks, and specifically CNNs trained for image recognition. To employ curriculum learning, the training algorithm must resolve 2 problems: (i) sort the training examples by difficulty; (ii) compute a series of mini-batches that exhibit an increasing level of difficulty. We address challenge (i) using two methods: transfer learning from some competitive “teacher" network, and bootstrapping. In our empirical evaluation, both methods show similar benefits in terms of increased learning speed and improved final performance on test data. We address challenge (ii) by investigating different pacing functions to guide the sampling. The empirical investigation includes a variety of network architectures, using images from CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and subsets of ImageNet. We conclude with a novel theoretical analysis of curriculum learning, where we show how it effectively modifies the optimization landscape. We then define the concept of an ideal curriculum, and show that under mild conditions it does not change the corresponding global minimum of the optimization function.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes how training examples are sampled so that mini-batches become progressively more difficult. This paper studies its effects on deep networks, particularly convolutional networks for image recognition. It separates curriculum design into two problems: determining example difficulty and deciding how quickly training should move toward harder examples.

The authors estimate difficulty using either transfer from a competitive teacher network or bootstrapping. They investigate pacing functions to control the progression of sampled batches. Across several architectures and experiments involving CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet subsets, both difficulty-estimation approaches show similar benefits: faster learning and improved final performance on test data.

The paper also provides a theoretical analysis of how curriculum learning changes the optimization landscape. It defines an ideal curriculum and shows that, under mild conditions, this curriculum preserves the corresponding global minimum of the optimization objective. This is a conditional result about the defined ideal curriculum, alongside empirical evidence that practical sampling schedules can improve the training process.
summary.tldr: Difficulty-based training schedules improve learning in image experiments, while a theoretical ideal curriculum preserves the global minimum under mild conditions.

title: On The Power of Curriculum Learning in Training Deep Networks

abstract: In this paper we study the problem of robust influence maximization in the independent cascade model under a hyperparametric assumption. In social networks users influence and are influenced by individuals with similar characteristics and as such they are associated with some features. A recent surging research direction in influence maximization focuses on the case where the edge probabilities on the graph are not arbitrary but are generated as a function of the features of the users and a global hyperparameter. We propose a model where the objective is to maximize the worst-case number of influenced users for any possible value of that hyperparameter. We provide theoretical results showing that proper robust solution in our model is NP-hard and an algorithm that achieves improper robust optimization. We make-use of sampling based techniques and of the renowned multiplicative weight updates algorithm. Additionally we validate our method empirically and prove that it outperforms the state-of-the-art robust influence maximization techniques.

paragraphs: Influence maximization chooses where to initiate a spreading process in a network. This paper studies robustness when the probabilities of influence along edges are generated from user features and a shared global hyperparameter. Under this assumption, uncertainty is tied together through that parameter rather than specified independently for every edge.

The objective is to maximize the worst-case number of influenced users across possible hyperparameter values in the independent cascade model. This asks for a decision that remains effective despite uncertainty about the parameter. The authors show that obtaining a proper robust solution is NP-hard and develop an algorithm for improper robust optimization.

Their algorithm uses sampling techniques and multiplicative weight updates. The distinction between proper and improper optimization matters: the paper does not claim an efficient exact solution to the hard proper formulation. It also provides empirical validation and reports superiority over state-of-the-art robust influence-maximization techniques. The combined contribution is a feature-based uncertainty model, an analysis of its computational difficulty, and an algorithmic approach to its robust objective.
summary.tldr: The paper optimizes worst-case network influence when edge probabilities depend on user features and an uncertain shared hyperparameter.

title: Robust Influence Maximization for Hyperparametric Models

abstract: Streaming algorithms are generally judged by the quality of their solution, memory footprint, and computational complexity. In this paper, we study the problem of maximizing a monotone submodular function in the streaming setting with a cardinality constraint $k$. We first propose SIEVE-STREAMING++, which requires just one pass over the data, keeps only $O(k)$ elements and achieves the tight $\frac{1}{2}$-approximation guarantee. The best previously known streaming algorithms either achieve a suboptimal $\frac{1}{4}$-approximation with $\Theta(k)$ memory or the optimal $\frac{1}{2}$-approximation with $O(k\log k)$ memory. Next, we show that by buffering a small fraction of the stream and applying a careful filtering procedure, one can heavily reduce the number of adaptive computational rounds, thus substantially lowering the computational complexity of SIEVE-STREAMING++. We then generalize our results to the more challenging multi-source streaming setting. We show how one can achieve the tight $\frac{1}{2}$-approximation guarantee with $O(k)$ shared memory, while minimizing not only the rounds of computations but also the total number of communicated bits. Finally, we demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithms on real-world data summarization tasks for multi-source streams of tweets and of YouTube videos.

paragraphs: The paper studies selecting at most k elements from a stream to maximize a monotone submodular objective. Such objectives capture diminishing returns: an additional element can contribute less when the selected set already contains useful information. A streaming algorithm must balance solution quality with limited storage and the cost of processing incoming data.

SIEVE-STREAMING++ makes one pass, stores O(k) elements, and achieves the tight one-half approximation guarantee. Earlier methods described in the abstract either used comparable memory for a one-quarter guarantee or required O(k log k) memory for a one-half guarantee. The new result combines the stronger approximation with storage proportional to the allowed selection size.

The authors further reduce sequentially dependent computational rounds by buffering a small fraction of the stream and filtering it carefully. They extend the results to multiple data sources, retaining the one-half guarantee with O(k) shared memory while addressing computation rounds and communicated bits. Experiments on tweet and YouTube-video summarization demonstrate the algorithms' efficiency for real-world streams.
summary.tldr: SIEVE-STREAMING++ achieves a tight one-half approximation with linear storage, with extensions reducing adaptive computation and multi-source communication.

title: Submodular Streaming in All Its Glory: Tight Approximation, Minimum Memory and Low Adaptive Complexity

abstract: Many privacy mechanisms reveal high-level information about a data distribution through noisy measurements. It is common to use this information to estimate the answers to new queries. In this work, we provide an approach to solve this estimation problem efficiently using graphical models, which is particularly effective when the distribution is high-dimensional but the measurements are over low-dimensional marginals. We show that our approach is far more efficient than existing estimation techniques from the privacy literature and that it can improve the accuracy and scalability of many state-of-the-art mechanisms.

paragraphs: Privacy mechanisms often release noisy measurements that summarize a data distribution. A subsequent task is to use those measurements to estimate answers to additional questions about the data. This paper focuses on making that estimation process efficient, using graphical models to organize the information available in the noisy summaries.

The approach is particularly effective when the data have many dimensions but each measurement concerns a low-dimensional marginal, meaning a distribution over a small subset of variables. This distinction is central to the problem: the full distribution may be large even though the released measurements each describe only a limited portion of it.

The authors show that their approach is substantially more efficient than existing estimation techniques from the privacy literature. They also show that it can improve the accuracy and scalability of many state-of-the-art privacy mechanisms. The contribution concerns how released measurements are used for inference, making graphical modeling a practical component of a broader private data-analysis process.
summary.tldr: Graphical models make inference from noisy private measurements more efficient, especially for high-dimensional data summarized by low-dimensional marginals.

title: Graphical-model based estimation and inference for differential privacy

abstract: We study the Gibbs sampling algorithm for discrete and continuous $k$-determinantal point processes. We show that in both cases, the spectral gap of the chain is bounded by a polynomial of $k$ and it is independent of the size of the domain. As an immediate corollary, we obtain sublinear time algorithms for sampling from discrete $k$-DPPs given access to polynomially many processors. In the continuous setting, our result leads to the first class of rigorously analyzed efficient algorithms to generate random samples of continuous $k$-DPPs. We achieve this by showing that the Gibbs sampler for a large family of continuous $k$-DPPs can be simulated efficiently when the spectrum is not concentrated on the top $k$ eigenvalues.

paragraphs: This paper studies Gibbs sampling for determinantal point processes that select exactly k points, covering both discrete and continuous domains. The central question is whether this sampling procedure can be given rigorous efficiency guarantees. The analysis focuses on the chain's spectral gap, a mathematical quantity connected to how quickly the sampler approaches its target distribution.

The authors establish a spectral-gap bound with polynomial dependence on k and no dependence on domain size. For discrete processes, this yields sublinear-time sampling algorithms when polynomially many processors are available. The processor requirement is part of that result: the stated speedup relies on parallel computational resources.

For continuous processes, the paper also addresses whether the Gibbs sampler can actually be simulated efficiently. It proves this for a large family whose spectrum is not concentrated on the top k eigenvalues. Together, these results provide a rigorously analyzed class of efficient continuous k-DPP samplers. The contribution links control of the chain's convergence with conditions that make its computational steps feasible.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes domain-size-independent Gibbs-sampling bounds for k-DPPs and efficient continuous sampling under a spectral condition.

title: A Polynomial Time MCMC Method for Sampling from Continuous Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: In this paper, we present a Bayesian Moment Matching (BMM) based method aimed at solving the initialization problem in Boolean SAT solvers. The initialization problem can be stated as follows: given a SAT formula $\phi$, compute an initial order over the variables of $\phi$ and values/polarity for these variables such that the runtime of SAT solvers on input $\phi$ is minimized. At the start of a solver run, our BMM-based methods compute a posterior probability distribution for an assignment to the variables of the input formula after analyzing its clauses, which will then be used by the solver to initialize its search. We perform extensive experiments to evaluate the efficacy of our BMM-based heuristic against 4 other initialization methods (random, survey propagation, Jeroslow-Wang, and default) in state-of-the-art solvers, MapleCOMSPS and MapleLCMDistChronotBT over the SAT competition 2018 application benchmark, as well as the best-known solvers in the cryptographic category, namely, CryptoMiniSAT, Glucose, and MapleSAT. On the cryptographic benchmark, BMM-based solvers out-perform all other initialization methods. Further, the BMM-based MapleCOMSPS significantly out-perform the same solver using all other initialization methods by 12 additional instances solved and better average runtime, over the SAT 2018 competition benchmark.

paragraphs: A Boolean satisfiability solver searches for variable assignments that satisfy a formula. Its starting choices include which variables to consider first and which truth values to try. This paper addresses that initialization problem, aiming to reduce runtime by choosing an initial variable ordering and polarity based on the formula's clauses.

The proposed heuristic uses Bayesian Moment Matching. At the beginning of a run, it analyzes the clauses to compute a posterior probability distribution over variable assignments. The solver then uses this distribution to initialize its search. The contribution is therefore a probabilistic method for guiding the starting search configuration within existing SAT solvers.

BMM-based solvers outperform the other initialization methods on the cryptographic benchmark. On the SAT competition application benchmark, BMM-based MapleCOMSPS solves 12 additional instances and has better average runtime than its alternatives. These findings demonstrate measured gains from changing initialization in the evaluated solver and benchmark combinations.
summary.tldr: Bayesian Moment Matching uses a SAT formula's clauses to choose better search initialization, improving results on the reported benchmarks.

title: Online Bayesian Moment Matching based SAT Solver Heuristics

abstract: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) represent the given data in a low-dimensional latent space, which is generally assumed to be Euclidean. This assumption naturally leads to the common choice of a standard Gaussian prior over continuous latent variables. Recent work has, however, shown that this prior has a detrimental effect on model capacity, leading to subpar performance. We propose that the Euclidean assumption lies at the heart of this failure mode. To counter this, we assume a Riemannian structure over the latent space, which constitutes a more principled geometric view of the latent codes, and replace the standard Gaussian prior with a Riemannian Brownian motion prior. We propose an efficient inference scheme that does not rely on the unknown normalizing factor of this prior. Finally, we demonstrate that this prior significantly increases model capacity using only one additional scalar parameter.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders represent data in a lower-dimensional latent space, usually treated as Euclidean. This assumption naturally motivates a standard Gaussian prior. The paper argues that the Euclidean assumption underlies a failure mode in which that prior restricts model capacity and leads to poorer performance.

The proposed alternative gives the latent space a Riemannian structure and replaces the Gaussian prior with a Riemannian Brownian motion prior. The change ties the prior to a different geometric view of the latent codes. It therefore addresses the proposed source of the capacity problem through both latent-space geometry and the probability distribution placed on it.

A practical obstacle is the prior's unknown normalizing factor. The authors introduce an efficient inference scheme that does not require that factor, making the proposed model usable despite it. They demonstrate a significant increase in model capacity using only one additional scalar parameter. The result supports geometric changes to the prior as a compact way to improve the representational capacity of the evaluated VAEs.
summary.tldr: A Riemannian Brownian motion prior increases demonstrated VAE capacity with one additional scalar parameter and a tractable inference scheme.

title: Variational Autoencoders with Riemannian Brownian Motion Priors

abstract: Heretofore, neural networks with external memory are restricted to single memory with lossy representations of memory interactions. A rich representation of relationships between memory pieces urges a high-order and segregated relational memory. In this paper, we propose to separate the storage of individual experiences (item memory) and their occurring relationships (relational memory). The idea is implemented through a novel Self-attentive Associative Memory (SAM) operator. Found upon outer product, SAM forms a set of associative memories that represent the hypothetical high-order relationships between arbitrary pairs of memory elements, through which a relational memory is constructed from an item memory. The two memories are wired into a single sequential model capable of both memorization and relational reasoning. We achieve competitive results with our proposed two-memory model in a diversity of machine learning tasks, from challenging synthetic problems to practical testbeds such as geometry, graph, reinforcement learning, and question answering.

The idea is implemented through a novel Self-attentive Associative Memory (SAM) operator. The two memories are wired into a single sequential model capable of both memorization and relational reasoning. We achieve competitive results with our proposed two-memory model in a diversity of machine learning tasks, from challenging synthetic problems to practical testbeds such as geometry, graph, reinforcement learning, and question answering.

paragraphs: The paper proposes separating two kinds of information in a neural network with external memory: individual experiences and relationships among those experiences. Its motivation is that a single memory can provide a lossy account of interactions between stored items. Separate item and relational memories are intended to support richer relationship representations.

The Self-attentive Associative Memory operator, or SAM, constructs relational memory from item memory. Based on an outer-product operation, it forms associative memories representing hypothetical higher-order relationships between arbitrary pairs of memory elements. The two memories are then connected within one sequential model, giving the system mechanisms for both retaining items and reasoning about their relationships.

The authors evaluate the model across synthetic problems and practical tasks involving geometry, graphs, reinforcement learning, and question answering. They report competitive results across this range. The contribution is an explicit architectural treatment of stored experiences and their relationships, with empirical evidence that the combined model can support both memorization and relational reasoning in diverse tasks.
summary.tldr: SAM connects separate item and relational memories to support memorization and relationship reasoning, with competitive results across diverse tasks.

title: Self-Attentive Associative Memory

abstract: Structured predictors require solving a combinatorial optimization problem over a large number of structures, such as dependency trees or alignments. When embedded as structured hidden layers in a neural net, argmin differentiation and efficient gradient computation are further required. Recently, SparseMAP has been proposed as a differentiable, sparse alternative to maximum a posteriori (MAP) and marginal inference. SparseMAP returns an interpretable combination of a small number of structures; its sparsity being the key to efficient optimization. However, SparseMAP requires access to an exact MAP oracle in the structured model, excluding, e.g., loopy graphical models or logic constraints, which generally require approximate inference. In this paper, we introduce LP-SparseMAP, an extension of SparseMAP addressing this limitation via a local polytope relaxation. LP-SparseMAP uses the flexible and powerful language of factor graphs to define expressive hidden structures, supporting coarse decompositions, hard logic constraints, and higher-order correlations. We derive the forward and backward algorithms needed for using LP-SparseMAP as a structured hidden or output layer. Experiments in three structured tasks show benefits versus SparseMAP and Structured SVM.

When that choice appears inside a neural network, training also requires gradients through the optimization step. SparseMAP addresses this with an interpretable combination of a few structures, but it depends on an exact maximum a posteriori inference oracle.

LP-SparseMAP extends that approach using a local polytope relaxation. This addresses the exact-inference requirement that prevents ordinary SparseMAP from handling models such as loopy graphical models or general logic constraints. Factor graphs provide the language for expressing the hidden structures, including hard logical rules, higher-order correlations, and coarse decompositions.

Experiments on three structured tasks show benefits over SparseMAP and Structured SVM. The central contribution is broader access to differentiable structured modeling: a relaxation makes more expressive constraints and interactions usable within a trainable layer, while retaining the sparse modeling approach.
summary.tldr: LP-SparseMAP uses a local polytope relaxation to extend differentiable sparse structured prediction beyond models requiring exact MAP inference.

title: LP-SparseMAP: Differentiable Relaxed Optimization for Sparse Structured Prediction

abstract: Deep neural networks are shown to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This motivates robust learning techniques, such as the adversarial training, whose goal is to learn a network that is robust against adversarial attacks. However, the sample complexity of robust learning can be significantly larger than that of “standard” learning. In this paper, we propose improving the adversarial robustness of a network by leveraging the potentially large test data seen at runtime. We devise a new defense method, called runtime masking and cleansing (RMC), that adapts the network at runtime before making a prediction to dynamically mask network gradients and cleanse the model of the non-robust features inevitably learned during the training process due to the size limit of the training set. We conduct experiments on real-world datasets and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of RMC empirically.

paragraphs: Making a neural network robust to adversarial attacks can require substantially more training data than ordinary prediction. This paper asks whether robustness can also benefit from the potentially large amount of test data encountered during use. Its approach moves part of the defense into the period immediately before a prediction.

The proposed method, runtime masking and cleansing, adapts the network at runtime. It combines dynamic masking of network gradients with an attempt to remove non-robust features learned during training. The paper connects those features to the limited size of the training set, framing runtime adaptation as a way to address weaknesses left by the original learning process.

Experiments on real-world datasets provide empirical support for the defense. The stated finding is that runtime adaptation can improve adversarial robustness in the evaluated settings. The contribution is the use of data encountered during operation to modify the predictor before it responds, expanding the role of robustness methods beyond the initial training stage.
summary.tldr: Runtime masking and cleansing adapts a network before prediction, using test-time data to improve adversarial robustness empirically.

title: Adversarial Robustness via Runtime Masking and Cleansing

abstract: Effective caching is crucial for performance of modern-day computing systems. A key optimization problem arising in caching – which item to evict to make room for a new item – cannot be optimally solved without knowing the future. There are many classical approximation algorithms for this problem, but more recently researchers started to successfully apply machine learning to decide what to evict by discovering implicit input patterns and predicting the future. While machine learning typically does not provide any worst-case guarantees, the new field of learning-augmented algorithms proposes solutions which leverage classical online caching algorithms to make the machine-learned predictors robust. We are the first to comprehensively evaluate these learning-augmented algorithms on real-world caching datasets and state-of-the-art machine-learned predictors. We show that a straightforward method – blindly following either a predictor or a classical robust algorithm, and switching whenever one becomes worse than the other – has only a low overhead over a well-performing predictor, while competing with classical methods when the coupled predictor fails, thus providing a cheap worst-case insurance.

paragraphs: A cache must choose which stored item to remove when space is needed, but the optimal choice depends on future requests. Learned predictors can exploit patterns in requests, while classical online algorithms provide robustness without accurate forecasts. Learning-augmented caching combines these strengths so that prediction errors do not leave the system entirely dependent on unreliable advice.

The paper evaluates such algorithms on real-world caching datasets using state-of-the-art learned predictors. Its central finding favors a straightforward switching method: follow either the predictor or a classical robust algorithm, and switch when the currently followed option becomes worse than the other. This gives the system a mechanism for responding when the relative usefulness of prediction changes.

The experiments show low overhead when the predictor performs well and competitiveness with classical methods when it fails. The result supports a simple form of worst-case insurance for learned caching. Its significance is practical: the evaluated combination preserves much of a good predictor’s benefit while offering a robust alternative during poor predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that switching between a learned caching predictor and a robust classical algorithm provides inexpensive protection against prediction failures.

title: Robust Learning-Augmented Caching: An Experimental Study

abstract: In this paper, we provide finite-sample convergence guarantees for an off-policy variant of the natural actor-critic (NAC) algorithm based on Importance Sampling. In particular, we show that the algorithm converges to a global optimal policy with a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}\log^2(1/\epsilon))$ under an appropriate choice of stepsizes. In order to overcome the issue of large variance due to Importance Sampling, we propose the $Q$-trace algorithm for the critic, which is inspired by the V-trace algorithm (Espeholt et al., 2018). This enables us to explicitly control the bias and variance, and characterize the trade-off between them. As an advantage of off-policy sampling, a major feature of our result is that we do not need any additional assumptions, beyond the ergodicity of the Markov chain induced by the behavior policy.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes an off-policy natural actor-critic algorithm, which learns using observations generated by a behavior policy. Importance sampling accounts for the difference between that policy and the policy being learned. The central question is how much data the algorithm needs to approach a globally optimal policy, rather than merely whether it improves eventually.

Importance sampling can introduce large variance into learning. To address this, the authors propose Q-trace for the critic, drawing inspiration from V-trace. Q-trace allows them to explicitly control bias and variance and describe their trade-off. This makes the critic's estimation behavior part of the convergence analysis rather than leaving it as an uncontrolled source of error.

With appropriately chosen step sizes, the authors establish a sample complexity of O(ε⁻³ log²(1/ε)) for convergence to global optimality at the specified accuracy. They emphasize that their result requires no additional assumptions beyond ergodicity of the Markov chain generated by the behavior policy. The guarantee thus ties finite-data performance to a stated sampling condition and a suitable step-size choice.
summary.tldr: An off-policy natural actor-critic analysis gives finite-sample guarantees using Q-trace to control the critic's bias and variance.

title: Finite-Sample Analysis of Off-Policy Natural Actor-Critic Algorithm

abstract: We introduce algorithms based on natural actor-critic and analyze their sample complexity for solving two player zero-sum Markov games in the tabular case. Our results improve the best-known sample complexities of policy gradient/actor-critic methods for convergence to Nash equilibrium in the multi-agent setting. We use the error propagation scheme in approximate dynamic programming, recent advances for global convergence of policy gradient methods, temporal difference learning, and techniques from stochastic primal-dual optimization. Our algorithms feature two stages, requiring agents to agree on an etiquette before starting their interactions, which is feasible for instance in self-play. However, the agents only access to joint reward and joint next state and not to each other’s actions or policies. Our complexity results match the best-known results for global convergence of policy gradient algorithms for single agent RL. We provide numerical verification of our methods for a two player bandit environment and a two player game, Alesia. We observe improved empirical performance as compared to the recently proposed optimistic gradient descent-ascent variant for Markov games.
