paragraphs: This paper studies how two opposing agents can learn strategies in a zero-sum Markov game, where one agent’s gain is the other’s loss. It develops natural actor-critic algorithms and analyzes how many samples they need to approach a Nash equilibrium. The analysis covers the tabular setting, where states and actions are represented explicitly.

The algorithms use two stages and require the agents to agree on an interaction protocol before learning begins. That coordination is feasible in settings such as self-play. During interaction, however, agents observe the joint reward and next state without accessing the other agent’s actions or policy. The analysis combines policy optimization, temporal difference learning, approximate dynamic programming, and stochastic optimization.

The resulting sample bounds improve the best previously known bounds for policy gradient and actor-critic methods in this multi-agent setting, while matching known global-convergence results for single-agent policy gradient methods. Experiments in a two-player bandit environment and Alesia also show improved performance over an optimistic gradient descent-ascent approach. These findings connect theoretical learning efficiency with empirical improvements in the evaluated games.
summary.tldr: Natural actor-critic algorithms improve sample-complexity guarantees for tabular zero-sum Markov games under an agreed interaction protocol.

title: A Natural Actor-Critic Framework for Zero-Sum Markov Games

abstract: Current techniques for explaining outliers cannot tell what caused the outliers. We present a formal method to identify "root causes" of outliers, amongst variables. The method requires a causal graph of the variables along with the functional causal model. It quantifies the contribution of each variable to the target outlier score, which explains to what extent each variable is a "root cause" of the target outlier. We study the empirical performance of the method through simulations and present a real-world case study identifying "root causes" of extreme river flows.

paragraphs: Explaining why an observation looks unusual does not by itself identify what caused it. This paper addresses that distinction by developing a formal method for assigning root-cause contributions to variables involved in an outlier. The target is an explanation of how variables contribute to the unusual outcome, beyond simply describing its abnormal features.

The method requires both a causal graph describing relationships among variables and a functional causal model describing those relationships. Using this causal information, it quantifies each variable’s contribution to the target outlier score. The resulting attribution expresses the extent to which each variable counts as a root cause within that model.

The authors investigate empirical performance through simulations and present an application to extreme river flows. This case study connects the formal attribution task to a real-world unusual event. The causal graph and functional model are essential inputs to the approach, so its contribution is a way to analyze outliers using an available causal description.
summary.tldr: Given a causal graph and functional causal model, the method attributes a target outlier score to contributions from individual variables.

title: Causal structure-based root cause analysis of outliers

abstract: The problem of learning functions over spaces of probabilities - or distribution regression - is gaining significant interest in the machine learning community. The main challenge in these settings is to identify a suitable representation capturing all relevant properties of a distribution. The well-established approach in this sense is to use kernel mean embeddings, which lift kernel-induced similarity on the input domain at the probability level. This strategy effectively tackles the two-stage sampling nature of the problem, enabling one to derive estimators with strong statistical guarantees, such as universal consistency and excess risk bounds. However, kernel mean embeddings implicitly hinge on the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a metric on probabilities, which is not the most suited to capture geometrical relations between distributions. In contrast, optimal transport (OT) metrics, are potentially more appealing. In this work, we propose an OT-based estimator for distribution regression. We build on the Sliced Wasserstein distance to obtain an OT-based representation. We study the theoretical properties of a kernel ridge regression estimator based on such representation, for which we prove universal consistency and excess risk bounds. Preliminary experiments complement our theoretical findings by showing the effectiveness of the proposed approach and compare it with MMD-based estimators.

paragraphs: Distribution regression learns predictions whose inputs are probability distributions. A central challenge is representing each distribution in a way that preserves the properties relevant to prediction. Existing kernel mean embeddings offer strong statistical foundations, but the metric they implicitly use, maximum mean discrepancy, may be less suitable for capturing geometric relationships between distributions.

The paper proposes a representation based on Sliced Wasserstein distance, drawing on optimal transport. It uses this representation to build a kernel ridge regression estimator. The aim is to incorporate a geometry-sensitive comparison of distributions while retaining the kind of statistical guarantees available for established kernel approaches.

The authors prove universal consistency and excess risk bounds for the proposed estimator. These results address its statistical behavior, including the challenge that distributions are themselves observed through samples. Preliminary experiments demonstrate effectiveness and compare the method with MMD-based estimators. The contribution is therefore primarily a theoretically supported alternative representation, with initial empirical evidence for using transport geometry in distribution-level prediction.
summary.tldr: Sliced Wasserstein kernels bring optimal-transport geometry to distribution regression while supporting consistency and excess risk guarantees.

title: Distribution Regression with Sliced Wasserstein Kernels

abstract: Across applications spanning supervised classification and sequential control, deep learning has been reported to find “shortcut” solutions that fail catastrophically under minor changes in the data distribution. In this paper, we show empirically that DNNs can be coaxed to avoid poor shortcuts by providing an additional “priming” feature computed from key input features, usually a coarse output estimate. Priming relies on approximate domain knowledge of these task-relevant key input features, which is often easy to obtain in practical settings. For example, one might prioritize recent frames over past frames in a video input for visual imitation learning, or salient foreground over background pixels for image classification. On NICO image classification, MuJoCo continuous control, and CARLA autonomous driving, our priming strategy works significantly better than several popular state-of-the-art approaches for feature selection and data augmentation. We connect these empirical findings to recent theoretical results on DNN optimization, and argue theoretically that priming distracts the optimizer away from poor shortcuts by creating better, simpler shortcuts.

paragraphs: Deep networks can solve a training task using shortcuts that break when the data distribution changes slightly. This paper investigates whether an additional input feature can steer learning toward more useful evidence. The proposed priming feature is computed from task-relevant inputs and is usually a rough estimate of the desired output.

Priming depends on approximate domain knowledge about which parts of the input matter. Examples include emphasizing recent video frames for visual imitation learning or foreground pixels for image classification. The approach gives the network an accessible summary of relevant evidence, and the authors argue theoretically that it attracts optimization toward better, simpler shortcuts instead of poor ones.

Priming performs significantly better than several leading feature-selection and data-augmentation approaches in these evaluations. The paper connects these empirical findings to recent theory on neural-network optimization, supporting the idea that useful guidance can work with the optimizer’s preference for simple solutions.
summary.tldr: Priming networks with a rough prediction from task-relevant features helps steer learning away from harmful shortcuts in the reported experiments.

title: Fighting Fire with Fire: Avoiding DNN Shortcuts through Priming

abstract: In practical federated learning scenarios, the participating devices may have different bitwidths for computation and memory storage by design. However, despite the progress made in device-heterogeneous federated learning scenarios, the heterogeneity in the bitwidth specifications in the hardware has been mostly overlooked. We introduce a pragmatic FL scenario with bitwidth heterogeneity across the participating devices, dubbed as Bitwidth Heterogeneous Federated Learning (BHFL). BHFL brings in a new challenge, that the aggregation of model parameters with different bitwidths could result in severe performance degeneration, especially for high-bitwidth models. To tackle this problem, we propose ProWD framework, which has a trainable weight dequantizer at the central server that progressively reconstructs the low-bitwidth weights into higher bitwidth weights, and finally into full-precision weights. ProWD further selectively aggregates the model parameters to maximize the compatibility across bit-heterogeneous weights. We validate ProWD against relevant FL baselines on the benchmark datasets, using clients with varying bitwidths. Our ProWD largely outperforms the baseline FL algorithms as well as naive approaches (e.g. grouped averaging) under the proposed BHFL scenario.

paragraphs: Devices participating in federated learning may store and compute model weights using different numbers of bits. This paper studies that hardware mismatch explicitly through Bitwidth Heterogeneous Federated Learning. Its central concern is that combining parameters represented at different precisions can seriously degrade model performance, particularly for models using higher precision.

The proposed ProWD framework places a trainable weight dequantizer at the central server. It progressively reconstructs low-bitwidth weights into higher-bitwidth weights and eventually full-precision weights. ProWD also selectively combines model parameters to improve compatibility across these different representations. These two components address both how incoming weights are reconstructed and how they are aggregated.

The authors evaluate ProWD on benchmark datasets with clients using varying bitwidths. In this setting, it substantially outperforms relevant federated learning baselines and straightforward approaches such as grouped averaging. The results identify numerical precision as a meaningful form of device heterogeneity and support treating it explicitly during server-side aggregation. The stated gains apply to the proposed mixed-bitwidth setting rather than establishing an advantage for every federated deployment.
summary.tldr: ProWD improves federated learning across devices with different numerical precisions by progressively reconstructing and selectively aggregating their weights.

title: Bitwidth Heterogeneous Federated Learning with Progressive Weight Dequantization

abstract: Learning structured representations of the visual world in terms of objects promises to significantly improve the generalization abilities of current machine learning models. While recent efforts to this end have shown promising empirical progress, a theoretical account of when unsupervised object-centric representation learning is possible is still lacking. Consequently, understanding the reasons for the success of existing object-centric methods as well as designing new theoretically grounded methods remains challenging. In the present work, we analyze when object-centric representations can provably be learned without supervision. To this end, we first introduce two assumptions on the generative process for scenes comprised of several objects, which we call compositionality and irreducibility. Under this generative process, we prove that the ground-truth object representations can be identified by an invertible and compositional inference model, even in the presence of dependencies between objects. We empirically validate our results through experiments on synthetic data. Finally, we provide evidence that our theory holds predictive power for existing object-centric models by showing a close correspondence between models’ compositionality and invertibility and their empirical identifiability.

paragraphs: Representing a visual scene as a collection of objects could help models generalise, but empirical success alone does not explain when such representations can be recovered without supervision. This paper develops conditions under which object-centric learning is theoretically possible, connecting assumptions about scene generation to properties of the inference model.

The authors introduce two assumptions on how multi-object scenes are generated: compositionality and irreducibility. Under this generative process, an inference model that is both invertible and compositional can identify the underlying object representations. The result allows dependencies between objects, so its stated guarantee does not require objects to be independent of one another.

Synthetic-data experiments validate the theoretical results. The authors also examine existing object-centric models and find a close relationship between their compositionality and invertibility and their empirical identifiability. This provides evidence that the theory helps predict which models recover object structure. The contribution is a conditional account of learnability together with empirical support for its relevance to current approaches, offering principles for understanding and designing object-based visual representations.
summary.tldr: Under compositionality and irreducibility assumptions, invertible compositional inference models can identify object representations even when objects are dependent.

title: Provably Learning Object-Centric Representations

abstract: Learning agent behaviors from observational data has shown to improve our understanding of their decision-making processes, advancing our ability to explain their interactions with the environment and other agents. While multiple learning techniques have been proposed in the literature, there is one particular setting that has not been explored yet: multi agent systems where agent identities remain anonymous. For instance, in financial markets labeled data that identifies market participant strategies is typically proprietary, and only the anonymous state-action pairs that result from the interaction of multiple market participants are publicly available. As a result, sequences of agent actions are not observable, restricting the applicability of existing work. In this paper, we propose a Policy Clustering algorithm, called K-SHAP, that learns to group anonymous state-action pairs according to the agent policies. We frame the problem as an Imitation Learning (IL) task, and we learn a world-policy able to mimic all the agent behaviors upon different environmental states. We leverage the world-policy to explain each anonymous observation through an additive feature attribution method called SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). Finally, by clustering the explanations we show that we are able to identify different agent policies and group observations accordingly. We evaluate our approach on simulated synthetic market data and a real-world financial dataset. We show that our proposal significantly and consistently outperforms the existing methods, identifying different agent strategies.

That anonymity prevents reconstruction of individual action sequences, limiting methods that depend on them. This paper studies how to group such observations by the policies behind them, motivated by financial markets where participant strategies and identities may be unavailable.

K-SHAP first treats the combined observations as an imitation learning problem. It trains a shared world-policy to mimic the agents' behavior across environmental states. The method then uses SHAP, an additive feature attribution technique, to explain each anonymous observation through that policy. Finally, it clusters the explanations to group observations associated with different agent policies.

The central idea is that explanations of decisions can provide a useful basis for separating behaviors within a mixed dataset. Evaluations on synthetic market simulations and a real financial dataset show significant, consistent improvements over existing methods in identifying different strategies. The reported outcome concerns recovering policy groupings from anonymous observations, making behavioral analysis possible in the setting the paper targets.
summary.tldr: K-SHAP clusters explanations from a shared imitation policy to identify different strategies in anonymous state-action observations.

title: K-SHAP: Policy Clustering Algorithm for Anonymous Multi-Agent State-Action Pairs

abstract: Concept shift is a prevailing problem in natural tasks like medical image segmentation where samples usually come from different subpopulations with variant correlations between features and labels. One common type of concept shift in medical image segmentation is the "information imbalance" between label-sparse samples with few (if any) segmentation labels and label-dense samples with plentiful labeled pixels. Existing distributionally robust algorithms have focused on adaptively truncating/down-weighting the "less informative" (i.e., label-sparse in our context) samples. To exploit data features of label-sparse samples more efficiently, we propose an adaptively weighted online optimization algorithm — AdaWAC — to incorporate data augmentation consistency regularization in sample reweighting. Our method introduces a set of trainable weights to balance the supervised loss and unsupervised consistency regularization of each sample separately. At the saddle point of the underlying objective, the weights assign label-dense samples to the supervised loss and label-sparse samples to the unsupervised consistency regularization. We provide a convergence guarantee by recasting the optimization as online mirror descent on a saddle point problem. Our empirical results demonstrate that AdaWAC not only enhances the segmentation performance and sample efficiency but also improves the robustness to concept shift on various medical image segmentation tasks with different UNet-style backbones.

The paper studies this information imbalance as a form of concept shift, where relationships between features and labels vary across subpopulations. Simply reducing the influence of sparsely labeled images can leave their visual information underused.

summary.tldr: AdaWAC adaptively assigns supervised and consistency-based learning signals to make better use of medical images with uneven label availability.

title: Adaptively Weighted Data Augmentation Consistency Regularization for Robust Optimization under Concept Shift

abstract: In this work, we provide a large-scale empirical study of the scaling properties of multilingual neural machine translation models. We examine how increases in the model size affect the model performance and investigate the role of the individual language pair weights on the scaling behavior. We find that these weights only affect the multiplicative factor of the scaling law, and in particular, the scaling exponent is unaffected by them. Through a novel joint scaling law formulation, we compute the effective number of parameters allocated to each language pair and examine the role of language similarity in the scaling behavior of our models. We find little evidence that language similarity has any impact. In contrast, “direction” of the multilinguality plays a significant role, with models translating from multiple languages into English having a larger number of effective parameters per task than their reversed counterparts. Finally, we leverage our observations to predict the performance of multilingual models trained with any language weighting at any scale, greatly reducing efforts required for language balancing in large multilingual models. Our findings apply to both in-domain and out-of-domain test sets and to multiple evaluation metrics, such as ChrF and BLEURT.

paragraphs: Multilingual translation models share capacity across language pairs, so model size and the relative training weight of each pair both matter. This paper empirically studies how those choices interact. The authors find that language-pair weights change the multiplicative factor in their scaling law while leaving its scaling exponent unaffected.

A joint scaling-law formulation lets them estimate an effective parameter allocation for each translation task. They use this description to investigate language similarity and translation direction. The study finds little evidence of an effect from language similarity. They provide an empirical basis for planning capacity and language balance in the studied multilingual translation setting.
summary.tldr: An empirical scaling framework predicts multilingual translation performance across model sizes and language weights, with translation direction influencing effective task capacity.

title: Scaling Laws for Multilingual Neural Machine Translation

abstract: State space models (SSMs) have high performance on long sequence modeling but require sophisticated initialization techniques and specialized implementations for high quality and runtime performance. We study whether a simple alternative can match SSMs in performance and efficiency: directly learning long convolutions over the sequence. We find that a key requirement to achieving high performance is keeping the convolution kernels smooth. We find that simple interventions-such as squashing the kernel weights-result in smooth kernels and recover SSM performance on a range of tasks including the long range arena, image classification, language modeling, and brain data modeling. Next, we develop FlashButterfly, an IO-aware algorithm to improve the runtime performance of long convolutions. FlashButterfly appeals to classic Butterfly decompositions of the convolution to reduce GPU memory IO and increase FLOP utilization. FlashButterfly speeds up convolutions by 2.2$\times$, and allows us to train on Path256, a challenging task with sequence length 64K, where we set state-of-the-art by 29.1 points while training 7.2$\times$ faster than prior work. Lastly, we introduce an extension to FlashButterfly that learns the coefficients of the Butterfly decomposition, increasing expressivity without increasing runtime. Using this extension, we outperform a Transformer on WikiText103 by 0.2 PPL with 30% fewer parameters.

paragraphs: State space models perform well on long sequences but can require sophisticated initialization and specialized implementations. It finds that smooth convolution kernels are important for strong performance, and simple changes such as squashing kernel weights recover state-space-model performance across several task families.

An extension learns the coefficients of the Butterfly decomposition, increasing expressivity without increasing runtime. summary.tldr: Smooth learned kernels and FlashButterfly make long convolutions a competitive, hardware-efficient approach to sequence modeling.

title: Simple Hardware-Efficient Long Convolutions for Sequence Modeling

abstract: We study the design of loss functions for click-through rates (CTR) to optimize (social) welfare in advertising auctions. Existing works either only focus on CTR predictions without consideration of business objectives (e.g., welfare) in auctions or assume that the distribution over the participants’ expected cost-per-impression (eCPM) is known a priori, then use various additional assumptions on the parametric form of the distribution to derive loss functions for predicting CTRs. In this work, we bring back the welfare objectives of ad auctions into CTR predictions and propose a novel weighted rankloss to train the CTR model. Compared to existing literature, our approach provides a provable guarantee on welfare but without assumptions on the eCPMs’ distribution while also avoiding the intractability of naively applying existing learning-to-rank methods. Further, we propose a theoretically justifiable technique for calibrating the losses using labels generated from a teacher network, only assuming that the teacher network has bounded $\ell_2$ generalization error. Finally, we demonstrate the advantages of the proposed loss on synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Predicting whether an advertisement will be clicked is part of an auction decision, so prediction quality alone need not capture the auction’s welfare objective. This paper designs the training loss for click-through-rate models around that downstream objective. Its proposed weighted ranking loss links model training to the welfare of advertising auctions.

The approach gives a provable welfare guarantee without assuming a distribution for participants’ expected cost per impression. That removes a distributional requirement used in earlier loss designs. It also avoids the computational intractability associated with naively applying existing learning-to-rank methods to this setting.

The authors additionally develop a theoretically justified way to calibrate the losses using labels from a teacher network. This part assumes that the teacher has bounded squared generalization error. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate advantages of the proposed loss. The contribution is therefore both an objective aligned with auction welfare and a supported method for incorporating teacher predictions, with the teacher’s error bound remaining an explicit condition.
summary.tldr: A weighted ranking loss aligns click-through-rate training with auction welfare and provides guarantees without assumptions on the eCPM distribution.

title: Pairwise Ranking Losses of Click-Through Rates Prediction for Welfare Maximization in Ad Auctions

abstract: Identifying invariants is an important program analysis task with applications towards program understanding, bug finding, vulnerability analysis, and formal verification. Existing tools for identifying program invariants rely on dynamic analysis, requiring traces collected from multiple executions in order to produce reliable invariants. We study the application of large language models to invariant prediction, finding that models trained on source code and fine-tuned for invariant generation can perform invariant prediction as static rather than dynamic analysis. Using a scratchpad approach where invariants are predicted sequentially through a program gives the best performance, finding invariants statically of quality comparable to those obtained by a dynamic analysis tool with access to five program traces.

paragraphs: Program invariants describe properties that hold at relevant points during program execution. Identifying them helps with understanding code, finding bugs, analyzing vulnerabilities, and formal verification. Existing tools discussed in this paper infer invariants from traces collected across multiple executions, so their analysis depends on actually running the program and observing its behavior.

The authors investigate whether large language models can predict invariants directly from source code. They use models trained on code and fine-tuned for invariant generation, allowing the prediction task to be performed statically. Their best-performing approach uses a scratchpad that predicts invariants sequentially through a program, organizing the analysis as a progression through the code.

In the reported study, this static approach produces invariants of quality comparable to a dynamic analysis tool supplied with five program traces. That finding supports code-based invariant prediction as a useful capability of the studied models. The comparison concerns the quality of predicted invariants; it does not turn those predictions into a general guarantee of program correctness.
summary.tldr: Code-trained language models can predict program invariants statically, with sequential scratchpads achieving quality comparable to a tool using five execution traces.

title: Can Large Language Models Reason about Program Invariants?

abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have relied heavily on the use of large Transformers due to their ability to learn at scale. However, the core building block of Transformers, the attention operator, exhibits quadratic cost in sequence length, limiting the amount of context accessible. Existing subquadratic methods based on low-rank and sparse approximations need to be combined with dense attention layers to match Transformers at scale, indicating a gap in capability. In this work, we propose Hyena, a subquadratic drop-in replacement for attention constructed by interleaving implicitly parametrized long convolutions and data-controlled gating. In challenging reasoning tasks on sequences of thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens, Hyena improves accuracy by more than 50 points over operators relying on state-space models, transfer functions, and other implicit and explicit methods, matching attention-based models. We set a new state-of-the-art for dense-attention-free architectures on language modeling in standard datasets WikiText103 and The Pile, reaching Transformer quality with a 20% reduction in training compute required at sequence length 2k. Hyena operators are 2x faster than highly optimized attention at sequence length 8k, with speedups of 100x at 64k.

paragraphs: Attention becomes expensive as sequences grow because its cost scales quadratically with sequence length. This paper introduces Hyena as a subquadratic replacement for attention. Its construction alternates implicitly parameterized long convolutions with data-controlled gates, combining long-range sequence processing with operations whose behavior depends on the input.

The authors evaluate Hyena on reasoning tasks spanning thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens. They report accuracy gains of more than 50 points over the compared state-space, transfer-function, and other implicit and explicit operators, while matching attention-based models. These results address whether lower-cost sequence operators can retain capabilities associated with attention.

On WikiText103 and The Pile, Hyena sets a reported state of the art among architectures without dense attention. It reaches Transformer quality with 20% less training compute at sequence length 2k. Operator measurements show twice the speed of highly optimized attention at 8k and a hundredfold speedup at 64k. These findings distinguish model-quality results from operator-speed measurements while showing advantages at the evaluated sequence lengths.
summary.tldr: Hyena combines long convolutions and input-dependent gating to match attention-based models in reported evaluations with lower sequence-processing costs.

title: Hyena Hierarchy: Towards Larger Convolutional Language Models

abstract: To reduce the difficulty of annotation, partial label learning (PLL) has been widely studied, where each example is ambiguously annotated with a set of candidate labels instead of the exact correct label. PLL assumes that the candidate label set contains the correct label, which induces disambiguation, i.e., identification of the correct label in the candidate label set, adopted in most PLL methods. However, this assumption is impractical as no one could guarantee the existence of the correct label in the candidate label set under real-world scenarios. Therefore, Unreliable Partial Label Learning (UPLL) is investigated where the correct label of each example may not exist in the candidate label set. In this paper, we propose a fusion framework of refinement and disambiguation named FREDIS to handle the UPLL problem. Specifically, with theoretical guarantees, not only does disambiguation move incorrect labels from candidate labels to non-candidate labels but also refinement, an opposite procedure, moves correct labels from non-candidate labels to candidate labels. Besides, we prove that the classifier trained by our framework could eventually approximate the Bayes optimal classifier. Extensive experiments on widely used benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

paragraphs: Partial label learning gives each training example several possible labels and asks the model to identify the correct one. Standard approaches assume that the correct answer is somewhere in that candidate set. This paper considers unreliable partial labels, where the correct label may be missing entirely. Under that condition, simply choosing among the supplied candidates cannot fix every annotation.

FREDIS combines two complementary procedures. Disambiguation moves incorrect labels out of the candidate set, while refinement brings correct labels into it from the non-candidate set. Allowing movement in both directions addresses both ambiguity within the annotations and omissions from them. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for these procedures.

They also prove that a classifier trained within their framework could eventually approximate the Bayes optimal classifier, the best classifier for the underlying data distribution. That is a theoretical approximation result, rather than a claim that every trained model already reaches that ideal. Experiments on widely used benchmarks support the effectiveness of combining refinement with disambiguation.
summary.tldr: FREDIS handles unreliable candidate labels by removing incorrect options and adding missing correct ones within a theoretically supported framework.

title: FREDIS: A Fusion Framework of Refinement and Disambiguation for Unreliable Partial Label Learning

abstract: The performance of learning models often deteriorates when deployed in out-of-sample environments. To ensure reliable deployment, we propose a stability evaluation criterion based on distributional perturbations. Conceptually, our stability evaluation criterion is defined as the minimal perturbation required on our observed dataset to induce a prescribed deterioration in risk evaluation. In this paper, we utilize the optimal transport (OT) discrepancy with moment constraints on the (sample, density) space to quantify this perturbation. Therefore, our stability evaluation criterion can address both data corruptions and sub-population shifts—the two most common types of distribution shifts in real-world scenarios. To further realize practical benefits, we present a series of tractable convex formulations and computational methods tailored to different classes of loss functions. The key technical tool to achieve this is the strong duality theorem provided in this paper. Empirically, we validate the practical utility of our stability evaluation criterion across a host of real-world applications. These empirical studies showcase the criterion’s ability not only to compare the stability of different learning models and features but also to provide valuable guidelines and strategies to further improve models.

paragraphs: A model’s performance can deteriorate when deployment data differ from the observed dataset. This paper proposes measuring stability by asking how much the data distribution must change to cause a specified deterioration in evaluated risk. The criterion turns sensitivity to distribution shift into a minimum-perturbation problem.

The authors quantify perturbations using optimal transport with moment constraints over a space that includes both samples and density. This formulation accommodates changes to the data themselves as well as changes in the relative prevalence of subpopulations. It therefore provides a common framework for analyzing data corruption and subpopulation shift.

To make the criterion usable, the paper establishes a strong duality theorem and derives tractable convex formulations and computational methods for different loss-function classes. Empirical studies across real-world applications show that the criterion can compare the stability of models and features and help guide model improvement. The contribution combines a concrete question about distributional sensitivity with mathematical and computational tools for evaluating it.
summary.tldr: The proposed stability criterion measures the smallest distributional perturbation needed to cause a specified increase in risk.

title: Stability Evaluation through Distributional Perturbation Analysis

abstract: Large-scale pre-trained vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) have shown powerful zero-shot transfer capabilities in image recognition tasks. Recent approaches typically employ supervised fine-tuning methods to adapt CLIP for zero-shot multi-label image recognition tasks. However, obtaining sufficient multi-label annotated image data for training is challenging and not scalable. In this paper, we propose a new language-driven framework for zero-shot multi-label recognition that eliminates the need for annotated images during training. Leveraging the aligned CLIP multi-modal embedding space, our method utilizes language data generated by LLMs to train a cross-modal classifier, which is subsequently transferred to the visual modality. During inference, directly applying the classifier to visual inputs may limit performance due to the modality gap. To address this issue, we introduce a cross-modal mapping method that maps image embeddings to the language modality while retaining crucial visual information. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms other zero-shot multi-label recognition methods and achieves competitive results compared to few-shot methods.

paragraphs: Multi-label image recognition asks a model to identify several applicable labels in one image. Adapting vision-language models for this task often requires images annotated with multiple labels, which are difficult to obtain at scale. This paper proposes training the task classifier from language data without requiring annotated images.

The method uses language generated by large language models together with CLIP’s aligned image and text embedding space. A classifier trained in the language modality is then transferred to visual inputs. This approach makes the shared embedding space the connection between the training information supplied as text and the images classified at inference.

Direct transfer can lose performance because image and language embeddings still differ. The authors therefore introduce a mapping that moves image embeddings toward the language modality while retaining crucial visual information. Experiments show improvements over other zero-shot multi-label recognition methods and competitive performance against few-shot methods. These findings support combining language-driven classifier training with an explicit correction for the modality gap.
summary.tldr: The framework trains a multi-label image classifier from generated language and maps image embeddings into the language modality for effective transfer.

title: Language-Driven Cross-Modal Classifier for Zero-Shot Multi-Label Image Recognition

abstract: The decoder-only Transformer architecture with causal masking and relative position encoding (RPE) has become the de facto choice in language modeling. Despite its exceptional performance across various tasks, we have identified two limitations: First, it prevents all attended tokens from having zero weights during the softmax stage, even if the current embedding has sufficient self-contained information. This compels the model to assign disproportional excessive attention to specific tokens. Second, RPE-based Transformers are not universal approximators due to their limited capacity at encoding absolute positional information, which limits their application in position-critical tasks. In this work, we propose StableMask: a parameter-free method to address both limitations by refining the causal mask. It introduces pseudo-attention values to balance attention distributions and encodes absolute positional information via a progressively decreasing mask ratio. StableMask’s effectiveness is validated both theoretically and empirically, showing significant enhancements in language models with parameter sizes ranging from 71M to 1.4B across diverse datasets and encoding methods. We further show that it supports integration with existing optimization techniques, making it easily usable in practical applications.

paragraphs: This paper identifies two limitations in decoder-only Transformers that combine causal masking with relative position encoding. First, softmax attention forces some weight onto attended tokens even when the current embedding already contains sufficient information. Second, limited representation of absolute position prevents the studied relative-position Transformers from being universal approximators.

StableMask addresses both issues by changing the causal mask without adding parameters. It introduces pseudo-attention values to balance attention distributions and uses a progressively decreasing mask ratio to encode absolute positional information. The mask thus helps control both how attention is distributed and what positional information the model can represent.

The authors support the method with theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation. They report significant improvements across language models ranging from 71 million to 1.4 billion parameters, using varied datasets and encoding methods. StableMask also integrates with existing optimization techniques. The contribution shows how a change to masking can address representational and attention-allocation issues within the decoder-only architecture.
summary.tldr: StableMask modifies causal masking without extra parameters to improve attention allocation and encode absolute position.

title: StableMask: Refining Causal Masking in Decoder-only Transformer

abstract: In the evolving landscape of natural language processing (NLP), fine-tuning pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) with first-order (FO) optimizers like SGD and Adam has become standard. Yet, as LLMs grow in size, the substantial memory overhead from back-propagation (BP) for FO gradient computation presents a significant challenge. Addressing this issue is crucial, especially for applications like on-device training where memory efficiency is paramount. This paper proposes a shift towards BP-free, zeroth-order (ZO) optimization as a solution for reducing memory costs during LLM fine-tuning, building on the initial concept introduced by (Malladi et al., 2023). Unlike traditional ZO-SGD methods, ou让work expands the exploration to a wider array of ZO optimization techniques, through a comprehensive, first-of-its-kind benchmarking study across five LLM families, three task complexities, and five fine-tuning schemes. Our study unveils previously overlooked optimization principles, highlighting the importance of task alignment, the role of the forward gradient method, and the balance between algorithm complexity and fine-tuning performance. We further introduce novel enhancements to ZO optimization, including block-wise descent, hybrid training, and gradient sparsity. Our study offers a promising direction for achieving further memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. Codes to reproduce all our experiments will be made public.
originalAbstract: In the evolving landscape of natural language processing (NLP), fine-tuning pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) with first-order (FO) optimizers like SGD and Adam has become standard. Yet, as LLMs grow in size, the substantial memory overhead from back-propagation (BP) for FO gradient computation presents a significant challenge. Addressing this issue is crucial, especially for applications like on-device training where memory efficiency is paramount. This paper proposes a shift towards BP-free, zeroth-order (ZO) optimization as a solution for reducing memory costs during LLM fine-tuning, building on the initial concept introduced by (Malladi et al., 2023). Unlike traditional ZO-SGD methods, ou让work expands the exploration to a wider array of ZO optimization techniques, through a comprehensive, first-of-its-kind benchmarking study across five LLM families, three task complexities, and five fine-tuning schemes. Our study unveils previously overlooked optimization principles, highlighting the importance of task alignment, the role of the forward gradient method, and the balance between algorithm complexity and fine-tuning performance. We further introduce novel enhancements to ZO optimization, including block-wise descent, hybrid training, and gradient sparsity. Our study offers a promising direction for achieving further memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. Codes to reproduce all our experiments will be made public.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large language models with optimizers such as SGD and Adam normally requires backpropagation, whose memory demands become challenging as models grow. This benchmark investigates zeroth-order optimization as a route to adaptation without backpropagation. The motivation is especially relevant when training must fit within limited memory, including on-device settings.

The study broadens the investigation beyond conventional zeroth-order SGD. It compares techniques across five language-model families, three levels of task complexity, and five fine-tuning schemes. This scope lets the authors examine how optimization choices interact with the task and adaptation setup, rather than treating memory-efficient fine-tuning as a single algorithmic choice.

The reported findings emphasize task alignment, the role of the forward gradient method, and the balance between algorithmic complexity and fine-tuning performance. The paper also introduces enhancements involving block-wise descent, hybrid training, and gradient sparsity. Its contribution is both a comparative assessment and a set of directions for improving zeroth-order methods. The findings present a promising path toward lower-memory fine-tuning, with performance tied to the choices made about training and optimization.
summary.tldr: This benchmark studies a broad range of backpropagation-free fine-tuning methods and identifies optimization choices that matter for memory-efficient LLM adaptation.

title: Revisiting Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning: A Benchmark

abstract: Scaling laws are powerful tools to predict the performance of large language models. However, current scaling laws fall short of accounting for inference costs. In this work, we first show that model architecture affects inference latency, where models of the same size can have up to $3.5\times$ difference in latency. To tackle this challenge, we modify the Chinchilla scaling laws to co-optimize the model parameter count, the number of training tokens, and the model architecture. Due to the reason that models of similar training loss exhibit gaps in downstream evaluation, we also propose a novel method to train inference-efficient models based on the revised scaling laws. We perform extensive empirical studies to fit and evaluate our inference-aware scaling laws. We vary model parameters from 80M to 1B, training tokens from 1.6B to 30B, and model shapes, training 63 models. Guided by our inference-efficient scaling law and model selection method, we release the Morph-1B model, which improves inference latency by $1.8\times$ while maintaining accuracy on downstream tasks compared to open-source models, pushing the Pareto frontier of accuracy-latency tradeoff. Notably, our experiments reveal that wider and shallower models can yield efficiency gains while preserving accuracy.

paragraphs: A language model's parameter count does not fully determine how quickly it runs. The authors find latency differences of up to 3.5 times among models of the same size. This motivates scaling laws that account for architecture and inference cost alongside the training resources normally used to predict performance.

The paper modifies Chinchilla scaling laws to jointly consider parameter count, training-token count, and model architecture. It also introduces a method for training inference-efficient models because similar training losses can still correspond to different downstream performance. The empirical study trains 63 models, spanning 80 million to one billion parameters and 1.6 billion to 30 billion training tokens, with varied shapes.

The resulting Morph-1B model improves inference latency by a factor of 1.8 while maintaining downstream accuracy relative to the compared open-source models. The experiments also show that wider, shallower designs can preserve accuracy while improving efficiency. These findings make model shape a practical part of choosing the accuracy–latency tradeoff, alongside size and training duration.
summary.tldr: Inference-aware scaling laws jointly optimize model size, training tokens, and architecture to improve language-model latency while preserving downstream accuracy.

title: Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models

abstract: Watermarking, the process by which Large Language Model (LLM) servers imbed an imperceptible signal at inference time in order to detect text generated by their own models, has grown in importance due to the significant improvements in natural language processing tasks by modern LLMs. Current approaches are often impractical due to generation latency, detection time, degradation in text quality, or robustness; such problems often arise due to the focus on token level watermarking, which ignores the inherent structure of text. In this work, we introduce a new scheme, GaussMark, that is simple and efficient to implement, has formal statistical guarantees, comes at no cost in generation latency, and embeds the watermark into the weights of the model itself, providing a structural watermark. Our approach is based on Gaussian independence testing and is motivated by recent empirical observations that minor additive corruptions to LLM weights can result in models of identical (or even improved) quality. We provide formal statistical bounds on the validity and power of our procedure and, through an extensive suite of experiments, demonstrate that GaussMark is reliable, efficient, relatively robust to corruption, and can be instantiated with essentially no loss in model quality.

paragraphs: Language-model watermarking aims to make generated text detectable as coming from a particular model. Existing approaches can introduce costs in generation speed, detection, text quality, or resistance to modification. GaussMark places the watermark in model weights, creating a structural signal without adding generation latency.

The method is based on Gaussian independence testing. It is motivated by observations that small additive changes to language-model weights can preserve, and sometimes improve, model quality. The paper develops formal statistical bounds for the watermarking procedure's validity and power, addressing both the reliability of its statistical conclusions and its ability to detect the embedded signal.

Experiments characterize GaussMark as efficient, reliable, and relatively resistant to corruption. They also show that it can be configured with essentially no loss of model quality. These findings support a practical route to watermarking through the model itself. The robustness claim remains qualified: the reported resistance to corruption is relative, rather than a claim that the watermark survives every possible alteration.
summary.tldr: GaussMark embeds statistically testable watermarks in language-model weights without adding generation latency and with essentially no quality loss in reported experiments.

title: GaussMark: A Practical Approach for Structural Watermarking of Language Models

abstract: Long-tailed learning has garnered increasing attention due to its practical significance. Among the various approaches, the fine-tuning paradigm has gained considerable interest with the advent of foundation models. However, most existing methods primarily focus on leveraging knowledge from these models, overlooking the inherent biases introduced by the imbalanced training data they rely on. In this paper, we examine how such imbalances from pre-training affect long-tailed downstream tasks. Specifically, we find the imbalance biases inherited in foundation models on downstream task as parameter imbalance and data imbalance. During fine-tuning, we observe that parameter imbalance plays a more critical role, while data imbalance can be mitigated using existing re-balancing strategies. Moreover, we find that parameter imbalance cannot be effectively addressed by current re-balancing techniques, such as adjusting the logits, during training, unlike data imbalance. To tackle both imbalances simultaneously, we build our method on causal learning and view the incomplete semantic factor as the confounder, which brings spurious correlations between input samples and labels. To resolve the negative effects of this, we propose a novel backdoor adjustment method that learns the true causal effect between input samples and labels, rather than merely fitting the correlations in the data. Notably, we achieve an average performance increase of about 1.67% on each dataset.

paragraphs: Long-tailed learning deals with datasets in which some classes appear much more often than others. Foundation models bring useful pretrained knowledge to these tasks, but they can also carry biases from imbalanced pre-training data. This paper separates the inherited effects into parameter imbalance and data imbalance.

The authors observe that parameter imbalance plays the more important role during fine-tuning. Existing rebalancing strategies can mitigate data imbalance, but techniques such as training-time logit adjustment do not effectively address the parameter imbalance they identify. Their method uses causal learning, treating an incomplete semantic factor as a confounder that creates spurious relationships between inputs and labels.

A proposed backdoor adjustment aims to recover the causal effect between inputs and labels while addressing both forms of imbalance. The authors report an average performance increase of about 1.67% on each dataset. The contribution is to distinguish imbalance embedded in pretrained parameters from imbalance in downstream data, then design an adjustment around that distinction. The findings explain why ordinary data rebalancing may leave an important source of bias unresolved.
summary.tldr: The paper distinguishes pretrained parameter imbalance from data imbalance and proposes causal backdoor adjustment to address both.

title: Rethinking the Bias of Foundation Model under Long-tailed Distribution

abstract: World models (WMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in prediction, generation, and planning tasks. Existing WMs primarily focus on unstructured data while cannot leverage the ubiquitous structured data, often represented as graphs, in the digital world. While multiple graph foundation models have been proposed, they focus on graph learning tasks and cannot extend to diverse multi-modal data and interdisciplinary tasks. To address these challenges, we propose the Graph World Model (GWM), a world model that supports both unstructured and graph-structured states with multi-modal information and represents diverse tasks as actions. The core of a GWM is a generic message-passing algorithm to aggregate structured information, either over a unified multi-modal token space by converting multi-modal data into text (GWM-T) or a unified multi-modal embedding space by modality-specific encoders (GWM-E). Notably, GWM introduces action nodes to support diverse tasks, where action nodes are linked to other nodes via direct reference or similarity computation. Extensive experiments on 6 tasks from diverse domains, including multi-modal generation and matching, recommendation, graph prediction, multi-agent, retrieval-augmented generation, and planning and optimization, show that the same GWM outperforms or matches domain-specific baselines’ performance, benefits from multi-hop structures, and demonstrate strong zero-shot/few-shot capabilities on unseen new tasks. Our codes for GWM is released at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/GWM.

paragraphs: Graph World Model aims to bring graph structure and multimodal information into a single world-model framework. The paper identifies a gap between world models centered on unstructured data and graph foundation models centered on graph-learning tasks. Its approach supports both graph-structured and unstructured states, while representing different tasks as actions within the model.

The core operation passes messages to aggregate information across structure. One version, GWM-T, converts multimodal data into text and works in a common token space. Another, GWM-E, uses modality-specific encoders to create a common embedding space. Action nodes connect tasks to other nodes through direct references or computed similarities, allowing the same framework to express different operations.

Across evaluations spanning generation, matching, recommendation, graph prediction, and other domains, the authors report performance matching or exceeding domain-specific baselines. They also find benefits from multihop structure and strong zero-shot or few-shot performance on unseen tasks. These findings support the usefulness of a shared structured representation for tasks usually addressed by separate specialized models.
summary.tldr: Graph World Model uses message passing and action nodes to handle diverse tasks over graph-structured and unstructured multimodal information.

title: Graph World Model

abstract: Solving the Nash equilibrium in normal-form games with large-scale strategy spaces presents significant challenges. Open-ended learning frameworks, such as PSRO and its variants, have emerged as effective solutions. However, these methods often lack an efficient metric for evaluating strategy improvement, which limits their effectiveness in approximating equilibria. In this paper, we introduce a novel evaluative metric called Advantage, which possesses desirable properties inherently connected to the Nash equilibrium, ensuring that each strategy update approaches equilibrium. Building upon this, we propose the Advantage Policy Space Response Oracle (A-PSRO), an innovative unified open-ended learning framework applicable to both zero-sum and general-sum games. A-PSRO leverages the Advantage as a refined evaluation metric, leading to a consistent learning objective for agents in normal-form games. Experiments showcase that A-PSRO significantly reduces exploitability in zero-sum games and improves rewards in general-sum games, outperforming existing algorithms and validating its practical effectiveness.

paragraphs: Finding a Nash equilibrium becomes difficult when a game offers a very large set of strategies. Open-ended methods such as Policy Space Response Oracle expand the strategies under consideration as learning proceeds. This paper addresses a weakness in that process: evaluating whether a newly learned strategy actually moves the system toward equilibrium.

The authors introduce a metric called Advantage, designed around mathematical properties connected to Nash equilibrium. They establish that the metric makes each strategy update approach equilibrium. Their A-PSRO framework uses this measure to give agents a consistent learning objective across both zero-sum games, where interests directly oppose one another, and general-sum games.

Experiments report lower exploitability in zero-sum games and higher rewards in general-sum games, outperforming the algorithms evaluated. These outcomes reflect different practical goals: resisting an opponent's ability to take advantage of a strategy, and improving rewards when interests are not strictly opposed. The contribution combines a theoretically motivated measure of progress with a framework that uses it to guide strategy learning.
summary.tldr: A-PSRO uses an equilibrium-linked Advantage metric to guide strategy learning in both zero-sum and general-sum games.

title: A-PSRO: A Unified Strategy Learning Method with Advantage Metric for Normal-form Games

abstract: Denoising diffusion models have driven significant progress in the field of Bayesian inverse problems. Recent approaches use pre-trained diffusion models as priors to solve a wide range of such problems, only leveraging inference-time compute and thereby eliminating the need to retrain task-specific models on the same dataset. To approximate the posterior of a Bayesian inverse problem, a diffusion model samples from a sequence of intermediate posterior distributions, each with an intractable likelihood function. This work proposes a novel mixture approximation of these intermediate distributions. Since direct gradient-based sampling of these mixtures is infeasible due to intractable terms, we propose a practical method based on Gibbs sampling. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on image inverse problems, utilizing both pixel- and latent-space diffusion priors, as well as on source separation with an audio diffusion model. The code is available at https://www.github.com/badr-moufad/mgdm.

paragraphs: Bayesian inverse problems seek an underlying signal that could explain an observation while accounting for uncertainty. A pretrained diffusion model can provide prior knowledge about plausible signals, allowing different reconstruction problems to be tackled at inference time without retraining a separate model for each task.

The difficulty is combining that prior with the observation throughout the diffusion sampling process. The intermediate distributions needed for posterior sampling have likelihood terms that cannot be evaluated tractably. The paper proposes approximating these distributions with mixtures. However, this alone does not make ordinary gradient-based sampling feasible: some required terms remain intractable. The authors therefore develop a practical sampling method based on Gibbs sampling.

The approach is evaluated on image inverse problems using diffusion priors operating both directly on pixels and in latent spaces, and on audio source separation. These experiments support the framework across different signal types and representations. Its central contribution is a mixture approximation paired with a sampling procedure that makes that approximation usable.
summary.tldr: A mixture approximation and Gibbs-based sampling method use pretrained diffusion models to solve inverse problems without task-specific retraining.

title: A Mixture-Based Framework for Guiding Diffusion Models

abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) struggles with coordination in sparse reward environments. Macro-actions —sequences of actions executed as single decisions— facilitate long-term planning but introduce asynchrony, complicating Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE). Existing CTDE methods use padding to handle asynchrony, risking misaligned asynchronous experiences and spurious correlations. We propose the Agent-Centric Actor-Critic (ACAC) algorithm to manage asynchrony without padding. ACAC uses agent-centric encoders for independent trajectory processing, with an attention-based aggregation module integrating these histories into a centralized critic for improved temporal abstractions. The proposed structure is trained via a PPO-based algorithm with a modified Generalized Advantage Estimation for asynchronous environments. Experiments show ACAC accelerates convergence and enhances performance over baselines in complex MARL tasks.

paragraphs: Teams of learning agents face a timing problem when their decisions represent extended sequences of actions. These macro-actions help with long-term planning when rewards are sparse, but different agents can finish them at different times. That makes it harder to train agents together while allowing each to operate independently afterward.

Existing approaches handle unequal timing by padding experience sequences. The paper identifies a risk that this can misalign experiences and introduce misleading correlations. Agent-Centric Actor-Critic, or ACAC, instead processes each agent’s trajectory independently through an agent-specific perspective. An attention-based module then brings those histories together for a centralized critic, which evaluates behavior using information across the team.

ACAC trains this structure with a PPO-based method and modifies Generalized Advantage Estimation to accommodate asynchronous experience. The experiments report faster convergence and better performance than baselines on complex multi-agent tasks. The contribution connects the representation of individual histories with the training procedure, allowing centralized learning to account for agents whose meaningful decisions occur on different schedules.
summary.tldr: ACAC improves asynchronous multi-agent learning by processing each agent’s history independently before combining histories in a centralized critic.

title: Agent-Centric Actor-Critic for Asynchronous Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Detailed image captioning is essential for tasks like data generation and aiding visually impaired individuals. High-quality captions require a balance between precision and recall, which remains challenging for current multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In this work, we hypothesize that this limitation stems from weakening and increasingly noisy visual attention as responses lengthen. To address this issue, we propose SPARC (Selective Progressive Attention ReCalibration), a training-free method that enhances the contribution of visual tokens during decoding. SPARC is founded on three key observations: (1) increasing the influence of all visual tokens reduces recall; thus, SPARC selectively amplifies visual tokens; (2) as captions lengthen, visual attention becomes noisier, so SPARC identifies critical visual tokens by leveraging attention differences across time steps; (3) as visual attention gradually weakens, SPARC reinforces it to preserve its influence. Our experiments, incorporating both automated and human evaluations, demonstrate that existing methods improve the precision of MLLMs at the cost of recall. In contrast, our proposed method enhances both precision and recall with minimal computational overhead.

paragraphs: Detailed image captions must include relevant content while keeping their claims accurate. The paper hypothesizes that multimodal language models struggle with this balance because attention to the image becomes weaker and noisier as a response grows. It proposes SPARC, a method that adjusts visual attention during generation without additional training.

SPARC selectively strengthens visual tokens rather than boosting every visual token. The authors observe that indiscriminate amplification reduces recall. To identify important tokens despite increasing noise, the method uses differences in attention across generation steps. It also progressively reinforces visual attention to maintain the image’s influence as the caption becomes longer.

Automated and human evaluations show that existing methods improve precision at the expense of recall, whereas SPARC improves both with minimal computational overhead. In practical terms, the reported captions become more accurate while also covering more relevant image content. The findings support selective attention adjustment as a useful intervention during decoding, while the proposed weakening-and-noise explanation is introduced as the authors’ hypothesis about the underlying problem.
summary.tldr: SPARC selectively reinforces visual attention during caption generation, improving both precision and recall without additional training.

title: Visual Attention Never Fades: Selective Progressive Attention ReCalibration for Detailed Image Captioning in Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Foundation Models have demonstrated significant success across various domains in Artificial Intelligence (AI), yet their capabilities for brainwave modeling remain unclear. In this paper, we comprehensively evaluate current Large Brainwave Foundation Models (LBMs) through systematic fine-tuning experiments across multiple Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) benchmark tasks, including memory tasks and sleep stage classification. Our extensive analysis shows that state-of-the-art LBMs achieve only marginal improvements (0.5%) over traditional deep architectures while requiring significantly more parameters (millions vs thousands), raising important questions about their efficiency and applicability in BCI contexts. Moreover, through detailed ablation studies and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), we significantly reduce trainable parameters without performance degradation, while demonstrating that architectural and training inefficiencies limit LBMs’ current capabilities. Our experiments span both full model fine-tuning and parameter-efficient adaptation techniques, providing insights into optimal training strategies for BCI applications. We pioneer the application of LoRA to LBMs, revealing that performance benefits generally emerge when adapting multiple neural network components simultaneously. These findings highlight the critical need for domain-specific development strategies to advance LBMs, suggesting that current architectures may require redesign to fully leverage the potential of foundation models in brainwave analysis.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates whether large brainwave foundation models deliver practical benefits for brain-computer interfaces. The authors systematically fine-tune existing models across benchmark tasks, including memory tasks and sleep-stage classification. They examine both full-model adaptation and methods that update only a small portion of the model's parameters.

In the reported experiments, leading brainwave foundation models improve performance by only 0.5% over traditional deep architectures, despite using millions of parameters where the traditional models use thousands. Ablation studies and Low-Rank Adaptation show that the number of trainable parameters can be substantially reduced without degrading performance. These findings distinguish the cost of adapting a large model from the predictive benefit it actually delivers.

The authors also find that LoRA's benefits generally emerge when several network components are adapted together. Their analysis attributes current limitations partly to architectural and training inefficiencies. The results therefore motivate development tailored to brainwave data, and suggest that architecture redesign may be needed to realize stronger foundation-model benefits in these applications.
summary.tldr: Brainwave foundation models show small benchmark gains despite large parameter counts, while LoRA reduces adaptation costs without degrading performance.

title: Are Large Brainwave Foundation Models Capable Yet ? Insights from Fine-Tuning

abstract: Multimodal Reward Models (MM-RMs) are crucial for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences, particularly as LLMs increasingly interact with multimodal data. However, we find that MM-RMs trained on existing datasets often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution data due to their reliance on unimodal spurious correlations, primarily text-only shortcuts within the training distribution, which prevents them from leveraging true multimodal reward functions. To address this, we introduce a Shortcut-aware MM-RM learning algorithm that mitigates this issue by dynamically reweighting training samples, shifting the distribution toward better multimodal understanding, and reducing dependence on unimodal spurious correlations. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in generalization, downstream task performance, and scalability, establishing a more robust framework for multimodal reward modeling. Our source code is provided on https://github.com/alignrm/Generalizable-MM-RM.

However, we find that MM-RMs trained on existing datasets often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution data due to their reliance on unimodal spurious correlations, primarily text-only shortcuts within the training distribution, which prevents them from leveraging true multimodal reward functions. To address this, we introduce a Shortcut-aware MM-RM learning algorithm that mitigates this issue by dynamically reweighting training samples, shifting the distribution toward better multimodal understanding, and reducing dependence on unimodal spurious correlations. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in generalization, downstream task performance, and scalability, establishing a more robust framework for multimodal reward modeling. Our source code is provided on https://github.com/alignrm/Generalizable-MM-RM.

paragraphs: Multimodal reward models judge outputs according to human preferences when multiple types of information are involved. The paper finds that models trained on existing datasets can rely heavily on text-only shortcuts. These correlations may be useful within the training distribution but fail on unfamiliar data, preventing the reward model from learning a genuinely multimodal basis for its judgments.

The proposed shortcut-aware learning algorithm dynamically reweights training examples. By changing their relative influence, it shifts the effective training distribution toward examples that encourage multimodal understanding and away from reliance on misleading single-modality correlations. The intervention therefore targets how the available data shapes reward learning, with shortcut dependence treated as a central obstacle to generalization.

Experiments report significant improvements in generalization, downstream task performance, and scalability. These findings connect a specific training failure—successful prediction through unimodal cues—to broader weaknesses in reward-model behavior. The contribution is both diagnostic and methodological: it identifies an observed source of poor transfer and presents a sample-weighting approach that reduces its influence in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Shortcut-aware sample reweighting improves multimodal reward models by reducing their dependence on misleading text-only correlations.

title: The Devil Is in the Details: Tackling Unimodal Spurious Correlations for Generalizable Multimodal Reward Models

abstract: Causal estimands can vary significantly depending on the relationship between outcomes in treatment and control groups, leading to wide partial identification (PI) intervals that impede decision making. Incorporating covariates can substantially tighten these bounds, but requires determining the range of PI over probability models consistent with the joint distributions of observed covariates and outcomes in treatment and control groups. This problem is known to be equivalent to a conditional optimal transport (COT) optimization task, which is more challenging than standard optimal transport (OT) due to the additional conditioning constraints. In this work, we study a tight relaxation of COT that effectively reduces it to standard OT, leveraging its well-established computational and theoretical foundations. Our relaxation incorporates covariate information and ensures narrower PI intervals for any value of the penalty parameter, while becoming asymptotically exact as a penalty increases to infinity. This approach preserves the benefits of covariate adjustment in PI and results in a data-driven estimator for the PI set that is easy to implement using existing OT packages. We analyze the convergence rate of our estimator and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive simulations, highlighting its practical use and superior performance compared to existing methods.

Covariates can narrow these partial identification intervals by restricting which probability models fit the observations. Extensive simulations demonstrate effectiveness and better performance than existing methods. The contribution combines tighter causal bounds with an accessible computational formulation, preserving benefits of covariate adjustment while drawing on established optimization tools.
summary.tldr: A covariate-aware optimal transport relaxation tightens causal identification intervals and approaches the exact conditional solution as its penalty grows.

title: Tightening Causal Bounds via Covariate-Aware Optimal Transport

abstract: Temporal sequences, even after stationarization, often exhibit leptokurtic distributions with fat tails and persistent distribution shifts. These properties destabilize feature dynamics, amplify model variance, and hinder model convergence in time series forecasting. To address this, we propose Morphing-Flow (MoF), a framework that combines a spline-based transform layer (Flow) and a test-time-trained method (Morph), which adaptively normalizes non-stationary, fat-tailed distributions while preserving critical extreme features. MoF ensures that inputs remain within a network’s effective activation space—a structured, normal-like distribution—even under distributional drift. Experiments across eight datasets show that MoF achieves state-of-the-art performance: With a simple linear backbone architecture, it matches the performance of state-of-the-art models on datasets such as Electricity and ETTh2. When paired with a patch-based Mamba architecture, MoF outperforms its closest competitor by 6.3% on average and reduces forecasting errors in fat-tailed datasets such as Exchange by 21.7%. Moreover, MoF acts as a plug-and-play module, boosting performance in existing models without architectural changes.

These properties can destabilize learned features, increase model variance, and make training harder. Morphing-Flow addresses the distribution presented to the forecasting network, aiming to normalize it while retaining the extreme values that carry useful information.

The framework combines Flow, a spline-based transformation layer, with Morph, a method trained at test time. Together they adapt nonstationary, fat-tailed inputs toward a structured, normal-like distribution within the network's effective activation range. The design explicitly seeks to preserve critical extreme features while adapting to distributional drift.
