With a patch-based Mamba architecture, it improves on its closest competitor by 6.3% on average and reduces forecasting errors by 21.7% on Exchange. It also improves existing models as a plug-and-play module without architectural changes. These results support adaptive input normalization as a useful contributor to forecasting performance across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Morphing-Flow adaptively normalizes shifting, fat-tailed time series while preserving important extremes and improving forecasting.

title: Slimming the Fat-Tail: Morphing-Flow for Adaptive Time Series Modeling

abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has shown effectiveness in aligning multi-modal large language models (MLLM) with human preferences. However, existing methods exhibit an imbalanced responsiveness to the data of varying hardness, tending to overfit on the easy-to-distinguish data while underfitting on the hard-to-distinguish data. In this paper, we propose Data- and Model-aware DPO (DAMA) to dynamically adjust the optimization process from two key aspects: (1) a data-aware strategy that incorporates data hardness, and (2) a model-aware strategy that integrates real-time model responses. By combining the two strategies, DAMA enables the model to effectively adapt to data with varying levels of hardness. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that DAMA not only significantly enhances the trustworthiness, but also improves the effectiveness over general tasks. For instance, on the Object HalBench, our DAMA-7B reduces response-level and mentioned-level hallucination by 90.0% and 95.3%, respectively, surpassing the performance of GPT-4V.

paragraphs: Preference training examples differ in how easily a model can distinguish the preferred response. The paper identifies an imbalance in existing Direct Preference Optimization methods for multimodal language models: they tend to overfit easy comparisons while underfitting difficult ones. Treating examples without adequately accounting for that difference can therefore distort the alignment process.

Data- and Model-aware DPO, or DAMA, adjusts optimization using two sources of information. Its data-aware component incorporates example hardness, while its model-aware component uses the model’s current responses. Combining them lets training respond both to the character of an example and to how the model presently handles it, supporting adaptation across difficulty levels.

Experiments on five benchmarks show improvements in trustworthiness and general task effectiveness. On Object HalBench, DAMA-7B reports reductions of 90.0% in response-level hallucination and 95.3% in mentioned-level hallucination, surpassing GPT-4V on that evaluation. These results support dynamically adjusting preference optimization as a way to improve alignment, with the stated hallucination gains tied to the named benchmark.
summary.tldr: DAMA adapts multimodal preference training to example difficulty and current model behavior, improving trustworthiness and general task performance.

title: DAMA: Data- and Model-aware Alignment of Multi-modal LLMs

abstract: We study the design of adaptive, sequential experiments for unbiased average treatment effect (ATE) estimation in the design-based potential outcomes setting. Our goal is to develop adaptive designs offering sublinear Neyman regret, meaning their efficiency must approach that of the hindsight-optimal nonadaptive design. Recent work [Dai et al, 2023] introduced ClipOGD, the first method achieving $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ expected Neyman regret under mild conditions. In this work, we propose adaptive designs with substantially stronger Neyman regret guarantees. In particular, we modify ClipOGD to obtain anytime $\widetilde{O}(\log T)$ Neyman regret under natural boundedness assumptions. Further, in the setting where experimental units have pre-treatment covariates, we introduce and study a class of contextual “multigroup” Neyman regret guarantees: Given a set of possibly overlapping groups based on the covariates, the adaptive design outperforms each group’s best non-adaptive designs. In particular, we develop a contextual adaptive design with $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ anytime multigroup Neyman regret. We empirically validate the proposed designs through an array of experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential experiments designed to estimate an average treatment effect without bias in the design-based potential-outcomes setting. It measures efficiency using Neyman regret: the gap relative to the best nonadaptive design chosen with hindsight. Sublinear regret means that the adaptive design approaches that benchmark’s efficiency as the experiment grows.

The authors modify ClipOGD to improve its previous square-root expected regret guarantee to an anytime logarithmic guarantee, up to suppressed logarithmic factors, under natural boundedness assumptions. The anytime property makes the guarantee applicable throughout the sequence of experimental units. The improvement strengthens the theoretical account of how quickly an adaptive design can approach the hindsight benchmark.

The paper also considers units with pretreatment covariates and possibly overlapping groups defined from them. It introduces multigroup guarantees that compare the adaptive design with each group’s best nonadaptive design. A contextual algorithm achieves anytime square-root multigroup regret, again with suppressed logarithmic factors. Experiments validate the proposed designs, complementing guarantees for both overall efficiency and performance across overlapping groups.
summary.tldr: Adaptive experimental designs achieve stronger Neyman regret bounds, including logarithmic regret under boundedness assumptions and contextual guarantees across overlapping groups.

title: Stronger Neyman Regret Guarantees for Adaptive Experimental Design

abstract: A recent line of work has shown promise in using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable features in neural network representations. However, the simple linear-nonlinear encoding mechanism in SAEs limits their ability to perform accurate sparse inference. Using compressed sensing theory, we prove that an SAE encoder is inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference, even in solvable cases. We then decouple encoding and decoding processes to empirically explore conditions where more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders. Our results reveal substantial performance gains with minimal compute increases in correct inference of sparse codes. We demonstrate this generalises to SAEs applied to large language models, where more expressive encoders achieve greater interpretability. This work opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations and analysing large language model activations.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders aim to explain neural network representations using a small set of active features. Their usefulness therefore depends partly on correctly identifying which features are present in an activation. This paper examines whether the usual encoder, consisting of a linear transformation followed by a nonlinearity, is expressive enough to perform that inference accurately.

Using compressed sensing theory, the authors prove that this encoding mechanism can be insufficient even when the underlying sparse inference problem is solvable. This establishes a gap between the existence of a recoverable sparse code and the encoder’s ability to find it. The authors then separate encoding from decoding to investigate when more sophisticated inference procedures recover codes more accurately.

Their experiments show substantial gains in correct sparse inference with only small increases in computation. They also apply more expressive encoders to sparse autoencoders for large language models and report greater interpretability. The findings identify inference quality as an important part of representation analysis: improving how features are recovered can improve the explanations obtained from them.
summary.tldr: Standard sparse autoencoder encoders have provable inference limits, while more expressive alternatives improve sparse recovery and reported interpretability with modest extra compute.

title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Many machine learning models require setting a parameter that controls their size before training, e.g. number of neurons in DNNs, or inducing points in GPs. Increasing capacity typically improves performance until all the information from the dataset is captured. After this point, computational cost keeps increasing, without improved performance. This leads to the question "How big is big enough?" We investigate this problem for Gaussian processes (single-layer neural networks) in continual learning. Here, data becomes available incrementally, and the final dataset size will therefore not be known before training, preventing the use of heuristics for setting a fixed model size. We develop a method to automatically adjust model size while maintaining near-optimal performance. Our experimental procedure follows the constraint that any hyperparameters must be set without seeing dataset properties, and we show that our method performs well across diverse datasets without the need to adjust its hyperparameter, showing it requires less tuning than others.

paragraphs: A model can waste computation when its capacity exceeds what the data support, but too little capacity can limit accuracy. Continual learning makes this choice harder because the final amount of data is unknown. This paper studies how to adjust Gaussian-process model size as observations arrive incrementally.

The proposed method changes model size automatically while maintaining near-optimal performance. It focuses on avoiding a fixed capacity chosen from advance knowledge of the dataset, such as a predetermined number of inducing points. This makes the size decision part of the continual-learning procedure rather than a one-time configuration based on a completed dataset.

Experiments enforce that hyperparameters are chosen without observing dataset properties. Under that constraint, the method works across diverse datasets without retuning its hyperparameter, demonstrating reduced tuning needs relative to alternatives. The contribution is adaptive capacity management for continual Gaussian processes; the abstract does not provide the detailed rule or a universal numerical threshold for when additional capacity stops helping.
summary.tldr: An adaptive model-size method lets continual Gaussian processes grow as needed without dataset-specific capacity tuning.

title: Adjusting Model Size in Continual Gaussian Processes: How Big is Big Enough?

abstract: Implicit neural representation (INR) has now been thrust into the limelight with its flexibility in high-fidelity flow field reconstruction tasks. However, the lack of standard benchmarking datasets and the grid independence assumption for INR-based methods hinder progress and adoption in real-world simulation scenarios. Moreover, naive adoptions of existing INR frameworks suffer from limited accuracy in capturing fine-scale structures and spatiotemporal dynamics. Tacking these issues, we first introduce HFR-Beach, a 5.4 TB public large-scale CFD dataset with 33,600 unsteady 2D and 3D vector fields for reconstructing high-fidelity flow fields. We further present PEINR, a physics-enhanced INR framework, to enrich the flow fields by concurrently enhancing numerical-precision and grid-resolution. Specifically, PEINR is mainly composed of physical encoding and transformer-based spatiotemporal fuser (TransSTF). Physical encoding decouples temporal and spatial components, employing Gaussian coordinate encoding and localized encoding techniques to capture the nonlinear characteristics of spatiotemporal dynamics and the stencil discretization of spatial dimensions, respectively. TransSTF fuses both spatial and temporal information via transformer for capturing long-range temporal dependencies. Qualitative and quantitative experiments and demonstrate that PEINR outperforms state-of-the-art INR-based methods in reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: Reconstructing fluid flow requires preserving small structures and changes across both space and time. Existing implicit neural representations can struggle with these details, and their assumption of grid independence can complicate use in simulation settings. This paper addresses the modeling problem alongside the shortage of standardized evaluation data.

The authors introduce HFR-Beach, a public 5.4-terabyte computational fluid dynamics dataset containing 33,600 unsteady two- and three-dimensional vector fields. Their PEINR model aims to improve numerical precision and grid resolution together. Its physical encoding separates temporal and spatial components, using Gaussian coordinate encoding and localized encoding to represent nonlinear dynamics and the spatial stencil structure.

A transformer-based spatiotemporal component then combines spatial and temporal information to capture dependencies over longer time spans. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations show better reconstruction quality than the state-of-the-art implicit representation methods compared. The contribution connects coordinate-based representation with simulation-relevant spatial structure and temporal information, while providing a large dataset for studying high-fidelity flow reconstruction.
summary.tldr: PEINR combines physical encoding and temporal attention to improve flow reconstruction, alongside a large public simulation dataset.

title: PEINR: A Physics-enhanced Implicit Neural Representation for High-Fidelity Flow Field Reconstruction

abstract: Extrapolating ultra-long contexts (text length $>$128K) remains a major challenge for large language models (LLMs), as most training-free extrapolation methods are not only severely limited by memory bottlenecks, but also suffer from the attention sink, which restricts their scalability and effectiveness in practice. In this work, we propose ParallelComp, a parallel long-context compression method that effectively overcomes the memory bottleneck, enabling 8B-parameter LLMs to extrapolate from 8K to 128K tokens on a single A100 80GB GPU in a training-free setting. ParallelComp splits the input into chunks, dynamically evicting redundant chunks and irrelevant tokens, supported by a parallel KV cache eviction mechanism. Importantly, we present a systematic theoretical and empirical analysis of attention biases in parallel attention—including the attention sink, recency bias, and middle bias—and reveal that these biases exhibit distinctive patterns under ultra-long context settings. We further design a KV cache eviction technique to mitigate this phenomenon. Experimental results show that ParallelComp enables an 8B model (trained on 8K context) to achieve 91.17% of GPT-4’s performance under ultra-long contexts, outperforming closed-source models such as Claude-2 and Kimi-Chat. We achieve a 1.76x improvement in chunk throughput, thereby achieving a 23.50x acceleration in the prefill stage with negligible performance loss and pave the way for scalable and robust ultra-long contexts extrapolation in LLMs. We release the code at https://github.com/menik1126/ParallelComp.

paragraphs: ParallelComp extends the amount of text a language model can process without additional training. It addresses both the memory demands of long inputs and attention biases that can distort which information receives emphasis. The reported system lets an 8-billion-parameter model trained for 8K tokens handle 128K tokens on one A100 GPU with 80GB of memory.

The method divides input into chunks and removes redundant chunks and irrelevant tokens through parallel key-value cache eviction. The authors also analyze attention sink, recency, and middle biases in parallel attention. Their theoretical and empirical findings show distinctive patterns at very long context lengths, motivating an eviction technique that mitigates these effects.

In the reported evaluation, the model reaches 91.17% of GPT-4’s performance and surpasses Claude-2 and Kimi-Chat. The paper reports 1.76 times higher chunk throughput and 23.50 times faster prefill with negligible performance loss. These results connect selective retention of context with both reduced memory pressure and faster processing in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: ParallelComp uses parallel context compression and cache eviction to extend an 8K-context model to 128K tokens without training.

title: ParallelComp: Parallel Long-Context Compressor for Length Extrapolation

abstract: Appropriate parameter initialization strategies are essential for reducing the high computational costs of training large pretrained models in various task scenarios. Graph HyperNetwork (GHN), a parameter initialization method, has recently demonstrated strong performance in initializing models. However, GHN still faces several challenges, including limited effectiveness in initializing larger models, poor performance on smaller datasets, and the requirement of task-specific GHN training, where each new task necessitates retraining the GHN model, leading to increased computational and storage overhead. To overcome these challenges, motivated by the recently proposed Learngene framework, we propose a novel method called Task-Aware Learngene (TAL). Briefly, our approach pretrains a TAL model under the guidance of a well-trained model and then performs multi-task tuning to obtain a shared TAL model that enables parameter prediction based on both model architectures and task-specific characteristics. Extensive experiments show the superiority of TAL. Models initialized with TAL outperform those initialized using GHN method by an average of 24.39% in terms of accuracy across Decathlon datasets.

paragraphs: Task-Aware Learngene, or TAL, focuses on choosing useful starting parameters for models before training. The paper builds on parameter prediction with Graph HyperNetworks, which it identifies as struggling with larger models, smaller datasets, and the need to train a separate initializer for each task. These difficulties increase computational and storage costs.

TAL first learns under the guidance of an already trained model. It then undergoes multi-task tuning to produce a shared initializer. This model predicts parameters using both the architecture being initialized and the characteristics of the target task, bringing structural and task information into the same parameter-generation process.

Experiments report that models initialized with TAL outperform those initialized with GHN by an average of 24.39% in accuracy across Decathlon datasets. The result supports the usefulness of a shared, task-aware initialization model in the evaluated setting. More broadly, the approach makes adaptation part of parameter prediction, addressing the overhead associated with maintaining separate task-specific initializers.
summary.tldr: TAL learns a shared initializer that predicts model parameters from architecture and task information, outperforming GHN initialization on Decathlon datasets.

title: Learngene Tells You How to Customize: Task-Aware Parameter Initialization at Flexible Scales

abstract: Large output spaces, also referred to as Extreme multilabel classification (XMC), is a setting that arises, e.g., in large-scale tagging and product-to-product recommendation, and is characterized by the number of labels ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions. This means that the linear classification head, usually only a tiny fraction of the overall model, turns into the main driver for compute and memory demand. Current state-of-the-art XMC methods predominantly rely on FP16-FP32 mixed-precision training, which we show can be unstable, and inefficient in terms of memory usage and computational overhead. Meanwhile, existing low-precision methods typically retain higher precision for the classification layer. In this work, we propose ELMO, a pure low-precision training framework for XMC models using BFloat16 and Float8 data types. By leveraging Kahan summation and stochastic rounding, we demonstrate that XMC models can be effectively trained entirely in Float8, without relying on single-precision master weights or tensor scaling. Low-precision training, combined with our proposed memory optimizations—gradient fusion and chunking—enables significant reductions in GPU memory usage. For example, we train a 3-million-label XMC model with only 6.6 GiB of GPU memory, compared to the 39.7GiB required by the optimized SOTA method, Renee without compromising accuracy.

For example, we train a 3-million-label XMC model with only 6.6 GiB of GPU memory, compared to the 39.7GiB required by the optimized SOTA method, Renee without compromising accuracy.

paragraphs: When a classification problem has hundreds of thousands or millions of possible labels, the output layer becomes a major computational expense. ELMO targets this extreme multilabel setting, including large-scale tagging and product recommendations. The authors show that commonly used FP16–FP32 mixed-precision training can be unstable and impose unnecessary memory and computation costs.

ELMO provides a low-precision training framework using BFloat16 and Float8. It combines Kahan summation and stochastic rounding to train models entirely in Float8 without single-precision master weights or tensor scaling. This matters because retaining higher-precision copies or operations in the classification layer can preserve much of the cost that low-precision computation is intended to remove.

The framework also uses gradient fusion and chunking to reduce peak memory requirements. In a reported example with three million labels, training uses 6.6 GiB of GPU memory, compared with 39.7 GiB for the optimized Renee method, without compromising accuracy. The result demonstrates how numerical techniques and memory management can work together to make very large output spaces more manageable.
summary.tldr: ELMO combines low-precision training and memory optimizations to train a three-million-label model with substantially less GPU memory and no accuracy loss.

title: ELMO : Efficiency via Low-precision and Peak Memory Optimization in Large Output Spaces

abstract: The exponential growth in the parameter scale of Large Language Models (LLMs) has precipitated an urgent demand for efficient compression techniques to facilitate practical deployment. To address this challenge, low-rank decomposition based on Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) offers a principled, hardware-friendly pathway for compressing LLMs without retraining. However, existing training-free approaches predominantly rely on uniform rank allocation, implicitly assuming homogeneous redundancy across the model depth and thereby neglecting the inherent non-uniformity of representational evolution. To bridge this gap, we introduce CGSVD, a Cascaded Granular Singular Value Decomposition framework that leverages a dual-level non-uniform allocation strategy to maximize semantic preservation. Specifically, we quantify inter-layer significance via angular distance and assess intra-layer compressibility through spectral entropy, enabling precise identification of critical architectural components. Furthermore, we propose an Iterative Residual Filling (IRF) mechanism to bridge the parameter gap caused by integer-rank truncation and ensure strict adherence to global compression targets. Extensive experiments on representative LLM families ranging from 3B to 13B parameters verify the superiority of our approach. Notably, under a 30% compression ratio on the LLaMA3.1-8B model, CGSVD achieves a remarkable average zero-shot accuracy boost of 6.08% and reduces perplexity by 15.46 compared to the baseline. We release the code to facilitate future research.

paragraphs: Singular value decomposition can compress language-model weight matrices into smaller low-rank representations without retraining. A central choice is how much capacity to retain in each part of the model. CGSVD challenges uniform allocation because different layers and components need not contain equal amounts of redundancy or contribute equally to preserving representations.

The method distributes retained capacity at two levels. Angular distance measures significance across layers, while spectral entropy assesses compressibility within layers. These signals guide where compression should be more or less aggressive. Because matrix ranks must be integers, the initial allocation can miss the requested total parameter budget. Experiments cover language-model families with 3B to 13B parameters. At a reported 30% compression ratio for LLaMA3.1-8B, CGSVD improves average zero-shot accuracy by 6.08% and lowers perplexity by 15.46 compared with the baseline. summary.tldr: CGSVD compresses language models without retraining by allocating low-rank capacity according to layer importance and component compressibility.

title: CGSVD: Cascaded Granular Singular Value Decomposition for Large Language Model Compression

abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to specialized domains typically incurs high data and computational overhead. While prior efficiency efforts have largely treated data selection and parameter-efficient fine-tuning as isolated processes, our empirical analysis suggests they may be intrinsically coupled. We posit the Strong Map Hypothesis: a sparse subset of attention heads plays a dominant role in task-specific adaptation, acting as keys that unlock specific data patterns. Building on this observation, we propose From Parameters to Data (P2D), a unified framework that leverages these task-sensitive attention heads as a dual compass for both sample mining and structural pruning. To rigorously quantify the total pipeline cost, we introduce the Alignment Efficiency Ratio (AER) metric for both selection latency and training time. Mechanistically, P2D identifies critical heads via a lightweight proxy and uses them as a functional filter to curate high-affinity data, establishing a synergistic pipeline. Empirically, by updating merely 10% of attention heads on 10% of the data, P2D achieves an 8.3 pp performance gain over strong baselines and delivers a 7.0x end-to-end time speedup. These results validate that precise parameter-data synchronization eliminates redundancy, offering a new paradigm for efficient alignment.

paragraphs: Efficient language-model adaptation often treats choosing training examples and choosing trainable parameters as separate problems. These findings support coordinating parameter and data choices as a practical efficiency strategy, while the proposed attention-head relationship remains framed as a hypothesis.
summary.tldr: P2D uses task-sensitive attention heads to coordinate parameter pruning and data selection, improving reported adaptation efficiency and performance.

title: From Parameters to Data: A Task-Parameter-Guided Fine-Tuning Pipeline for Efficient LLM Alignment

abstract: Long-sequence modeling faces a fundamental trade-off between the efficiency of compressive fixed-size memory in RNN-like models and the fidelity of lossless growing memory in attention-based Transformers. Inspired by the Multi-Store Model in cognitive science, we introduce a memory framework of artificial neural networks. Our method maintains a sliding window of the Transformer’s KV cache as lossless short-term memory, while a learnable module termed Artificial Hippocampus Network (AHN) recurrently compresses out-of-window information into a fixed-size compact long-term memory. To validate this framework, we instantiate AHNs using modern RNN-like architectures, including Mamba2, DeltaNet, and GatedDeltaNet to augment open-weight base LLMs. We also propose an efficient self-distillation method where the base model’ all parameters are frozen and only the parameters from AHNs are optimized. For inference, our method sets a default large sliding window size of 32k for attention, and AHNs activate only when the sequence length exceeds the 32k window, addressing the quadratic-complexity issue of attention that emerges at that scale. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks LV-Eval and InfiniteBench demonstrate that AHN-augmented models consistently outperform sliding window baselines and achieve performance comparable or even superior to full-attention models, while substantially reducing computational and memory requirements. For instance, augmenting the Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with AHNs reduces inference FLOPs by 40.5% and memory cache by 74.0%, while improving its average score on LV-Eval (128k sequence length) from 4.41 to 5.88.

paragraphs: Long-context models face a memory trade-off: compressing earlier information saves resources but can lose detail, while retaining a growing attention cache becomes expensive. This paper combines these approaches through separate short-term and long-term memories. Recent information stays in a sliding window of the Transformer’s attention cache, while an Artificial Hippocampus Network recurrently compresses information that leaves the window.

At inference, the default attention window holds 32k tokens, and the additional memory module activates only when the sequence exceeds that length.

summary.tldr: Artificial Hippocampus Networks compress older context into fixed-size memory while retaining recent attention, improving long-context efficiency and benchmark performance.

title: Artificial Hippocampus Networks for Efficient Long-Context Modeling

abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for reasoning, but reliable PRMs often require step annotations or heavy verification pipelines, making them costly to scale and refresh during online RL. Implicit PRMs reduce this cost by training log-likelihood-ratio rewards from trajectory-level outcome labels. However, the log-ratio is constrained only as a sequence-level aggregate during training, while inference decomposes it into token- or step-level scores for partial prefixes. This train–inference mismatch leaves local credits weakly identified, so distribution-wide scoring can amplify misleading advantages. We propose Implicit Prefix-Value Reward Model (IPVRM), which directly learns the probability of eventual correctness for each prefix from outcome labels. Step signals are then obtained as temporal-difference (TD) differences between consecutive prefix values, aligning the training target with inference-time use. IPVRM markedly improves step-verification F1 on ProcessBench. To exploit these prefix values during policy optimization, we further introduce Distribution-Level RL (DistRL), which applies TD advantages to both sampled tokens and high-probability candidate tokens, providing dense counterfactual updates without additional rollouts. Experiments show that DistRL brings limited gains with unreliable implicit rewards, but consistently improves downstream reasoning when paired with IPVRM. The implementation of our method is available at https://github.com/gaoshiping/IPVRM .

paragraphs: Reasoning models benefit from feedback on intermediate steps, but collecting step annotations or running extensive verification is costly. Implicit process rewards use whole-trajectory outcomes instead. The paper identifies a mismatch in log-likelihood-ratio approaches: training constrains an aggregate sequence score, while inference treats its components as meaningful local scores for unfinished reasoning.

Distribution-Level RL delivers limited gains with unreliable implicit rewards and consistently improves downstream reasoning when paired with IPVRM, making reward quality central to the combined approach.
summary.tldr: IPVRM learns correctness probabilities for reasoning prefixes, enabling reliable step rewards and more effective distribution-level reinforcement learning.

title: Unleashing Implicit Rewards: Prefix-Value Learning for Distribution-Level Optimization

abstract: The evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) agents for software engineering (SWE) is constrained by the scarcity of verifiable datasets, a bottleneck stemming from the complexity of constructing executable environments across diverse languages. To address this, we introduce MEnvAgent, a Multi-language framework for automated Environment construction that facilitates scalable generation of verifiable task instances. MEnvAgent employs a multi-agent Planning-Execution-Verification architecture to autonomously resolve construction failures and integrates a novel Environment Reuse Mechanism that reduces computational overhead by incrementally patching historical environments. Evaluations on MEnvBench, a new benchmark comprising 1,000 tasks across 10 languages, demonstrate that MEnvAgent outperforms baselines, improving Fail-to-Pass (F2P) rates by 8.6% while reducing time costs by 43%. Additionally, we demonstrate the utility of MEnvAgent by constructing MEnvData-SWE, the largest open-source polyglot dataset of realistic verifiable Docker environments to date, alongside solution trajectories that enable consistent performance gains on SWE tasks across a wide range of models.

paragraphs: Software-engineering tasks become more useful for training and evaluation when proposed solutions can run in a working environment. Building those environments across programming languages is difficult, limiting the supply of verifiable tasks. MEnvAgent automates this construction process to support larger, multilingual software-engineering datasets.

The framework uses multiple agents organized around planning, execution, and verification to resolve construction failures. It also reuses historical environments by applying incremental patches, reducing the need to rebuild everything for each task. This reuse mechanism addresses computational overhead alongside the practical challenge of obtaining an executable environment.

On MEnvBench, which contains 1,000 tasks across 10 languages, MEnvAgent improves Fail-to-Pass rates by 8.6% and reduces time costs by 43% relative to baselines. The authors also use it to construct MEnvData-SWE, described as the largest open-source polyglot dataset of realistic verifiable Docker environments to date. Associated solution trajectories yield consistent software-engineering performance gains across a wide range of models, connecting environment construction to downstream learning utility.
summary.tldr: MEnvAgent automates and reuses executable environments across programming languages, enabling more efficient construction of verifiable software-engineering tasks.

title: MEnvAgent: Scalable Polyglot Environment Construction for Verifiable Software Engineering

abstract: Image-to-Video diffusion models leverage input images to generate visually stunning content, yet frequently produce motion that violates physical laws. We reveal a surprising finding: a 2-step generation often exhibits better physical consistency than a 50-step output from the same model. Through spectral analysis, we trace this to phase erosion during denoising; the phase degrades significantly (dropping by $\approx 18%$ from step 2 to step 50), whereas the magnitude remains relatively stable. Building on this insight, we propose PhaseLock, a training-free framework that preserves the valid motion priors from few-step inference throughout the denoising trajectory. Rather than relying on full-step inference for physical consistency, PhaseLock extracts a motion prior from just 2 steps and enforces it onto high-fidelity generation via Latent Delta Guidance. Our approach effectively mitigates phase degradation, improving physical consistency by an average of 6.2 points across diverse models while largely maintaining visual fidelity, with negligible overhead ($1.06\times$ time, $1.02\times$ memory) and reduced reliance on expensive external guidance methods ($\sim5\times$ time).

summary.tldr: PhaseLock preserves motion information from two-step video generation to improve physical consistency during later visual refinement.

title: Physics in 2-Steps: Locking Motion Priors Before Visual Refinement Erases Them

abstract: This paper challenges the assumption that vision-language models (VLMs) require fixed patch-based 2D vision features. Analyzing fine-tuned vision encoders, we find that representations become increasingly abstract and less spatially coherent during VLM training. Notably, models trained with image-text alignment (such as SigLIP2) develop a small number of specialized tokens that effectively summarize global image content. Building on this, we introduce RADIO1D, which compresses images into a compact, variable-length 1D token sequence using multi-teacher knowledge distillation and an autoencoder design. The resulting representations exhibit strong hierarchical summarization, enabling accurate scene understanding–even with a single token–and support improved composition-aware image retrieval. In VLMs, RADIO1D provides flexible accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs through adjustable token counts, delivering competitive performance on diverse multimodal benchmarks with lower computational overhead and better accuracy. We release our models under a permissive license.

paragraphs: Vision-language models commonly represent images as fixed grids of patch features. This paper examines whether that spatial format remains necessary after training. It combines knowledge distillation from multiple teachers with an autoencoder design. The resulting representations support hierarchical summarization, allowing the number of tokens to change according to the desired balance between accuracy and computational cost.

The authors report accurate scene understanding even with a single token, improved composition-aware image retrieval, and competitive multimodal benchmark performance with reduced overhead and better accuracy. These findings support compact, adjustable representations as a useful alternative to fixed patch features in the evaluated tasks. The contribution connects an analysis of learned visual abstraction to a representation designed to exploit it.
summary.tldr: RADIO1D compresses images into adjustable-length token sequences, supporting efficient vision-language processing and strong hierarchical scene summaries.

title: RADIO1D: Elastic Representations for Condensed Vision Modeling

abstract: Many combinatorial optimization problems admit quadratic unconstrained binary formulations (QUBO) which can often be relaxed to the box $[0,1]^n$ and optimized using scalable gradient-based methods. However, the resulting non-convex landscape can often contain local optima that are spurious or infeasible. In this paper, we establish sufficient structural conditions on quadratic penalties that rule out these failures, guaranteeing that every local minimizer of the relax problem is both binary and feasible. For each problem we study, we examine existing QUBO formulations when available, identify why they fail when they do, and propose alternative relaxed QUBOs that satisfy our conditions. We show for several common combinatorial problems, including open-pit mining, knapsack, and traveling salesman formulations, that these constructions allow gradient-based methods such as projected gradient descent and Adam to be safely applied to obtain valid binary solutions. Our results clarify when differentiable optimization is a reliable local solver for quadratic combinatorial objectives.

paragraphs: Many combinatorial problems can be expressed as quadratic objectives over binary variables, with penalties encoding constraints. Relaxing the variables to values between zero and one makes gradient-based optimization possible. However, a local minimum of the resulting continuous problem can contain fractional values or violate the original constraints, leaving the solver with an unusable answer.

The paper establishes sufficient structural conditions on quadratic penalties that prevent these failures. When those conditions hold, every local minimizer of the relaxed problem is binary and feasible. This is a guarantee about the validity of local solutions; it does not say that every such solution is globally optimal.

The authors examine existing formulations where available, explain failures, and construct alternatives meeting their conditions. Examples include open-pit mining, knapsack, and traveling salesman formulations. They show how these constructions support the use of projected gradient descent and Adam to obtain valid binary solutions. The contribution identifies when continuous optimization has a trustworthy connection to the original discrete problem, rather than relying on the hope that relaxed solutions will become valid.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient penalty conditions ensuring that every local minimum of certain relaxed binary optimization problems is binary and feasible.

title: Local Minima in Quadratic-Penalty Relaxations of Binary Linear Programs

abstract: Connectivity structure shapes neural computation, but inferring this structure from population recordings is degenerate: multiple connectivity structures can generate identical dynamics. Recent work uses low-rank recurrent neural networks (lrRNNs) to infer low-dimensional latent dynamics and connectivity from observed activity, enabling a mechanistic interpretation of the dynamics. However, standard approaches for training lrRNNs can recover spurious structures irrelevant to the underlying dynamics. We first characterize the identifiability of connectivity structures in lrRNNs and determine conditions under which a unique solution exists. To find such solutions, we develop an inference framework based on maximum entropy and continuous normalizing flows (CNFs), trained via flow matching. Instead of estimating a single connectivity matrix, our method learns a distribution over connection weights that is maximally unbiased over unidentifiable components while matching the observed dynamics. This approach captures complex yet necessary distributions such as heavy-tailed connectivity found in empirical data. We validate our method on synthetic datasets with connectivity structures that generate multistable attractors, limit cycles, and ring attractors, and demonstrate its applicability in recordings from rat frontal cortex during decision-making. Our framework shifts circuit inference from recovering connectivity to identifying which connectivity structures are computationally required, and which are artifacts of underconstrained inference.

paragraphs: Observed neural activity does not necessarily determine a unique pattern of connections: different networks can generate identical dynamics. Consequently, fitting a low-rank recurrent neural network can produce apparent structure that the recordings do not actually require. This paper first analyzes which connectivity structures are identifiable and establishes conditions under which a unique solution exists.

The proposed inference framework learns a distribution of connection weights rather than selecting a single connectivity matrix. It combines a maximum-entropy principle with continuous normalizing flows trained through flow matching. The goal is to reproduce the observed dynamics while remaining maximally unbiased about components that cannot be identified. The distribution can also express complex features, including heavy tails, when those features are needed.

Validation covers synthetic systems with multiple stable attractors, limit cycles, and ring attractors, alongside recordings from rat frontal cortex during decision-making. The framework changes the interpretive question: which properties of connectivity are required to explain the computation, and which arise from choosing one solution to an underconstrained problem? That distinction makes uncertainty about circuit structure part of the inference itself.
summary.tldr: This framework infers distributions of neural connectivity to distinguish structure required by observed dynamics from underdetermined features.

title: Identifying Connectivity Distributions from Neural Dynamics Using Flows

abstract: Geometrical interpretations of deep learning models offer insightful perspectives into their underlying mathematical structures. In this work, we introduce a novel approach that leverages differential geometry, particularly concepts from Riemannian geometry, to integrate multiple models into a unified transfer learning framework. By aligning the Ricci curvature of latent space of individual models, we construct an interrelated architecture, namely Geometric Embedding Alignment via cuRvature matching in transfer learning (GEAR), which ensures comprehensive geometric representation across datapoints. This framework enables the effective aggregation of knowledge from diverse sources, thereby improving performance on target tasks. We evaluate our model on 23 molecular task pairs and demonstrate significant performance gains over existing benchmark models—achieving improvements of at least 14.4% under random splits and 8.3% under scaffold splits.
originalAbstract: Geometrical interpretations of deep learning models offer insightful perspectives into their underlying mathematical structures. In this work, we introduce a novel approach that leverages differential geometry, particularly concepts from Riemannian geometry, to integrate multiple models into a unified transfer learning framework. By aligning the Ricci curvature of latent space of individual models, we construct an interrelated architecture, namely Geometric Embedding Alignment via cuRvature matching in transfer learning (GEAR), which ensures comprehensive geometric representation across datapoints. This framework enables the effective aggregation of knowledge from diverse sources, thereby improving performance on target tasks. We evaluate our model on 23 molecular task pairs and demonstrate significant performance gains over existing benchmark models—achieving improvements of at least 14.4% under random splits and 8.3% under scaffold splits.

paragraphs: GEAR is a transfer learning framework that brings knowledge from multiple models into a shared architecture. Its central idea is to connect models through the geometry of their latent spaces—the internal representations they learn from data. This gives the framework a way to relate information learned from diverse sources when addressing a target task.

The approach draws on differential geometry, particularly Riemannian geometry, and aligns a geometric quantity called Ricci curvature across the individual models’ latent spaces. Curvature matching is the mechanism used to build connections among the models. The authors describe the resulting architecture as providing a comprehensive geometric representation across data points, supporting the aggregation of knowledge.

The evaluation covers 23 molecular task pairs. The authors report significant performance gains over existing benchmark models, with improvements of at least 14.4% under random splits and 8.3% under scaffold splits. These are results for the two stated evaluation settings; the abstract does not present them as guarantees for arbitrary transfer learning tasks.

The findings support geometry alignment as a useful approach to combining models in the evaluated molecular tasks. The broader contribution is a framework that makes the geometric structure of learned representations central to knowledge transfer, with the reported gains showing its practical value in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: GEAR combines knowledge from multiple models by matching latent-space Ricci curvature, reporting performance gains across 23 molecular task pairs.

title: Geometric Embedding Alignment via Curvature Matching in Transfer Learning

abstract: Code transformation is a foundational capability in the software development process, where its effectiveness relies on constructing a high-quality code representation to characterize the input code semantics and guide the transformation. Existing approaches treat code transformation as an end-to-end learning task, leaving the construction of the representation needed for semantic reasoning implicit in model weights or relying on rigid compiler-level abstractions. We present SemRep, a framework that improves code transformation through generative code representation learning. Our key insight is to employ the semantics-preserving transformations as the intermediate representation, which serves as both a generative mid-training task and the guidance for subsequent instruction-specific code transformations. Across general code editing and optimization tasks (e.g., GPU kernel optimization), SemRep outperforms the extensively finetuned baselines with strictly the same training budget by 6.9% in correctness, 1.1$\times$ in performance, 13.9% in generalization, and 6.7% in robustness. With the improved exploration of diverse code transformations, SemRep is particularly amenable to evolutionary search. Combined with an evolutionary coding agent, SemRep finds optimizations that 685B larger-weight baselines fail to discover while achieving the same performance with 25% less inference compute.

title: SemRep : Generative Code Representation Learning with Code Transformations

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to optimize policies from pre-collected datasets. A bottleneck of this paradigm is managing epistemic uncertainty, which arises from limited data coverage (sample-level) and the ambiguity in identifying transition dynamics from finite data (model-level). To provide a unified quantification of these uncertainties, Bayesian RL has been proposed by treating the dynamics model as a random variable and maintaining a corresponding belief. Despite its theoretical appeal, policy optimization in Bayesian RL remains computationally challenging as it requires solving composite objectives with expectations. Prior methods either employ search-based techniques with poor computational scalability or impose restrictive posterior assumptions that sacrifice the adaptability of Bayesian RL. To address these limitations, we propose Posterior Hybrid Bayesian Belief (PhyB), which reformulates the expectation as a convex combination over a subset of dynamics models. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the objective discrepancy induced by this approximation remains bounded. Based on PhyB, we develop an iterative regularized policy optimization algorithm that provides metric-agnostic guarantees for monotonic improvement until convergence. Empirical results demonstrate that PhyB achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve a policy using previously collected data. Uncertainty arises both because some situations are poorly covered and because finite observations can support multiple explanations of environment dynamics. Bayesian reinforcement learning represents this uncertainty through a belief over dynamics models, but optimizing policies across that belief can be computationally difficult.

Posterior Hybrid Bayesian Belief, or PhyB, approximates the relevant expectation with a convex combination over a subset of dynamics models. The paper proves that the resulting discrepancy in the objective is bounded. This provides a controlled approximation to the Bayesian calculation rather than requiring the optimization to handle the full expectation directly.

Using this representation, the authors develop an iterative regularized policy-optimization algorithm with metric-agnostic guarantees of monotonic improvement until convergence. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks. The theoretical and empirical contributions address different parts of the problem: bounding approximation error, establishing improvement of the optimization procedure, and testing whether the resulting approach performs well in practice.
summary.tldr: PhyB approximates Bayesian uncertainty over environment dynamics to enable regularized offline policy optimization with bounded approximation error and improvement guarantees.

title: Regularized Offline Policy Optimization with Posterior Hybrid Bayesian Belief

abstract: Large language models can represent a variety of personas but typically default to a helpful Assistant identity cultivated during post-training. Across several different models, we find an “Assistant Axis" in their activation space, which captures the extent to which a model is operating in its default Assistant mode. Steering towards the Assistant direction reinforces helpful and harmless behavior; steering away increases the model’s tendency to identify as other entities. Measuring deviations along the Assistant Axis predicts “persona drift,” a phenomenon where models slip into exhibiting harmful or bizarre behaviors that are uncharacteristic of their typical persona. We find that persona drift is often driven by conversations demanding meta-reflection on the model’s processes or featuring emotionally vulnerable users. We show that restricting activations to a fixed region along the Assistant Axis can stabilize model behavior in these scenarios—and also in the face of adversarial persona-based jailbreaks. Our results suggest that post-training steers models toward a particular region of persona space but only loosely tethers them to it, motivating work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.

paragraphs: This paper studies how language models maintain their usual helpful Assistant persona despite being able to represent many identities. Across several models, the authors identify an activation-space direction that tracks how strongly the model is operating in its default Assistant mode. They call this direction the Assistant Axis.

summary.tldr: An internal Assistant Axis predicts persona drift across several models, and constraining activations along it stabilizes behavior in tested scenarios.

title: The Assistant Axis: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models

abstract: Modeling unknown latent functions from finite, irregularly sampled measurements is a recurring challenge across science and engineering. Neural processes (NPs), a family of probabilistic functional models, are promising solutions—especially when endowed with domain-specific symmetries like translation equivariance, which improve sample efficiency and generalization. Yet existing translation-equivariant NPs face two limitations: (i) they stack generic components with non-linearities, obscuring the induced function class and limiting interpretability; and (ii) convolutional designs are limited by local receptive fields and the need to embed inputs onto a dense uniform grid, while attention-based alternatives lift these restrictions at quadratic cost in the number of observations. We address both with two contributions. First, using the Volterra expansion, we approximate continuous translation-equivariant operators by sums of higher-order convolutions, yielding analytical transparency while admitting efficient evaluation via first-order convolutions. Second, we introduce set Fourier convolutions (SFConvs), a frequency-domain parameterization that operates directly on irregularly sampled points, achieves approximately global receptive fields, and scales linearly in the number of observations. Building on these ideas, we propose two conditional NPs (CNPs): SFConvCNPs, which stack SFConv blocks with non-linearities, and SFVConvCNPs, which integrate the Volterra formulation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate our methods’ efficacy against state-of-the-art baselines.

Existing implementations face a trade-off: conventional convolutions need grids and have local reach, while attention can connect distant observations at quadratic cost.

The contribution combines a clearer account of the operators being learned with a computational design that handles irregular samples without first placing them on a dense uniform grid.
summary.tldr: Fourier convolutions and Volterra expansions give neural processes efficient global access to irregular observations and more explicit operator structure.

title: Revisiting Neural Processes via Fourier Transform and Volterra Series

abstract: Multi-agent LLM debates achieve strong performance on decision-making tasks as well as problem-solving benchmarks, yet their safety and fairness risks remain poorly understood. Notably, interaction can amplify the biases of single LLMs, raising concerns for real-world deployment. We identify the emergence of collective (often biased) norms in multi-agent LLM debates and show that noise (e.g., LLM sampling temperature) is a key driver. To explain this, we propose an analytical framework drawing on physics-inspired theoretical models of social dynamics. We predict a phase transition to collective bias when conformity surpasses a critical threshold given the LLMs’ initial bias and debate noise. We test the theoretical predictions through controlled experiments and observe a finite-size crossover consistent with an underlying phase transition. We further find that agent heterogeneity suppresses emergence by smoothing (rounding) this transition. Finally, we show that these insights generalize to realistic decision-making tasks, including investment decisions and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.

paragraphs: Debating language-model agents can perform well on reasoning and decision tasks, yet agreement among them can amplify individual biases. This paper examines how collective norms emerge through interaction. It identifies debate noise, including randomness controlled by sampling temperature, as an important part of that process.

The authors build an analytical framework using physics-inspired models of social dynamics. summary.tldr: A social-dynamics framework explains how conformity and debate noise can produce biased LLM consensus, with agent heterogeneity suppressing its emergence.

title: Emergence of Biased Consensus in Multi-Agent LLM Debates

abstract: Multi-hop reasoning for question answering (QA) plays a critical role in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for large language models (LLMs). Based on inherent relation-dependency and reasoning patterns, it is categorized into parallel fact-verification (simultaneously verifying independent sub-questions) and chained reasoning (sequential multi-step inference). Existing approaches adopt either LLM-based fact verification or KG path-based chain construction, failing to handle both categories well: the former underperforms on chained reasoning, while the latter suffers from redundant paths in parallel tasks. Inspired by the Dual Process Theory in cognitive science and Stanovich’s Cognitive Misers Theory, we propose an effective multi-hop QA framework DTKG (Dual-Track Knowledge Graph) through building a two-stage pipeline: i) Classification Stage (dynamic question categorization via few-shot prompting, emulating "unconscious processing"); and ii) Branch Processing Stage (tailored reasoning paths, emulating "conscious processing"). Multi-facet experiments on six datasets show DTKG achieves 5.0%-29.5% performance improvement. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DTKG-621F

paragraphs: Multi-hop questions do not all require the same reasoning structure. Some involve checking several independent facts, while others require a sequence in which one inference supplies information for the next. DTKG starts from this distinction and argues that a single processing strategy can be inefficient or ineffective across both kinds of question.

The framework first classifies the question using a language model prompted with a few examples. It then sends the question to a tailored reasoning branch. This design responds to complementary weaknesses identified in existing methods: language-model fact verification struggles with chained inference, while constructing knowledge-graph paths can create redundant work for independent fact checks. Cognitive theories motivate the separation between initial categorization and subsequent deliberate processing.

Experiments spanning six datasets report performance improvements ranging from 5.0% to 29.5%. The findings support selecting a reasoning structure according to the dependencies within a question. DTKG's contribution is the coordinated classification-and-branching pipeline, which lets different question types receive different forms of knowledge-graph-verified reasoning.
summary.tldr: DTKG classifies multi-hop questions and routes them to reasoning branches suited to independent fact checks or sequential inference.

title: DTKG: Dual-Track Knowledge Graph-Verified Reasoning Framework for Multi-Hop QA

abstract: Modern foundation models are evaluated through broad capabilities such as arithmetic, reasoning, safety, and robustness, yet it remains unclear in a principled sense when finite tests can meaningfully certify such claims. We develop a rigorous theory of capability evaluation by formalizing evaluation as inference over a task family and asking when guarantees over the full family can be inferred from a strict subset of tests. We analyze two canonical regimes. In stochastic multi-environment evaluation, we characterize when uniform certification is possible across multiple environments and show that the sample complexity is governed by a $\chi^2$-radius of the environment family, yielding near-optimal evaluation protocols with matching lower bounds under a natural overlap condition. In contrast, for worst-case, rule-like capabilities, we establish fundamental impossibility results. Even for structured model classes such as Boolean circuits of bounded size, black-box evaluation cannot, in general, certify global properties. Together, these results provide a principled framework for understanding when finite evaluation can and cannot certify capabilities.

summary.tldr: Finite tests can certify some statistical capabilities under suitable conditions, but generally cannot certify worst-case global rules through black-box evaluation.

title: Certifying Capabilities from Finite Tests: When Is It Possible?

abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is one of the most widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for adapting pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks. Although LoRA significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters and lowers fine-tuning costs, its performance is often limited by the inherent low-rank assumption. In this paper, we revisit the notion of rank for LoRA update matrices and show that the standard matrix rank fails to capture duplicated directions and redundancy in the update subspace. Motivated by this analysis, we argue that the Kruskal rank offers a more informative criterion for characterizing update diversity. We therefore propose Low Kruskal Rank Adaptation (LoKRA), a new PEFT algorithm with provable theoretical guarantees that mitigates the limitations of LoRA. We further introduce LoKRA$^+$, an enhanced variant that provides a tighter theoretical lower bound on the Kruskal rank and yields stronger empirical performance. Experiments on multiple LLMs show that our approach consistently outperforms LoRA and other baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance across a range of benchmarks. The code can be viewed at https://github.com/AMD-AGI/LoKRA.

The authors argue that it misses duplicated directions and redundancy within the update subspace, leaving an important aspect of adaptation uncharacterized.

summary.tldr: LoKRA uses Kruskal rank to address redundancy in parameter-efficient updates and reports improvements over LoRA across multiple language models.

title: Low Kruskal-Rank Adaptation

abstract: We systematically evaluate Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods under the paradigm of Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). RLVR incentivizes language models to enhance their reasoning capabilities through verifiable feedback; however, while methods like LoRA are commonly used, the optimal PEFT architecture for RLVR remains unidentified. In this work, we conduct the first comprehensive evaluation of over 12 PEFT methodologies across the DeepSeek-R1-Distill families on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Our empirical results challenge the default adoption of standard LoRA with three main findings. First, we demonstrate that structural variants, such as DoRA, AdaLoRA, and MiSS, consistently outperform LoRA. Second, we uncover a spectral collapse phenomenon in SVD-informed initialization strategies (e.g., PiSSA, MiLoRA), attributing their failure to a fundamental misalignment between principal-component updates and RL optimization. Furthermore, our ablations reveal that extreme parameter reduction (e.g., VeRA, Rank-1) severely bottlenecks reasoning capacity. We further conduct ablation studies and scaling experiments to validate our findings. This work provides a definitive guide for advocating for more exploration for parameter-efficient RL methods.

title: Evaluating Parameter Efficient Methods for RLVR

abstract: Irregular time series arise ubiquitously in real-world systems, where observations are sparse, asynchronous, and governed by underlying continuous-time dynamics. Existing continuous–discrete state-space models typically rely on path-based variational inference, which is computationally expensive or constrained by restrictive posterior assumptions. We propose SDEVI, a novel framework that performs variational inference directly on the joint distribution over discrete-time observations, while guaranteeing consistency with an underlying continuous process governed by a Stochastic Differential Equation(SDE). SDEVI employs a variational posterior induced by linear time-varying SDEs as a scalable inference backbone. To enable intricate dynamics modeling for real-world data, we introduce non-linear-SDE-induced variational inference and generalize our framework to the complex domain. Extensive experiments across healthcare, physics, climate, and IoT benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on interpolation, extrapolation, regression, and classification tasks.

Extensive experiments across healthcare, physics, climate, and IoT benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on interpolation, extrapolation, regression, and classification tasks.

paragraphs: Many time series contain observations taken at uneven intervals, even though the underlying system evolves continuously. Modeling these data requires connecting sparse, asynchronous measurements to continuous dynamics. Existing continuous–discrete state-space methods often perform inference over entire paths, which can be computationally expensive or depend on restrictive assumptions about the inferred distribution.

SDEVI instead performs variational inference directly over the joint distribution at discrete observation times. Its construction guarantees consistency with an underlying continuous process governed by a stochastic differential equation. This keeps the continuous-time foundation while moving inference toward the observations that are actually available. Linear time-varying stochastic differential equations induce the variational posterior used as its scalable backbone.

To represent more intricate dynamics, the authors introduce inference induced by nonlinear stochastic differential equations and extend the framework to the complex domain. Experiments cover healthcare, physics, climate, and Internet of Things benchmarks. The reported state-of-the-art results span interpolation, extrapolation, regression, and classification, indicating that the framework supports several uses of irregularly sampled data rather than a single prediction setting.
summary.tldr: SDEVI models irregular observations directly while preserving consistency with continuous stochastic dynamics.

title: Generative Modeling of Irregular Time Series via SDE-Induced Continuous-Discrete Variational Inference

abstract: Time series imputation benefits from leveraging cross-feature correlations, yet existing attention-based methods re-discover feature relationships at each layer, lacking persistent anchors to maintain consistent representations. To address this, we propose HELIX, which assigns each feature a learnable feature identity, a persistent embedding that captures intrinsic semantic properties throughout the network. Unlike graph-based methods that rely on predefined topology and assume homogeneous spatial relationships, HELIX learns arbitrary feature dependencies end-to-end from temporal co-variation, naturally handling datasets where features mix spatial locations with semantic variables. Integrated with hybrid temporal-feature attention, HELIX achieves the state-of-the-art performance, surpassing all 16 baselines on 5 public datasets across 21 experimental settings in our evaluation. Furthermore, our mechanistic analysis reveals that HELIX aligns learned feature identities and dependencies with latent physical and semantic structure progressively across layers, demonstrating that it more effectively translates cross-feature structure into imputation accuracy.

paragraphs: HELIX fills missing values in time series by improving how a network represents relationships among features. The paper argues that existing attention methods repeatedly rediscover these relationships at each layer, without persistent anchors. HELIX gives each feature a learned identity embedding that carries its intrinsic semantic properties throughout the network.

Those identities are combined with attention across time and features. Dependencies are learned end-to-end from how variables change together over time, rather than imposed through a predefined graph. This supports data whose features combine spatial locations with semantic variables, where assuming a uniform kind of spatial relationship may be inappropriate. Persistent identities give the changing attention computations a consistent reference for each feature.

In the reported evaluation, HELIX surpasses all 16 baselines on five public datasets across 21 settings. Mechanistic analysis also finds that learned identities and dependencies progressively align with underlying physical and semantic structure across layers. Together, these findings connect the persistent feature representation with a more effective use of cross-feature information for recovering missing observations.
summary.tldr: HELIX gives time-series features persistent learned identities, improving dependency modeling and missing-value recovery across the reported evaluation.

title: HELIX: Hybrid Encoding with Learnable Identity and Cross-dimensional Synthesis for Time Series Imputation

abstract: Parametric Computer-Aided-Design (CAD) modeling from human intent remains challenging, particularly during the conceptual design stage, where design goals are expressed through incomplete and unstructured modalities (e.g., hand-drawn sketches and textual descriptions). In this work, we rethink the human intent-to-CAD pipeline and propose a unified method that directly maps multi-level human intents to executable codes, without assuming the prior existence of target CAD models. To support our study, we construct HiCAD, the first large-scale dataset aligning hand-drawn sketches, textual descriptions, and parametric CAD codes. Based on this, we introduce HiCAD, a two-stage framework comprising Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment to bridge the representational gap between heterogeneous inputs, and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning to enforce geometric and topological consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines across multiple tasks, validating its effectiveness and robustness in transforming heterogeneous human intents into high-fidelity parametric CAD models. Our project page: https://zqwlearning.github.io/HiCAD.

paragraphs: Early design ideas are often incomplete sketches and loosely phrased descriptions, while parametric CAD requires executable, geometrically coherent instructions. This paper develops a direct mapping between those heterogeneous expressions of intent and CAD code. It does not require a finished target CAD model to exist beforehand.

The authors construct HiCAD, aligning hand-drawn sketches, text descriptions, and parametric CAD programs. Their two-stage framework first uses cooperative multi-task alignment to connect the input representations. Spatial-aware reinforcement learning then encourages geometric and topological consistency in the generated code.

Experiments across multiple tasks outperform existing baselines and demonstrate robust conversion of varied intent inputs into parametric models. The contribution combines a dataset with an alignment and optimization pipeline. The abstract does not establish that every generated design meets manufacturing constraints or fully resolves ambiguity in a user’s incomplete concept; those are distinct from producing a high-fidelity executable CAD representation.
summary.tldr: HiCAD aligns sketches and text with executable CAD programs, using multi-task training and spatial rewards to improve generation.

title: Rethinking Human Intent-to-CAD: Parametric CAD Model Generation via Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in complex medical reasoning yet face diminishing gains under inference scaling laws. While existing studies augment LLMs with various knowledge types, it remains unclear how effectively the additional costs translate into accuracy. In this paper, we explore how meta-cognition of LLMs, i.e., their self-assessment of their own cognitive states, can regulate the reasoning process. Specifically, we propose MedCoG, a Medical Meta-Cognition Agent with Knowledge Graph, where the meta-cognitive assessments of task complexity, familiarity, and knowledge density dynamically regulate utilization of procedural, episodic, and factual knowledge. The LLM-centric on-demand reasoning aims to mitigate the diminishing returns under scaling law by (1) reducing costs via avoiding indiscriminate scaling, (2) improving accuracy via filtering out distractive knowledge. To validate this, we empirically characterize the scaling curve and introduce inference density to quantify inference efficiency. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of MedCoG on five hard sets of medical benchmarks, yielding 6.2x inference density. Furthermore, the Oracle study highlights the significant potential of meta-cognitive regulation.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more reasoning resources or additional knowledge does not necessarily produce proportional accuracy gains. This paper studies that tradeoff in medical reasoning, where the usefulness of extra inference cost remains unclear. MedCoG uses the model's assessments of its own cognitive state to regulate when and how it draws on knowledge.

The framework combines a medical meta-cognition agent with a knowledge graph. Assessments of task complexity, familiarity, and knowledge density guide the use of procedural, episodic, and factual knowledge. This on-demand regulation aims to reduce costs from indiscriminate scaling and improve accuracy by filtering distracting information. The central mechanism is selective allocation of reasoning support according to the task.

The authors empirically characterize the scaling curve and introduce inference density as an efficiency measure. On five hard medical benchmark sets, they report effective, efficient performance and 6.2-fold inference density. An Oracle study indicates further potential for meta-cognitive regulation. The findings support examining how effectively added resources contribute to reasoning, alongside the accuracy reached with those resources.
summary.tldr: MedCoG uses model self-assessments to regulate medical knowledge use, reporting improved reasoning efficiency and 6.2-fold inference density.

title: MedCoG: Maximizing LLM Inference Density in Medical Reasoning via Meta-Cognitive Regulation

abstract: Non-stationary time series forecasting is challenged by evolving distribution shifts that static models struggle to capture. While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising paradigm for decoupling complex drift patterns, existing approaches are limited by fixed expert pools and memoryless routing, hampering their ability to adapt to abrupt regime shifts. To address this, we propose Dynamic TMoE, a framework that unifies architectural evolution with temporal continuity during learning phase. By detecting distribution shifts via Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), we dynamically instantiate heterogeneous experts and prune redundant ones to optimize capacity. Additionally, a temporal memory router leverages recurrent states and an anomaly repository to ensure stable, context-aware expert selection without requiring test-time updates. Experiments on nine benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, reducing MSE by 10.4% and MAE by 7.8%. Code is available at https://github.com/andone-07/Dynamic-TMoE.
