paragraphs: Time-series forecasting becomes harder when the process generating the observations changes over time. Mixture-of-experts models can divide prediction work among specialized components, but fixed expert collections and routing without memory limit their ability to handle abrupt changes. Dynamic TMoE addresses both the composition of the expert pool and how experts are selected.

During learning, the framework detects distribution shifts using Maximum Mean Discrepancy. It adds heterogeneous experts when needed and removes redundant ones, allowing model capacity to evolve. Its router combines recurrent state with a repository of anomalies, so expert selection can incorporate temporal context instead of treating each routing decision in isolation.

The framework is designed to use this learned structure and contextual routing without test-time updates. Across nine benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art forecasting results, with reductions of 10.4% in mean squared error and 7.8% in mean absolute error. These findings support combining adaptation of the architecture during learning with memory in routing, rather than relying solely on a fixed collection of specialists.
summary.tldr: Dynamic TMoE evolves its expert pool during learning and uses temporal routing memory to improve forecasting under distribution shifts.

title: Dynamic TMoE: A Drift-Aware Dynamic Mixture of Experts Framework for Non-Stationary Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Real-world data is rarely clean; it is plagued by severe class imbalance (long-tailed distributions) and label corruption. Current solutions lean heavily on "black-box" meta-learning to re-weight samples. However, this paradigm introduces a fatal circular dependency: it relies on pristine, balanced validation sets to guide the optimization, which are essentially non-existent in the wild. We propose ProMeCD, a self-referential framework that breaks this dependency by recasting optimization as an autonomous control problem. Instead of training an opaque neural meta-learner, we employ a transparent proportional-integral controller. The system monitors “cognitive entropy” that is a metric derived from von Mises-Fisher gradient statistics to assess learning uncertainty. To resolve the scalar ambiguity between tail and noisy samples, ProMeCD employs a decoupled control strategy: it boosts tail classes via integral accumulation of magnitude deficits when directional consistency is high, while suppressing noise via proportional feedback when consistency collapses. Theoretically, we prove that this mechanism guarantees convergence and formally prevents the minority initial drop, ensuring monotonic improvement for rare classes. Crucially, ProMeCD is fully white-box and validation-free. Experiments on CIFAR-LT, iNaturalist, CIFAR-N, mini WebVision, and Clothing1M confirm that ProMeCD is not merely efficient; it outperforms the recent meta-learner FMW-Net by over 10% in severe imbalance settings, proving that explicit control theory offers a superior path to handling imperfect data.

paragraphs: ProMeCD tackles two problems that can coexist in training data: rare classes and incorrect labels. Both can make examples difficult to learn, yet they call for different responses. The paper replaces sample reweighting guided by a clean, balanced validation set with a transparent control mechanism that uses signals from learning itself.

A proportional-integral controller monitors learning uncertainty through cognitive entropy derived from von Mises-Fisher gradient statistics. It distinguishes cases using gradient magnitude and directional consistency. When directions remain consistent, accumulated magnitude deficits boost rare classes. When consistency collapses, proportional feedback suppresses noisy examples. The separation is intended to avoid treating every difficult example as either valuable minority data or label noise.

The authors prove convergence and prevention of the initial minority-performance drop, with monotonic rare-class improvement in their theoretical treatment. Experiments cover imbalanced and noisy-label benchmarks, including iNaturalist and Clothing1M. They report gains exceeding 10% over FMW-Net under severe imbalance, supporting explicit, validation-free control as an effective way to handle these two data problems together.
summary.tldr: ProMeCD uses transparent feedback control to support rare classes and suppress label noise without a clean validation set.

title: ProMeCD: Unifying Long-Tailed and Noisy Label Learning via White-Box Control

abstract: Is monolithic scaling the only path to AGI? This paper challenges the dogma that purely scaling a single model is sufficient to achieve Artificial General Intelligence. Instead, we identify Agentic AI as a necessary paradigm for mastering the complex, heterogeneous distribution of real-world tasks. Through rigorous theoretical derivations, we contrast the optimization constraints of monolithic learners against the efficiency of Agentic systems, progressing from simple routing mechanisms to general Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) topologies. We demonstrate that Agentic AI achieves exponentially superior generalization and sample efficiency. Finally, we discuss the connection to Mixture-of-Experts, reinterpret the instability of current multi-agent frameworks, and call for greater research focus on Agentic AI.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the idea that increasing the scale of a single model is sufficient to reach artificial general intelligence. The authors argue that the varied and complex distribution of real-world tasks calls for agentic systems, and they take the strong position that this organization is a necessary paradigm for mastering that distribution.

The technical argument compares the optimization constraints of a single learner with those of agentic arrangements. It develops from simple routing, which directs work through different components, to general directed acyclic graph structures. Through theoretical derivations, the authors report exponentially better generalization and sample efficiency for agentic AI in their analysis. These are theoretical advantages presented in support of the proposed research direction.

The paper also connects agentic organization to Mixture-of-Experts and offers a reinterpretation of instability in current multi-agent frameworks. Its broader implication is that the organization of learning and computation deserves greater research attention alongside model scale. The work presents agentic AI as a foreseeable route toward AGI, rather than reporting an achieved AGI system.
summary.tldr: The authors argue for agentic AI as a necessary pathway toward AGI, supported by theoretical efficiency and generalization advantages.

abstract: Multi-view algorithms, such as co-training and co-EM, utilize unlabeled datawhen the available attributes can be split into independent and compatiblesubsets. Co-EM outperforms co-training for many problems, but it requires theunderlying learner to estimate class probabilities, and to learn fromprobabilistically labeled data. Therefore, co-EM has so far only been studiedwith naive Bayesian learners. We cast linear classifiers into a probabilisticframework and develop a co-EM version of the Support Vector Machine. Weconduct experiments on text classification problems and compare the family ofsemi-supervised support vector algorithms under different conditions,including violations of the assumptions underlying multi-view learning. Forsome problems, such as course web page classification, we observe the mostaccurate results reported so far.

paragraphs: Multi-view learning uses unlabeled examples when attributes can be divided into independent, compatible subsets. Co-EM is one such approach and has outperformed co-training on many problems. Its requirements, however, constrain the underlying learner: it must estimate class probabilities and learn from examples whose labels are probabilistic rather than fixed.

This paper develops a way to use support vector machines within co-EM. The authors place linear classifiers in a probabilistic framework, allowing an SVM-based learner to meet those requirements. This extends co-EM beyond the naive Bayesian learners with which it had previously been studied and connects it to semi-supervised support vector learning.

Experiments compare semi-supervised support vector algorithms on text classification tasks under different conditions. These include conditions that violate the assumptions behind multi-view learning, making those assumptions part of the investigation. For some tasks, including course web page classification, the authors report the most accurate results available at the time, rather than claiming an advantage across every problem.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic formulation enables SVMs to participate in co-EM, with strong reported results on some text classification tasks.

title: Co-EM support vector learning

abstract: A plausible representation of relational information among entities in dynamic systems such as a living cell or a social community is a stochastic network which is topologically rewiring and semantically evolving over time. While there is a rich literature on modeling static or temporally invariant networks, much less has been done toward modeling the dynamic processes underlying rewiring networks, and on recovering such networks when they are not observable. We present a class of hidden temporal exponential random graph models (htERGMs) to study the yet unexplored topic of modeling and recovering temporally rewiring networks from time series of node attributes such as activities of social actors or expression levels of genes. We show that one can reliably infer the latent timespecific topologies of the evolving networks from the observation. We report empirical results on both synthetic data and a Drosophila lifecycle gene expression data set, in comparison with a static counterpart of htERGM.

paragraphs: Relationships in a cell or social community can change over time, so a single fixed network may miss part of the system’s behavior. This paper studies networks whose connections evolve and may not be directly observable. The available evidence instead consists of measurements associated with individual nodes over time.

The authors introduce hidden temporal exponential random graph models to represent and recover these changing networks. Inputs can include time series of social actors’ activities or gene expression levels. The modeling task is to infer the hidden topology at particular times from those observed attributes, connecting changes in node measurements with changes in the underlying relational structure.

The paper reports that latent time-specific network structures can be inferred reliably and presents experiments on synthetic data and a Drosophila lifecycle gene-expression dataset. The evaluations include a static counterpart of the proposed model. This comparison addresses the value of explicitly modeling temporal rewiring. The stated contribution is a model-based route from observable node histories to otherwise hidden, evolving network connections.
summary.tldr: Hidden temporal graph models recover evolving network structures from time series of node attributes, with evidence from synthetic and gene-expression data.

title: Recovering temporally rewiring networks: a model-based approach
